  • Inter-band — carriers in different bands (e.g., 800 MHz + 1800 MHz).

Maximum: 5 carriers of 20 MHz = 100 MHz total → up to 3 Gbps peak (4×4 MIMO, 100 MHz, 64-QAM).

Deployment impact: allows operators with fragmented spectrum (common in most markets) to offer wider "virtual" channels.

docs.title: 5.6.2 Enhanced MIMO
docs.text:
• Downlink: 8×8 MIMO (8 layers) → 8× peak rate.
  • Uplink: 4×4 MIMO.

Peak rate with 8×8 MIMO + 20 MHz (no CA): 8 × 150 Mbps ≈ 1.2 Gbps.

With CA + 8×8 MIMO: 5 carriers × 8 streams × 150 Mbps = 6 Gbps.

docs.title: 5.6.3 Coordinated Multipoint (CoMP)
docs.text:
Multiple eNodeBs coordinate to serve a UE at the cell edge:

  • Joint transmission (JT) — multiple eNodeBs transmit the same data to the UE, which combines them. Requires tight timing sync and CSI sharing.
  • Dynamic point selection (DPS) — the UE is served by the best eNodeB at any given moment (fast switching).
  • Coordinated scheduling/beamforming (CS/CB) — eNodeBs coordinate their beams to reduce interference.

Benefit: cell-edge throughput improves by ~30–50% — significant because cell edge is where users experience the worst performance.

Challenge: requires X2 interface backhaul with sub-1 ms latency and high bandwidth — expensive to deploy. CoMP is deployed in limited form in real networks.

docs.title: 5.6.4 Relay nodes
docs.text:
Small low-power base stations that forward data from a macro eNodeB to UEs:

  • Decode-and-forward relay — receives, decodes, re-encodes, transmits.
  • Amplify-and-forward relay — simple analog amplification (lower latency, more noise).

Benefit: extend coverage to areas with weak macro coverage (rural, indoor) without full backhaul (relay uses the same spectrum for the backhaul, not fiber).

docs.title: 5.6.5 Peak rates table
docs.text:
Release Downlink peak Uplink peak Key features 8 (LTE) 150 Mbps 75 Mbps 20 MHz, 2×2 MIMO, 64-QAM 10 (LTE-A) 1 Gbps 500 Mbps 100 MHz (5×CA), 8×8 MIMO 12 (LTE-A Pro) 3 Gbps 1.5 Gbps Enhanced CA, 256-QAM DL 13 3.9 Gbps 1.5 Gbps 32-carrier CA (unlicensed) 14 4.5 Gbps 2.2 Gbps eLAA, feLAA

The path from Release 8 to Release 14 shows how 4G kept evolving — 30× the peak rate over 8 years.

docs.title: Worked example 5.5 — LTE-A carrier aggregation peak rate
docs.text:
Scenario: 5 carriers of 20 MHz each, intra-band contiguous. 4×4 MIMO on each carrier. 64-QAM, rate-3/4 coding.

Per carrier, per stream: ~100 Mbps (from Worked example 5.1, without MIMO's doubling).

4 streams per carrier: 400 Mbps per carrier.

5 carriers: 5 × 400 = 2 Gbps peak.

With 64-QAM (6 bits/symbol) and 8×8 MIMO (8 streams): 5 × 8 × 100 = 4 Gbps — matching the Release 10 specification of ~3 Gbps (the difference is due to control overhead and reference signals).

In practice: commercial LTE-A networks achieve 300–600 Mbps peak (with 60 MHz of aggregated spectrum), and 100–200 Mbps average in dense urban.

docs.title: 5.7 WiMAX
docs.text: WiMAX (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access) is the IEEE 802.16 family of standards for wireless metropolitan area networks. It was the "other" 4G standard — technically comparable to LTE, commercially eclipsed by it.

docs.title: 5.7.1 IEEE 802.16 family
docs.text:
Standard Year Purpose 802.16 2001 Fixed wireless (line-of-sight, 10–66 GHz) 802.16a 2003 Fixed wireless, 2–11 GHz (NLOS) 802.16d 2004 Fixed WiMAX (OFDM, 256 FFT) 802.16e 2005 Mobile WiMAX (OFDMA, 2048 FFT, scalable) 802.16m 2011 WiMAX 2 (WirelessMAN-Advanced, ITU-R IMT-Advanced)

Mobile WiMAX (802.16e) was the commercially relevant version — deployed in Korea (WiBro), USA (Sprint/Clearwire), Russia (Yota), Pakistan, and a few others.

docs.title: 5.7.2 Mobile WiMAX physical layer
docs.text:
OFDMA-based — very similar to LTE:

Parameter WiMAX (802.16e) LTE (Release 8) Multiple access (DL/UL) OFDMA / OFDMA OFDMA / SC-FDMA Subcarrier spacing 10.94 kHz (fixed) 15 kHz FFT size 128, 512, 1024, 2048 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048 Channel bandwidth 1.25, 5, 10, 20 MHz 1.4, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20 MHz Frame duration 5 ms 10 ms Cyclic prefix 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 Normal (4.7 μs), extended (16.67 μs) MIMO 2×2 (baseline), 4×4 (later) 2×2, 4×4, 8×8 Modulation QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM Duplex TDD (FDD optional) FDD or TDD

Key difference: WiMAX uses OFDMA in the uplink too (rather than LTE's SC-FDMA). This gives WiMAX better frequency-scheduling flexibility but worse PAPR — a UE power-efficiency penalty.

Another key difference: WiMAX's TDD-first design (FDD was optional) versus LTE's FDD-first design. TDD gives better uplink/downlink flexibility for data-heavy traffic but requires global time synchronization.

docs.title: 5.7.3 WiMAX architecture
docs.text:
ASN (Access Service Network) — the radio access network.

  • BS (Base Station) — the WiMAX base station.
  • ASN-GW (ASN Gateway) — controls one or more BSs, analogous to LTE's MME
  • S-GW combined.

CSN (Connectivity Service Network) — the core network.

  • HA (Home Agent) — Mobile IP home agent (for mobility).
  • AAA — Authentication, Authorization, Accounting (RADIUS/Diameter).
  • DHCP — IP address allocation.
  • PCRF — policy control (in WiMAX 2).

Key architectural difference from LTE: WiMAX has two core network nodes (BS + ASN-GW), vs. LTE's three (eNodeB + MME + S-GW/P-GW). LTE is flatter.

docs.title: 5.7.4 WiMAX capacity
docs.text:
WiMAX 802.16e peak rate (20 MHz, 2×2 MIMO, 64-QAM):

  • Downlink: ~75 Mbps (TDD, 3:1 DL/UL ratio).
  • Uplink: ~25 Mbps.

With 802.16m (WiMAX 2), 4×4 MIMO, and 100 MHz (via aggregation):

  • Downlink: ~1 Gbps peak.

In practice, Mobile WiMAX deployments achieved:

  • Peak: 20–40 Mbps DL per sector in well-deployed networks.
  • Average: 3–10 Mbps DL per user in loaded conditions.
  • Cell capacity: ~30–50 Mbps per sector (comparable to early LTE).

docs.title: Worked example 5.6 — WiMAX capacity per MHz per km²
docs.text:
Scenario: WiMAX 802.16e, TDD, 20 MHz channel, 3:1 DL/UL ratio, 2×2 MIMO. Sector throughput (DL) = 30 Mbps. Site has 3 sectors → 90 Mbps per site.

Cell area: With 2 km radius (typical suburban), each hexagonal cell has area ≈ \(2.598 \times R^2\) = 10.4 km². But 3 sites cover 3 cells, so per-cell area ≈ 10.4 km².

Capacity per site per MHz per km²:

\[ \frac{90\ \text{Mbps}}{20\ \text{MHz} \times 10.4\ \text{km}^2} \approx 0.43\ \text{bps/Hz/km}^2 \]

Comparison with early LTE: LTE at 20 MHz, 2×2 MIMO, 3-sector, 2 km cells achieved ~150 Mbps per site → 0.72 bps/Hz/km² — roughly 1.7× WiMAX. LTE's better uplink (SC-FDMA) and higher MIMO order are the main reasons.

docs.title: 5.8 WiMAX vs. LTE — the 4G battle
docs.text: Aspect WiMAX (802.16e/m) LTE (Release 8/10) PHY OFDMA (DL + UL) OFDMA (DL) + SC-FDMA (UL) Duplex TDD first, FDD optional FDD first, TDD optional Peak rate ~75 Mbps (Rel 1), ~1 Gbps (Rel 2) 150 Mbps (Rel 8), 1 Gbps (Rel 10) Latency ~30 ms ~10 ms MIMO 2×2 baseline, 4×4 later 2×2 to 8×8 Mobility 60–120 km/h Up to 350 km/h Ecosystem Small (backed by Intel, Samsung, Clearwire) Massive (backed by 3GPP, 200+ operators) Spectrum 2.5 GHz (mostly), 3.5 GHz, unlicensed 700/800/1800/2100/2600 MHz (legacy 2G/3G spectrum) Backward compatibility None — requires new spectrum Dual-mode with 2G/3G → seamless fallback Commercial deployment Limited (Korea, US, Russia, Pakistan) Global (every continent) Timeline 2006–2011 deployment 2009–present Market outcome Commercially dead (~2015) Global 4G standard

docs.title: 5.8.1 Why WiMAX lost
docs.text:
WiMAX lost for reasons outside the technical specs:

  1. Ecosystem. LTE inherited the global GSM/UMTS operator base — 200+ operators worldwide, each with existing spectrum and customers. WiMAX operators had to build networks and customer bases from scratch.

  2. Backward compatibility. LTE devices are dual-mode with 2G/3G → users can drop out of coverage gracefully. WiMAX devices only work on WiMAX.

  3. Standards process. 3GPP has a clear, predictable release cycle (new release every 12–18 months) with broad industry participation. IEEE 802.16 was less cohesive and slower to iterate.

  4. Device ecosystem. Qualcomm, Apple, Samsung, etc. built LTE chipsets — not WiMAX. By 2013, LTE handsets were everywhere; WiMAX handsets were scarce.

  5. Intel's exit. Intel (the driving force behind WiMAX) shut down its WiMAX division in 2010 and pivoted to LTE — a fatal blow.

  6. The TDD vs. FDD issue. WiMAX was TDD-first; most operators owned FDD spectrum (from 2G/3G). Using WiMAX meant not using their existing spectrum.

Technically, WiMAX was comparable to or in some ways slightly ahead of LTE (especially early — WiMAX supported 4×4 MIMO before LTE did). Commercially, it lost decisively to the much larger LTE ecosystem.

docs.title: 5.8.2 Legacy of WiMAX
docs.text:
Even though WiMAX lost as a cellular standard, its technology influenced:

  • LTE and 5G NR PHY — WiMAX proved OFDMA + MIMO at scale, which LTE adopted.
  • WiFi (802.11) — WiMAX's OFDMA influenced WiFi 4/5/6/7 (802.11n/ac/ax/be).
  • Fixed wireless access (FWA) — WiMAX lives on as a niche FWA technology; 5G FWA (using mmWave) is essentially its spiritual successor.

docs.title: 5.9 Radio and network components
docs.text: Modern 4G/5G networks use advanced radio and network infrastructure that goes beyond the "macro base station" model. Understanding these components is essential for network design.

docs.title: 5.9.1 Antenna systems
docs.text:
MIMO antenna arrays:

  • Co-located MIMO — multiple antennas at one site, closely spaced.
  • Distributed MIMO — antennas spread across cells, coordinated (used in CoMP).

Active Antenna Systems (AAS):

  • Traditional: passive antennas + remote radio unit (RRU) + feeder cable.
  • AAS: each antenna element has its own RF chain — enables massive MIMO (64–256 elements) and 3D beamforming (both horizontal and vertical).

Massive MIMO (precursor to 5G):

  • 64+ antennas at the base station.
  • Beamforming gain: up to 10 log₁₀(64) = 18 dB per beam.
  • Multi-user MIMO: serves multiple UEs simultaneously.
  • Used in 4G LTE-A Pro and 5G NR.

docs.title: 5.9.2 Remote Radio Head (RRH) and Baseband Unit (BBU)
docs.text:
Traditional base station: RF and baseband in one box at the tower → heavy, hard to maintain, and the feeder cable (coax) wastes power.

Modern split:

  • RRH (Remote Radio Head) — RF and antenna at the tower top. Small, light, power-efficient.
  • BBU (Baseband Unit) — baseband processing at the bottom of the tower or in a centralized location.
  • CPRI/OBSAI interface — fiber carrying digitized I/Q samples between RRH and BBU.

Advantages:

  • Higher power efficiency — no coax feeder losses.
  • Easier installation — lighter tower-top equipment.
  • Fiber transport — the BBU can be far away (up to 20 km with CPRI).

docs.title: 5.9.3 Cloud RAN (C-RAN)
docs.text:
C-RAN centralizes BBUs from many cell sites into a BBU hotel:

  • RRHs at the cell sites (tower tops).
  • Dark fiber from each RRH to the centralized BBU pool.
  • BBU pool — many BBUs co-located in one facility.

Advantages:

  • Statistical multiplexing — 100 BBUs can serve 300 cell sites, because each site's traffic varies throughout the day.
  • Easier upgrades — swap BBU pool hardware without visiting cell sites.
  • CoMP-ready — coordinated transmission is trivial when BBUs are co-located.
  • Power savings — centralize cooling and power supply.

Disadvantages:

  • Fiber dependency — every cell site needs dark fiber (a significant cost).
  • Latency — CPRI latency must be < 100 μs for tight coordination.
  • Single point of failure — if the BBU pool fails, all cells go down (mitigated by redundancy).

Adoption: Used in dense urban and 5G deployments; limited in rural areas where fiber is expensive.

docs.title: 5.9.4 Small cells
docs.text:
Small cells are low-power base stations for capacity and coverage in specific areas:

Type Power Coverage Use Femtocell 10–100 mW 10–50 m Home/small office Picocell 100–500 mW 50–200 m Enterprise, hotspot Microcell 1–5 W 200–1000 m Dense urban Macrocell 20–40 W 1–30 km Wide-area coverage

Heterogeneous network (HetNet) — mixing cell types to optimize coverage and capacity.

docs.title: 5.9.5 Backhaul
docs.text:
Backhaul connects cell sites to the core network. Options:

Technology Capacity Typical distance Use Fiber 1–100 Gbps up to 80 km Preferred; where available Microwave 100 Mbps–1 Gbps 1–30 km (LOS) Rural, difficult-to-reach sites E-band (70/80 GHz) 1–10 Gbps 1–3 km Dense urban Free-space optical 1–10 Gbps 1–2 km Line-of-sight only Satellite 10–100 Mbps Global Remote sites DSL 10–100 Mbps 1–5 km Small cells (limited)

Backhaul is the hidden bottleneck — a 4G site with 3 sectors × 300 Mbps peak needs ~1–3 Gbps of backhaul at peak. Fiber or microwave capacity often lags the radio capacity by 5–10 years, causing congestion at the cell.

5G target: 10–20 Gbps per site → nearly all 5G sites need fiber.

docs.title: 5.10.1 Spectral efficiency
docs.text:
Peak spectral efficiency (bps/Hz) is the theoretical maximum:

System Peak DL spectral efficiency Peak UL UMTS R99 0.4 bps/Hz 0.4 bps/Hz HSPA+ (R11) 8.4 bps/Hz 2.3 bps/Hz LTE (Release 8) 7.5 bps/Hz (2×2) 3.75 bps/Hz (1×2) LTE-Advanced (Release 10) 15 bps/Hz (8×8) 6.75 bps/Hz (4×4) LTE-A Pro (Release 13) 25 bps/Hz (massive MIMO) 9.6 bps/Hz 5G NR (Sub-6) 30 bps/Hz 15 bps/Hz 5G NR (mmWave) 60+ bps/Hz 30 bps/Hz

Peak is achievable only in ideal conditions — highest SNR, best MIMO rank, no interference. Average spectral efficiency in real networks is ~30–50% of peak.

docs.title: 5.10.2 Cell-edge performance
docs.text:
The cell-edge user is the one who experiences the worst signal — typically at the cell boundary, with interference from neighboring cells at full strength.

Metrics:

  • 5th percentile throughput — the throughput achieved by the slowest 5% of users.
  • Cell-edge spectral efficiency — bps/Hz at the 5th percentile.
System Average spectral efficiency Cell-edge spectral efficiency UMTS R99 0.5 bps/Hz/cell 0.03 bps/Hz/cell HSPA+ 2 bps/Hz/cell 0.15 bps/Hz/cell LTE (2×2) 3 bps/Hz/cell 0.1 bps/Hz/cell LTE-A (8×8 + CoMP) 6 bps/Hz/cell 0.2 bps/Hz/cell 5G NR (massive MIMO) 15 bps/Hz/cell 0.3 bps/Hz/cell

Cell-edge is 10–100× worse than average — this is the fundamental challenge of cellular design. CoMP, beamforming, and small cells all target cell-edge improvement.

docs.title: Worked example 5.7 — capacity per km² for LTE
docs.text:
Scenario: LTE Release 8, 20 MHz, 3-sector macro site, average spectral efficiency 2.5 bps/Hz/cell (average load).

Cell throughput: 2.5 bps/Hz × 20 MHz = 50 Mbps per cell. Per 3-sector site: 150 Mbps.

Site coverage area: In suburban deployment with 2 km cell radius:

  • Cell area ≈ \(2.598 R^2\) = 10.4 km² per cell.
  • 3 sectors per site = 3 cells.
  • Site coverage = 3 × 10.4 = 31.2 km².

Capacity per km²: 150 Mbps / 31.2 km² ≈ 4.8 Mbps/km².

With LTE-Advanced (8×8 MIMO, CA, ~2× spectral efficiency): ~10 Mbps/km².

With 5G NR (mmWave, dense small cells, ~10× spectral efficiency): 50–100 Mbps/km² in dense urban — the reason 5G is being deployed mainly in dense areas.

docs.title: 5.10.3 Traffic density and capacity planning
docs.text:
Traffic density (Gbps/km²) is the key design metric in modern networks:

Scenario Traffic density Cell density needed Rural 0.01–0.1 Gbps/km² Macro cells (10–30 km) Suburban 0.1–1 Gbps/km² Macro cells (1–3 km) Urban 1–10 Gbps/km² Macro + microcells (500 m) Dense urban 10–50 Gbps/km² Microcells + picocells (200–500 m) Ultra-dense 50–300 Gbps/km² Small cells + DAS (50–200 m)

Network densification — deploying more cells per km² — is the main way to increase capacity. But each cell needs backhaul, power, and site costs → the cost per Gbps grows nonlinearly as cell size shrinks.

5G mmWave enables very dense deployment (10+ cells/km²) at high cost — viable only in stadiums, airports, and dense commercial areas.

docs.title: 5.11 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. 4G was defined by IMT-Advanced requirements: 1 Gbps peak downlink, 100 Mbps high-mobility, all-IP, low latency. LTE and WiMAX both met these — LTE won the market for ecosystem reasons.
  2. OFDMA (downlink) and SC-FDMA (uplink) replace WCDMA — OFDMA for flexibility and MIMO compatibility, SC-FDMA for UE power efficiency.
  3. LTE resource blocks are 12 subcarriers × 7 symbols × 2 slots; 100 RBs in 20 MHz; each RB 180 kHz wide, 0.5 ms long. Subcarrier spacing is 15 kHz.
  4. MIMO provides spatial multiplexing (linear capacity growth with \(\min(N_t, N_r)\)), transmit diversity (reliability), and beamforming (coverage). This is the workhorse behind 100+ Mbps per 20 MHz.
  5. The EPC (Evolved Packet Core) is flat, all-IP: eNodeB → S-GW → P-GW → Internet, with MME and HSS for control. Latency < 10 ms vs. 50 ms in UMTS.
  6. The eNodeB combines RNC + NodeB functions; X2 interface enables inter-eNodeB handover without going through the core.
  7. LTE-Advanced adds carrier aggregation (up to 5 carriers, 100 MHz), higher-order MIMO (8×8), CoMP, and relays — pushing peak to 3 Gbps.
  8. WiMAX was technically comparable to LTE but lost commercially because of ecosystem, backward compatibility, and market dynamics. Its technology influenced LTE, WiFi, and 5G NR.
  9. Radio and network components — RRH, BBU, C-RAN, small cells, massive MIMO — are what make modern 4G/5G deployments possible. Backhaul is often the hidden bottleneck.
  10. Network capacity depends on spectral efficiency, cell-edge performance, and cell density. Cell-edge is 10–100× worse than average — that's the fundamental cellular challenge.
  11. Peak spectral efficiency grew from 0.4 bps/Hz (UMTS) to 60+ bps/Hz (5G mmWave). Average grew from ~0.5 to ~15 bps/Hz/cell — still 10× below peak, and cell-edge 10–100× below average.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice
docs.text:
1. IMT-Advanced (4G) requirements include peak downlink of: (a) 100 Mbps (b) 500 Mbps (c) 1 Gbps (d) 10 Gbps

  2. LTE uses which multiple access in the uplink? (a) OFDMA (b) SC-FDMA (c) CDMA (d) TDMA

  3. LTE's subcarrier spacing is: (a) 10.94 kHz (b) 15 kHz (c) 30 kHz (d) 60 kHz

  4. An LTE resource block consists of: (a) 12 subcarriers × 7 symbols (b) 15 subcarriers × 6 symbols (c) 24 subcarriers × 12 symbols (d) 100 subcarriers

  5. SC-FDMA reduces PAPR by approximately: (a) 1 dB (b) 3 dB (c) 6 dB (d) 10 dB

  6. Massive MIMO refers to: (a) 2×2 MIMO (b) 4×4 MIMO (c) 8×8 MIMO (d) 64+ antennas at the BS

  7. The EPC node that anchors user-plane handovers is: (a) eNodeB (b) MME (c) S-GW (d) P-GW

  8. The flat architecture of LTE compared with UMTS eliminates: (a) MSC (b) BSC/RNC (c) HLR (d) BTS

  9. Carrier aggregation in LTE-Advanced supports: (a) 1 carrier (b) up to 3 (c) up to 5 (d) up to 32

  10. WiMAX was standardized by: (a) 3GPP (b) IEEE 802.16 (c) ITU-T (d) ETSI

  11. CoMP (Coordinated Multipoint) primarily improves: (a) Peak rate (b) Cell-edge throughput (c) Latency (d) Battery life

  12. LTE-A Pro (Release 13) peak downlink rate is: (a) 150 Mbps (b) 1 Gbps (c) 3 Gbps (d) 10 Gbps

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. LTE downlink uses ____ for multiple access; uplink uses ____.
  2. An LTE resource block occupies ____ kHz of bandwidth and ____ ms of time.
  3. LTE subcarrier spacing is ____ kHz.
  4. The EPC's ____ handles control-plane signalling including NAS messages.
  5. The EPC's ____ anchors the user plane across handovers.
  6. The ____ allocates IP addresses and connects to external PDNs.
  7. LTE's X2 interface connects ____ to ____.
  8. LTE-Advanced supports ____ carriers aggregation, each up to 20 MHz, total 100 MHz.
  9. WiMAX uses OFDMA in both uplink and downlink, unlike LTE which uses ____ in uplink.
  10. Massive MIMO (64+ antennas) can provide beamforming gain up to ____ dB.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. State the IMT-Advanced requirements and explain how LTE-Advanced and WiMAX each meet them.
  2. Explain why LTE uses OFDMA in the downlink but SC-FDMA in the uplink. What is the PAPR trade-off?
  3. Describe the LTE resource block — bandwidth, time, subcarrier count, symbol count. How many RBs are there in 20 MHz?
  4. Compare spatial multiplexing, transmit diversity, and beamforming for MIMO. When is each used?
  5. Draw the LTE EPC architecture — eNodeB, MME, S-GW, P-GW, HSS. Explain the role of each and the interfaces between them.
  6. Explain why LTE's flat architecture matters — how does removing the RNC reduce latency?
  7. Describe LTE-Advanced enhancements: carrier aggregation, higher-order MIMO, CoMP, relays. What peak rate does each enable?
  8. Describe the WiMAX architecture (ASN, CSN). Compare with LTE's EPC. Why did WiMAX lose the 4G battle despite being technically competitive?
  9. Explain C-RAN and its advantages. What are the deployment challenges?
  10. Compute spectral efficiency per cell and per km² for LTE and LTE-A. Why is cell-edge throughput so much worse than average?
  11. Compare LTE vs. LTE-A vs. 5G NR on spectral efficiency, peak rate, latency, and MIMO configuration.
  12. A network operator has 60 MHz of spectrum (3 × 20 MHz carriers) and needs to support 100 Mbps peak downlink. Can LTE-Advanced with 2×2 MIMO achieve this? With 4×4 MIMO? With 8×8 MIMO? Show calculations.

docs.title: 5.13 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (c) — 1 Gbps peak.
  2. (b) — SC-FDMA.
  3. (b) — 15 kHz.
  4. (a) — 12 subcarriers × 7 symbols (per slot; 14 per subframe).
  5. (c) — ~6 dB.
  6. (d) — 64+ antennas at the BS.
  7. (c) — S-GW.
  8. (b) — BSC/RNC.
  9. (c) — up to 5.
  10. (b) — IEEE 802.16.
  11. (b) — cell-edge throughput.
  12. (c) — 3 Gbps.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. OFDMA; SC-FDMA.
  2. 180; 0.5.
  3. 15.
  4. MME.
  5. S-GW.
  6. P-GW.
  7. eNodeB; eNodeB.
  8. 5.
  9. SC-FDMA.
  10. ~18 dB (10 log 64).
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. IMT-Advanced requirements: 1 Gbps peak DL (low mobility), 100 Mbps (high mobility), 500 Mbps peak UL, 15 bps/Hz peak spectral efficiency, < 10 ms user-plane latency, all-IP, mobility up to 350 km/h. LTE-A meets them via carrier aggregation (100 MHz), 8×8 MIMO, CoMP, and relays → 3 Gbps peak,

    15 bps/Hz. WiMAX 802.16m meets them via 100 MHz aggregation, 4×4 MIMO, and advanced relaying → 1 Gbps peak. Both standards meet the requirements technically; LTE won commercially.

  2. Downlink OFDMA: the eNodeB has abundant power (mains-powered, no battery) and flexible frequency-scheduling needs → OFDMA's higher PAPR (10–12 dB) is acceptable, and its spectral flexibility is valuable. Uplink SC-FDMA: the UE is battery-powered — OFDMA's PAPR would require 10 dB PA backoff → inefficient → short battery + poor coverage. SC-FDMA's DFT-precoding reduces PAPR to 3–6 dB → the UE PA operates near saturation → +6 dB uplink power → ~2× cell radius. Trade-off: slightly lower spectral efficiency in the uplink (must allocate contiguous RBs), but coverage and battery life win.
  3. LTE resource block: 12 subcarriers × 180 kHz bandwidth × 7 symbols × 0.5 ms slot (normal CP). Time-frequency unit = 84 resource elements (REs). In 20 MHz: 100 RBs (20 MHz / 180 kHz ≈ 111, but guard band leaves 100 usable). Per subframe (1 ms): 100 RBs × 168 REs = 16,800 REs total, minus reference signals and control → ~100 RBs worth of data.
  4. Spatial multiplexing: multiple independent streams → linear capacity growth. Used when channel is high-rank (rich scattering, good SNR). Transmit diversity: same data duplicated across antennas with orthogonal codes (Alamouti/SFBC) → 3 dB gain in Rayleigh fading at half the rate. Used for control channels, cell edge, and low-SNR UEs. Beamforming: focus energy toward a specific UE → 10 log(N_t) dB gain. Used for coverage extension, interference reduction, and MU-MIMO.
  5. LTE EPC architecture: (a) eNodeB — base station, all radio functions + RRC. (b) MME — control plane, NAS, authentication, mobility, bearer management. (c) S-GW — user-plane anchor for handovers, charging. (d) P-GW — gateway to external PDN, IP allocation, QoS. (e) HSS — subscription database + authentication. Interfaces: Uu (UE-eNodeB), S1-MME (eNodeB-MME), S1-U (eNodeB-S-GW), S5/S8 (S-GW-P-GW), S6a (MME-HSS), S11 (MME-S-GW), X2 (eNodeB-eNodeB).
  6. Flat architecture: UMTS has NodeB → RNC → SGSN/MSC — three levels of signalling, each adding latency. LTE collapses NodeB+RNC into eNodeB and uses direct S1 to the core → two levels. Result: user-plane RTT drops from ~50 ms to ~10 ms; control-plane (idle→connected) from ~500 ms to ~50–100 ms. This was critical for interactive services (gaming, VoLTE, industrial IoT) that were impossible on 3G.
  7. LTE-A enhancements: (a) Carrier aggregation — up to 5 carriers × 20 MHz = 100 MHz → 5× rate → up to 1 Gbps with 2×2 MIMO. (b) Higher-order MIMO — 8×8 DL → 8× rate → up to 3 Gbps with CA. (c) CoMP — coordinated transmission from multiple eNodeBs improves cell-edge throughput 30–50%. (d) Relays — decode-and-forward or amplify-and-forward relays extend coverage to remote areas without new fiber backhaul.
  8. WiMAX architecture: (a) ASN — BS + ASN-GW. (b) CSN — HA (mobile IP), AAA, DHCP. Compare to LTE: WiMAX has 2 nodes (BS+ASN-GW) where LTE has 3 (eNodeB+MME+S/P-GW) — LTE is flatter. Why WiMAX lost: (i) ecosystem — LTE had 200+ operator backing, WiMAX had ~30; (ii) backward compatibility — LTE dual-mode with 2G/3G, WiMAX not; (iii) Intel's exit (2010) was fatal; (iv) TDD-first design didn't match most operators' FDD spectrum; (v) slower standards iteration.
  9. C-RAN: centralizes BBUs from many cell sites into a BBU pool; RRHs at cell sites; fiber (CPRI) carries digitized samples. Advantages: statistical multiplexing of BBU processing, easier upgrades, CoMP-ready, power savings. Challenges: fiber everywhere (huge cost), CPRI latency budget (< 100 μs), single point of failure at the BBU pool (needs redundancy), and the recent trend toward distributed/virtualized RAN (O-RAN) has shifted industry views.
  10. Spectral efficiency per cell: LTE ~3 bps/Hz/cell average (DL, 2×2 MIMO, 20 MHz). LTE-A ~6 bps/Hz/cell with 8×8 + CoMP. Per km²: LTE 50 Mbps/cell ÷ 10 km² cell ≈ 5 Mbps/km². LTE-A 100 Mbps/cell ÷ 10 km² = 10 Mbps/km². Cell-edge is worse because: at the cell boundary, the serving signal is weakest (max path loss) while interfering signals from adjacent cells are strongest (min path loss from neighbors) → SIR is worst. This yields 10–100× worse throughput. CoMP, beamforming, and small cells target this.
  11. LTE vs. LTE-A vs. 5G NR: (a) LTE — 150 Mbps peak, 2×2 MIMO, 20 MHz, ~10 ms latency, ~3 bps/Hz/cell average. (b) LTE-A — 3 Gbps peak, 8×8 MIMO, 100 MHz CA, ~10 ms latency, ~6 bps/Hz/cell average. (c) 5G NR — 20 Gbps peak (mmWave), 64–256 antenna massive MIMO, 400 MHz per carrier (mmWave), ~1 ms latency, ~15 bps/Hz/cell average (Sub-6), 30 bps/Hz/cell (mmWave).
  12. Calculation: (a) 2×2 MIMO: per carrier ~150 Mbps peak × 3 carriers = 450 Mbps — well exceeds 100 Mbps target. (b) 4×4 MIMO: ~300 Mbps per carrier × 3 = 900 Mbps. (c) 8×8 MIMO: ~600 Mbps per carrier × 3 = 1.8 Gbps. Answer: even 2×2 MIMO with 3× CA achieves 450 Mbps — easily satisfies 100 Mbps target. For a high-traffic cell, 4×4 MIMO gives 900 Mbps peak with room for multiple users at once.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• S. Sesia, I. Toufik & M. Baker, LTE — The UMTS Long Term Evolution: From Theory to Practice, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011 — the practical engineering reference; covers PHY, MAC, RRC, EPC in detail.
  • E. Dahlman, S. Parkvall & J. Sköld, 4G: LTE/LTE-Advanced for Mobile Broadband, 2nd ed., Academic Press, 2013 — the standard 4G textbook.
  • E. Dahlman, S. Parkvall & J. Sköld, 5G NR: The Next Generation Wireless Access Technology, 2nd ed., Academic Press, 2020 — the natural successor.
  • H. Holma & A. Toskala, LTE for UMTS: Evolution to LTE-Advanced, Wiley, 2011 — from the HSPA authors.
  • C. Cox, An Introduction to LTE: LTE, LTE-Advanced, SAE, VoLTE and 4G Mobile Communications, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2014 — accessible introduction.
  • A. Ghosh, J. Zhang, J. G. Andrews & R. Muhamed, Fundamentals of LTE, Prentice Hall, 2010 — well-written fundamentals.
  • J. G. Andrews, A. Ghosh & R. Muhamed, Fundamentals of WiMAX, Prentice Hall, 2007 — the WiMAX reference.
  • L. Nuaymi, WiMAX: Technology for Broadband Wireless Access, Wiley, 2007 — WiMAX architecture and PHY.
  • T. S. Rappaport, Wireless Communications: Principles and Practice, 2nd ed., Prentice Hall, 2002 — Ch 11 for MIMO basics.
  • A. Goldsmith, Wireless Communications, Cambridge, 2005 — Ch 10 for MIMO capacity.
  • D. Tse & P. Viswanath, Fundamentals of Wireless Communication, Cambridge, 2005 — Ch 7 for MIMO theory (free PDF online).
  • 3GPP TS 36.xxx series — LTE specifications:
  • TS 36.300 — Overall description.
  • TS 36.211 — Physical channels and modulation.
  • TS 36.212 — Multiplexing and channel coding.
  • TS 36.213 — Physical layer procedures.
  • TS 36.300 — E-UTRAN overall.
  • TS 23.401 — GPRS enhancements for E-UTRAN access (EPC).
  • TS 36.913 — Requirements for further advancements (LTE-Advanced).
  • IEEE 802.16e-2005 and 802.16m-2011 — WiMAX specifications.
  • NGMN Alliance — operator-driven 5G requirements (precursor to 5G NR).

docs.title: Suggested tutorial problems
docs.text:
1. IMT-Advanced check. For each requirement (peak DL, peak UL, spectral efficiency, latency), compute whether LTE-Advanced (Release 10) meets it. Show calculations and cite the standard's claims.

  2. Resource block count. Verify that 20 MHz LTE has 100 RBs. Show the arithmetic: 20 MHz / 180 kHz = 111.11. Where do the 11 missing RBs go?

  3. Peak throughput. Compute peak LTE throughput for: (a) 10 MHz, 2×2 MIMO, 64-QAM, rate-3/4; (b) 20 MHz, 4×4 MIMO, 64-QAM, rate-3/4; (c) 60 MHz (3×CA), 4×4 MIMO, 64-QAM, rate-3/4.

  4. SC-FDMA vs OFDMA. For a UE with 23 dBm PA and maximum PAPR limits: OFDMA allows 14 dBm average TX (10 dB backoff); SC-FDMA allows 19 dBm (4 dB backoff). Compute the cell radius for each, using path-loss exponent 3.5 and equal receiver sensitivity. Which is preferred and why?

  5. MIMO modes. A UE is at 10 dB SNR with rich scattering — which MIMO mode should the eNodeB choose? At 0 dB SNR with one dominant path — which mode? Justify.

  6. EPC latency. Trace the path of a packet from a UE to a Google server. List each network element and its contribution to latency. Total one-way and RTT.

  7. Carrier aggregation. Design an LTE-A configuration for an operator with spectrum at 800 MHz (10 MHz), 1800 MHz (20 MHz), and 2600 MHz (20 MHz). How many component carriers? What peak downlink rate with 4×4 MIMO? Note any deployment challenges (inter-band CA, antenna sharing).

  8. WiMAX capacity. For WiMAX 802.16e, 10 MHz TDD (3:1 DL/UL), 2×2 MIMO: compute peak DL and UL. Then compute the site capacity (3-sector) assuming 50% of peak average.

  9. Cell-edge improvement. A cell has average throughput 50 Mbps, cell-edge (5th percentile) 2 Mbps. CoMP provides a 3 dB SIR improvement at cell edge, translating to a 2× throughput improvement. Compute the new cell-edge throughput. What is the % of users below 1 Mbps before and after?

  10. Massive MIMO gain. A 64-antenna massive MIMO system beams to 8 UEs simultaneously. Compute the per-user SNR gain vs. a single antenna (10 log(64/8) = 9 dB per user). Compute the total capacity gain vs. 2×2 MIMO.

  11. Backhaul. A 4G LTE site has 3 sectors, each 20 MHz, 4×4 MIMO. Peak per sector is 600 Mbps. What fiber backhaul capacity does the site need at peak? At 60% average load?

  12. 5G vs 4G. Compare 5G NR (Sub-6, 100 MHz, massive MIMO) with LTE-A (20 MHz × 3, 4×4 MIMO) on: peak rate, average rate, latency, and capacity per km². What are the main reasons for 5G's advantage?

docs.title: Chapter 6 — Next Generation Networks (NGN)
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Contact hours: 3 lecture · Home study: 7 h · Part IV — Emerging technologies

Coverage (syllabus): overview of next generation networks · personal area networks (Bluetooth and ZigBee) · wireless data services (WiFi) · UWB · 5G mobile network technology and the Internet of Things (IoT).

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain what Next Generation Networks (NGN) means and how the concept evolved from all-IP convergence to the IoT era.
  2. Describe Bluetooth Classic and BLE — piconet topology, protocols, data rates, and power profiles — and choose between them for a given application.
  3. Analyse ZigBee — mesh topology, IEEE 802.15.4 PHY/MAC, AODV routing, and why it dominates low-power sensor networks.
  4. Compare the WiFi standards (802.11a/b/g/n/ac/ax/be) — rates, bands, MIMO, OFDMA — and select a WiFi generation for a given deployment.
  5. Explain UWB — impulse radio, timing, ranging — and its role in high-precision positioning.
  6. Describe LPWAN technologies (LoRa, NB-IoT, Sigfox) — range, data rate, battery life — and their role in IoT connectivity.
  7. Explain 5G network architecture — service-based core, network slicing, edge computing — and the three 5G use cases (eMBB, URLLC, mMTC).
  8. Compute IoT device battery life, coverage range, and network capacity for typical LPWAN/WiFi/BLE deployments.
  9. Design a connectivity strategy — WPAN, WLAN, LPWAN, cellular — for a real-world IoT application based on range, power, and data requirements.

docs.title: 6.1.1 From convergence to everything-over-IP
docs.text:
The term Next Generation Network (NGN) was defined by the ITU-T in the early 2000s as a packet-based network able to provide telecommunication services — voice, data, video — over a single IP infrastructure with guaranteed QoS.

The original NGN vision (2004 ITU-T Y.2001):

"A packet-based network able to provide telecommunication services and able to make use of multiple broadband, QoS-enabled transport technologies, in which service-related functions are independent from underlying transport-related technologies."

Key NGN principles:

  • Packet-based — everything rides on IP, not circuit switching.
  • Service / transport separation — services are decoupled from the underlying network via open APIs.
  • QoS-enabled — unlike the best-effort internet, NGN guarantees performance.
  • Any-access — fixed, mobile, wireless — all converge to one network.
  • Multi-service — voice, data, video, IoT over one infrastructure.

docs.title: 6.1.2 The stages of NGN evolution
docs.text:
Stage 1 (2000–2010): All-IP convergence.

  • Replace PSTN circuit switching with IP-based voice (VoIP).
  • Replace 2G/3G core networks with IP (R4 MSC Server + MGW → all-IP EPC in LTE).
  • Example: BT's 21CN project (UK), Verizon's FiOS (fiber to the home).
  • Key technologies: SIP, MPLS, IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS).

Stage 2 (2010–2020): Fixed-mobile convergence (FMC).

  • Unify fixed and mobile access under one core (EPC → 5G SBA).
  • Voice over WiFi (VoWiFi), LTE-WiFi aggregation (LWA).
  • Example: T-Mobile's VoWiFi, AT&T's small-cell deployment.
  • Key technologies: ANDSF, ePDG, 5G NSA/SA.

Stage 3 (2020s): IoT convergence.

  • Billions of devices — sensors, actuators, cameras — all IP-connected.
  • LPWAN (LoRa, NB-IoT, Sigfox) sits alongside WiFi and cellular for IoT.
  • 5G and beyond: network slicing, edge computing, massive machine-type communication.
  • Key technologies: MQTT, CoAP, 5G core, edge computing, ML.

The NGN concept broadened from "voice over IP" to "everything over IP" — the network becomes a platform for all digital services.

docs.title: 6.1.3 The NGN landscape in one picture
docs.text:
Category Standard Range Data rate Power WPAN (personal) Bluetooth Classic 10–100 m 1–3 Mbps Low Bluetooth LE 10–100 m 125 kbps–2 Mbps Very low ZigBee 10–100 m 250 kbps Very low UWB 1–10 m 100 Mbps–1 Gbps Low WLAN (local) WiFi 4/5/6/7 30–100 m 100 Mbps–30 Gbps High WMAN (metropolitan) WiMAX, 5G FWA 1–50 km 100 Mbps–1 Gbps High WWAN (wide) 4G LTE 1–30 km 100 Mbps–1 Gbps High 5G NR 100 m–10 km 1–20 Gbps High LPWAN (IoT) LoRa 2–15 km 0.3–37.5 kbps Extremely low NB-IoT 1–10 km 26–127 kbps Very low Sigfox 3–50 km 100 bps Extremely low Satellite GEO, LEO global 1–200 Mbps —

Each row is a different trade-off between range, rate, and power. The NGN is about making all of them work together — not replacing them.

docs.title: 6.2.1 Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR) — the original
docs.text:
Bluetooth Classic (Basic Rate / Enhanced Data Rate, BR/EDR) was defined in 1994 by Ericsson and standardized as IEEE 802.15.1 in 2002. Designed as a cable replacement for short-range connections (headphones, mice, keyboards).

Key parameters:

Parameter Value Frequency 2.4 GHz ISM band (2.400–2.4835 GHz) Channel spacing 1 MHz; 79 channels (or 40 in low-energy variants) Modulation GFSK (Basic Rate), π/4-DQPSK, 8-DPSK (EDR) Data rate 1 Mbps (BR), 2–3 Mbps (EDR) Range Class 1: 100 m, Class 2: 10 m, Class 3: 1 m Tx power Class 1: 20 dBm, Class 2: 4 dBm, Class 3: 0 dBm Topology Piconet (1 master + up to 7 active slaves)

The piconet:

  • One master device controls the piconet — it defines the hopping sequence, the slot timing, and the channel access rules.
  • Up to 7 active slaves simultaneously; more can be in parked or sniff mode (low-power standby).
  • Slots are 625 μs long; master and slave alternate transmissions.
  • Frequency hopping at 1600 hops/s (each slot on a different channel) — resist to interference and multi-path.

Scatternets. Multiple piconets can be interconnected by a device that belongs to two or more piconets simultaneously. This is limited in practice (the shared device is a bottleneck).

Protocol stack (simplified):

  • Radio → Baseband → LMP (Link Manager Protocol) → L2CAP (Logical Link Control and Adaptation) → RFCOMM (serial port) or A2DP (audio).
  • SDP (Service Discovery Protocol) — finds available services.
  • Profiles — application-level standards (HSP for headset, HFP for handsfree, A2DP for audio, HID for input devices, OPP for file transfer).

Why frequency hopping? The 2.4 GHz ISM band is shared by WiFi, ZigBee, microwaves, and Bluetooth itself. Hopping across 79 channels means a narrowband interferer only affects 1/79 of slots — Bluetooth retransmits the failed slots on different frequencies. Effective interference resistance without needing a coordination protocol.

docs.title: 6.2.2 Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) — the IoT version
docs.text:
BLE (Bluetooth Smart) was introduced in Bluetooth 4.0 (2010) as a fundamentally different radio optimized for IoT sensors and wearables.

Key design changes:

Aspect Bluetooth Classic BLE Target use Continuous data (audio, files) Bursty sensor data Channel count 79 × 1 MHz 40 × 2 MHz (3 advertising + 37 data) Connection setup ~seconds ~3 ms Peak current (TX) 30–40 mA ~10 mA Standby current 100 μA – 1 mA < 1 μA Duty cycle Continuous Bursty (advertise → sleep) Data rate (peak) 2–3 Mbps (EDR) 1 Mbps (BT 4.0), 2 Mbps (BT 5.0) Range (BT 5.0) 10–100 m 10–400 m (with coded PHY)

The BLE advertising model.

BLE devices don't need a connection. A peripheral broadcasts advertisement packets on 3 advertising channels; a central scans for them, then either reads the advertisement data (broadcast mode) or requests a connection.

Advertising interval — from 20 ms to 10.24 s. Longer intervals = lower power but higher latency.

GATT (Generic Attribute Profile).

BLE data is organized as services and characteristics: - Service — a group of related characteristics (e.g., "Heart Rate Service"). - Characteristic — a single data value (e.g., "Heart Rate Measurement") with properties (read, write, notify).

Standard profiles (Heart Rate, Battery, Device Information) are defined by the Bluetooth SIG; custom services are common for specific applications.

Bluetooth versions:

Version Year Key additions 4.0 2010 BLE introduced 4.1 2013 IoT-friendly coexistence with LTE 4.2 2014 IPv6/6LoWPAN support, faster 5.0 2016 2× speed (2 Mbps), 4× range (400 m), 8× advertising payload 5.1 2019 Direction finding (AoA/AoD) for indoor positioning 5.2 2020 LE Audio (LC3 codec, multi-stream) 5.3 2021 Periodic advertising, channel classification 5.4 2023 PAwR (periodic advertising with responses)

docs.title: Worked example 6.1 — BLE battery life
docs.text:
Scenario: A temperature sensor sends one 10-byte reading every 10 s. Advertising is not used (connection mode). Each transmission uses 2 ms at 10 mA; the MCU consumes 5 μA in sleep. Battery: 1000 mAh coin cell.

Energy per transmission:

  • Transmit: 2 ms × 10 mA = 20 μAh per transmission.
  • Sleep between transmissions: (10 s − 2 ms) × 5 μA ≈ 50 μAh per interval.
  • Total per 10 s: ~70 μAh × (10 s / 3600 s/h) ... let me redo:
  • 2 ms at 10 mA = 20 mA·ms = 0.00556 mAh per transmission.
  • 9998 ms at 5 μA = 0.0000139 mAh per interval.
  • Per 10 s interval: 0.00557 mAh.
  • Per hour: 360 intervals × 0.00557 = 2.0 mAh/h.
  • Battery life: 1000 mAh / 2.0 mA ≈ 500 hours ≈ 21 days.

Optimization: Increase advertising interval to 30 s and use a lower TX power:

  • Transmit: 2 ms × 5 mA = 0.00278 mAh per transmission.
  • Per hour: 120 intervals × 0.00278 = 0.334 mAh/h.
  • Battery life: 1000 / 0.334 ≈ 3000 hours ≈ 125 days (~4 months).

Realistic for IoT: A properly tuned BLE sensor (event-driven, not periodic) can last 1–3 years on a coin cell. Longer life requires LPWAN (ZigBee, LoRa, NB-IoT).

docs.title: 6.2.3 Bluetooth Classic vs. BLE — choosing
docs.text:
Application Recommended Wireless headphones Bluetooth Classic (A2DP) Fitness tracker / smartwatch BLE Wireless mouse / keyboard BLE (or Classic HID) Continuous audio streaming Bluetooth Classic (higher rate) Hearing aids BLE (LE Audio, BT 5.2) Indoor location beacon BLE (with 5.1 direction finding) File transfer between phones Bluetooth Classic Medical sensor BLE

Rule of thumb: if the data is continuous and needs a high rate → Classic. If it's bursty and power is critical → BLE.

docs.title: 6.3.1 What is ZigBee?
docs.text:
ZigBee (IEEE 802.15.4) is a low-power, low-data-rate, mesh-capable WPAN standard designed for sensor networks and home automation.

Key parameters:

Parameter Value Frequency 2.4 GHz (global, 16 channels), 868 MHz (EU), 915 MHz (US) Modulation OQPSK (2.4 GHz) or BPSK (sub-GHz) Data rate 250 kbps (2.4 GHz), 40 kbps (915 MHz), 20 kbps (868 MHz) Range 10–100 m per hop (typical); extended via mesh Topology Star, tree, or mesh Power (TX) ~30 mA Power (sleep) < 1 μA Network capacity 65,000+ nodes per network

docs.title: 6.3.2 The ZigBee protocol stack
docs.text:
Built on IEEE 802.15.4 (PHY + MAC), ZigBee adds:

  • NWK (Network) layer — mesh routing, address assignment, network formation.
  • APS (Application Support) layer — endpoint multiplexing, binding.
  • ZDO (ZigBee Device Object) — device discovery, service discovery.
  • Application profiles — standardized profiles (Home Automation 1.2, Smart Energy, Light Link) and manufacturer-specific profiles.

Device types:

  • Coordinator — forms the network, assigns addresses, maintains the network. Exactly one per network.
  • Router — forwards traffic, participates in mesh. Typically mains-powered.
  • End Device — leaves/actuators/sensors, sleeps most of the time. Typically battery-powered.

docs.title: 6.3.3 Mesh networking and AODV
docs.text:
ZigBee supports mesh topologies — any router can forward for any other. The routing protocol is AODV (Ad hoc On-demand Distance Vector):

  1. The source broadcasts a Route Request (RREQ) — "who has the destination?"
  2. Intermediate routers forward the RREQ, adding their address.
  3. The destination receives the RREQ and sends back a Route Reply (RREP) — tracing the reverse path.
  4. Routers cache the route for future use.
  5. Route maintenance: if a link breaks, an RERR (Route Error) propagates back; source initiates a new RREQ.

Why AODV? On-demand — no routing table is maintained proactively. For sensor networks (mostly idle), this saves energy.

docs.title: Worked example 6.2 — ZigBee mesh coverage
docs.text:
Scenario: A factory wants to cover 500 m × 500 m with ZigBee sensors. Each sensor has range 30 m. Floor has walls reducing effective range to 20 m.

Single-hop coverage: ~20 m.

Mesh approach: deploy routers every 15 m (overlap for reliability).

  • Row spacing: 15 m; column spacing: 15 m.
  • Number of routers: (500/15) × (500/15) ≈ 34 × 34 = 1,156 routers.
  • This is more than ZigBee can handle reliably (practical limit ~500 routers per network).

Alternative: hierarchical (cluster tree).

  • Divide area into 4 clusters of 250 × 250 m.
  • Each cluster has 1 coordinator + ~100 routers + many end devices.
  • Alternative: reduce coverage requirement — use fewer sensors, accept longer hops (multi-hop latency increases).

The trade-off: more hops = larger area but higher latency and lower throughput (each hop halves bandwidth). For typical building automation, a single-cell 10,000 m² deployment with 200-300 devices is comfortable for ZigBee; larger deployments need multiple networks or gateway bridges.

docs.title: 6.3.4 ZigBee vs. BLE
docs.text:
Aspect ZigBee BLE Topology Mesh Star (BLE Mesh is a newer standard) Data rate 250 kbps 1–2 Mbps Range per hop 10–100 m 10–100 m Network size 65,000+ ~10–20 typical; higher with BLE Mesh Power (idle) < 1 μA < 1 μA Latency 15–30 ms typical 3 ms Standard IEEE 802.15.4 Bluetooth SIG Ecosystem Smart home (Philips Hue, SmartThings) Wearables, phones, broad Best for Sensor networks Phone-tethered IoT

Rule of thumb: ZigBee when the network has many devices and needs mesh coverage; BLE when the device talks to a phone or the network is small.

docs.title: 6.4.1 The 802.11 family
docs.text:
WiFi (IEEE 802.11) dominates local wireless — home, office, public hotspot. Every WiFi generation has improved peak rate, spectral efficiency, and features:

Standard Year Brand Band Channel width Peak rate Key feature 802.11 1997 — 2.4 GHz 20 MHz 2 Mbps Original 802.11b 1999 — 2.4 GHz 20 MHz 11 Mbps DSSS, more range 802.11a 1999 — 5 GHz 20 MHz 54 Mbps OFDM 802.11g 2003 — 2.4 GHz 20 MHz 54 Mbps OFDM at 2.4 GHz 802.11n 2009 WiFi 4 2.4/5 GHz 40 MHz 600 Mbps MIMO, channel bonding 802.11ac 2013 WiFi 5 5 GHz 80/160 MHz 6.9 Gbps MU-MIMO DL, 256-QAM 802.11ax 2019 WiFi 6 2.4/5 GHz 160 MHz 9.6 Gbps OFDMA, MU-MIMO UL/DL, 1024-QAM, TWT 802.11be 2024 WiFi 7 2.4/5/6 GHz 320 MHz 46 Gbps 4096-QAM, Multi-Link (MLO), 16×16 MIMO 802.11ay 2024 — 60 GHz 2.16 GHz 100 Gbps mmWave, for VR/AR

The naming confusion. IEEE uses numbers (802.11ac); the WiFi Alliance introduced simpler names (WiFi 4, 5, 6, 7) starting in 2018 to avoid consumer confusion. Both are used; the numbered names are unambiguous for generations, so this course uses them.

docs.title: 6.4.2 Key PHY technologies
docs.text:
OFDM and its evolution:

  • WiFi 4 (802.11n) — OFDM, 20/40 MHz channels, MIMO.
  • WiFi 5 (802.11ac) — OFDM, 80/160 MHz, MU-MIMO downlink, 256-QAM.
  • WiFi 6 (802.11ax) — OFDMA, MU-MIMO uplink + downlink, 1024-QAM, longer OFDM symbol (4× — reduces guard band overhead).
  • WiFi 7 (802.11be) — 4096-QAM, 320 MHz channels, Multi-Link Operation (MLO — simultaneous transmission on multiple bands), 16×16 MIMO.

OFDMA in WiFi 6 — the biggest change since WiFi 4. Instead of scheduling one user per channel (all subcarriers), the AP allocates resource units (RUs) to multiple users simultaneously. This is exactly what LTE/5G do, and it massively improves efficiency in crowded environments (stadiums, airports, offices).

MIMO scaling:

Generation MIMO WiFi 4 4×4 WiFi 5 8×8 (with MU-MIMO DL) WiFi 6 8×8 (with MU-MIMO DL+UL) WiFi 7 16×16, plus Multi-Link

docs.title: Worked example 6.3 — WiFi 6 capacity in a crowded office
docs.text:
Scenario: Office with 200 users, each with a phone and laptop (400 devices). AP is WiFi 6, 5 GHz, 80 MHz channel, 4×4 MIMO.

Per-AP theoretical peak: ~2.4 Gbps (WiFi 6, 80 MHz, 4×4).

Realistic per-AP throughput: 40–60% of peak in dense environment → ~1.2 Gbps.

Per-user throughput (ideal 400 evenly split): 1.2 Gbps / 400 = 3 Mbps per device. Too slow for video calls.

With 8 APs deployed (typical office): 8 × 1.2 Gbps = 9.6 Gbps total → 24 Mbps per device — acceptable for most uses.

OFDMA advantage: WiFi 5 would give ~1 Gbps per AP but with one user per transmission (MU-MIMO limited to 4 DL streams). WiFi 6 OFDMA allows ~30 RUs per 80 MHz channel → up to 30 simultaneous users per transmission → much better at high density.

The lesson: WiFi 6's OFDMA is about capacity in dense environments, not peak rate per user. Its biggest benefit is that a stadium or airport full of people doesn't collapse the network.

docs.title: 6.4.3 WiFi bands and coexistence
docs.text:
Band Channels Interference 2.4 GHz 14 channels (varies by country), 20 MHz Very congested (Bluetooth, ZigBee, microwave) 5 GHz 25+ channels (varies), 20–160 MHz Congested but more channels 6 GHz (WiFi 6E) 59 channels of 20 MHz, or 14 of 160 MHz Empty — reserved for WiFi

The 6 GHz band (5.925–7.125 GHz) was allocated for WiFi 6E and WiFi 7 in 2020–2021. No legacy devices — every WiFi 6E device supports 6 GHz. Clean spectrum means better performance, especially in dense environments.

docs.title: 6.4.4 WiFi security
docs.text:
Standard Year Cipher Status WEP 1997 RC4 Broken (crackable in minutes) WPA 2003 TKIP Deprecated WPA2 2004 AES-CCMP Good, still widely used WPA3 2018 AES-GCMP, SAE Current standard

WPA3 improvements:

  • SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) — replaces the WPA2 PSK handshake, resistant to offline dictionary attacks.
  • Forward secrecy — captured traffic can't be decrypted even if the password is later compromised.
  • 192-bit security mode for enterprise/WPA3-Enterprise.

Rule: never deploy WEP or WPA. WPA2 is the minimum for compatibility; WPA3 is recommended for new deployments.

docs.title: 6.5.1 What is UWB?
docs.text:
Ultra-Wideband (UWB) is a radio technology that transmits very short impulses (< 1 ns) across a very wide bandwidth (> 500 MHz), at very low power spectral density.

FCC definition: any signal with fractional bandwidth > 20% or absolute bandwidth > 500 MHz, transmitting at power below −41.3 dBm/MHz.

Key properties:

Property Value Frequency 3.1–10.6 GHz Bandwidth > 500 MHz Pulse duration 0.1–1 ns Range 1–10 m (typical), up to 30 m Data rate 100 Mbps–1 Gbps (short range) Power 0.5 mW (very low) Position accuracy ~10 cm

docs.title: 6.5.2 Why UWB is different
docs.text:
Traditional radio (narrowband): transmission occupies a narrow slice of spectrum around a carrier; the signal must be modulated onto that carrier (AM, FM, PSK, QAM).

UWB: transmits impulses — extremely short pulses that inherently span a wide bandwidth. No carrier in the traditional sense; the "carrier" is the pulse repetition rate.

Fourier transform intuition: a pulse of duration \(\tau\) has bandwidth \(\approx 1/\tau\). A 1 ns pulse = 1 GHz bandwidth. UWB exploits this directly.

The advantage: wide bandwidth → fine time resolution → excellent ranging (position estimation). UWB can measure distances to cm precision by measuring time of flight.

docs.title: 6.5.3 Two flavours of UWB
docs.text:
1. Impulse Radio UWB (IR-UWB) — the original approach.

  • Transmit Gaussian pulses or monocycle pulses.
  • Data rate limited by pulse repetition frequency (typically 100–1000 Mbps).
  • Used in research and short-range radar.

2. Multi-Band OFDM (MB-OFDM) — a competitor (WiMedia Alliance).

  • Divide the 3.1–10.6 GHz band into 14 sub-bands of 528 MHz.
  • Use OFDM within each sub-band.
  • Higher data rate (~1 Gbps), more complex.
  • WiMedia dissolved around 2010; MB-OFDM is now rarely used.

3. IEEE 802.15.4z (the current standard) — supports both.

  • HRP (High Rate Pulse) UWB — for high data rate.
  • LRP (Low Rate Pulse) UWB — for low-power, precise ranging.
  • Focus on secure ranging (STS — Scrambled Timestamp Sequence) to prevent relay attacks.

docs.title: 6.5.4 UWB applications
docs.text:
High-precision indoor positioning.

  • Apple AirTag, Samsung SmartTag+ — UWB provides cm-level direction and distance, much better than Bluetooth RSSI.
  • Smart home — precise location of people and objects.
  • Warehouse logistics — track items to cm.

Secure car access.

  • Digital car keys use UWB ranging to verify the key is actually nearby (defeats relay attacks that fool Bluetooth/RSSI systems).
  • Standardized by the Car Connectivity Consortium (CCC Digital Key 3.0).

Industrial positioning.

  • Robots, tools, people in factories, mines, warehouses.
  • 10 cm precision, better than Bluetooth or WiFi for industrial use.

Short-range high-rate data.

  • Wireless USB (defunct).
  • VR/AR cable replacement (in some products).
  • Wireless HDMI (few consumer products).

docs.title: Worked example 6.4 — UWB ranging precision
docs.text:
UWB range resolution: governed by the pulse bandwidth \(B\):

\[ \boxed{\;\Delta d \approx \frac{c}{2B}\;} \]

For \(B = 1\) GHz: \(\Delta d \approx 3 \times 10^8 / (2 \times 10^9) = \mathbf{15\ cm}\).

For \(B = 500\) MHz: \(\Delta d \approx \mathbf{30\ cm}\).

Time-of-flight measurement: at \(d = 10\) m, the round-trip time is:

\[ t = \frac{2d}{c} = \frac{20}{3 \times 10^8} \approx 67\ \text{ns}. \]

A 1 ns timing error gives \(c \cdot t/2 = 15\) cm distance error — hence nanosecond-class timing is required for cm-level ranging. Modern UWB chips achieve < 100 ps timing precision.

The lesson: UWB's ranging accuracy comes from the short pulse (wide bandwidth). No narrowband technology can match this.

docs.title: 6.6 LPWAN — Low-Power Wide Area Networks
docs.text: Between WiFi (short-range, high-rate) and cellular (long-range, high-rate, power-hungry) there's a gap: long-range, very low power, low data rate, battery- powered. That's LPWAN — the IoT connectivity solution.

docs.title: 6.6.1 The LPWAN landscape
docs.text:
Technology Frequency Data rate Range Battery life Standard LoRa Sub-GHz ISM (868/915 MHz) 0.3–37.5 kbps 2–15 km 10+ years LoRa Alliance (proprietary PHY) NB-IoT Licensed LTE (700/800/900 MHz) 26–127 kbps 1–10 km 5–10 years 3GPP (Release 13) Sigfox Sub-GHz ISM (868/902 MHz) 100 bps 3–50 km 10+ years Sigfox (proprietary) LTE-M Licensed LTE 1 Mbps 1–10 km 5–10 years 3GPP (eMTC) Weightless Sub-GHz ISM 0.1–100 kbps 2–5 km 5+ years Weightless SIG

Rule of thumb: LoRa for unlicensed global deployment, NB-IoT for licensed spectrum (tied to cellular operators), Sigfox for ultra-low data rate, LTE-M for higher data rate than NB-IoT.

docs.title: 6.6.2 LoRa — the PHY and MAC
docs.text:
LoRa = Long Range. The physical layer is proprietary (Semtech); the MAC layer (LoRaWAN) is open and managed by the LoRa Alliance.

Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) — the modulation technique.

  • Each symbol is a frequency chirp (up-sweep or down-sweep).
  • Spreading factor (SF) controls chirp rate: SF7–SF12.
  • Higher SF = longer range (more spreading) but lower data rate.
  • SF12 gives ~-137 dBm sensitivity (very long range), at 250 bps.
  • SF7 gives ~-123 dBm, at ~5.5 kbps.

The trade-off:

SF Data rate Sensitivity Range (km) 7 5.5 kbps -123 dBm 2 9 1.8 kbps -129 dBm 6 11 0.5 kbps -134 dBm 10 12 0.25 kbps -137 dBm 15

LoRaWAN classes:

  • Class A (baseline) — bidirectional; uplink scheduled by the device, two short downlink windows after each uplink. Lowest power.
  • Class B — beacon-synchronized; scheduled downlink receive windows. Moderate power, low downlink latency.
  • Class C — continuous receive (except when transmitting). Highest power, lowest latency. For mains-powered devices.

Network architecture:

  • End devices — sensors that transmit.
  • Gateways — receive on multiple channels/SFs; forward to network server via IP (WiFi, Ethernet, cellular).
  • Network server — de-duplicates, manages devices, routing.
  • Application server — user applications.

The key advantage: LoRa is license-free (ISM bands) — anyone can deploy a LoRaWAN network. Enterprises deploy private LoRa for building automation, agriculture, industrial sensors. National LoRaWAN networks exist in many countries (mobile operators, IoT providers).

docs.title: 6.6.3 NB-IoT — cellular for IoT
docs.text:
NB-IoT (Narrowband IoT) is the 3GPP IoT standard (Release 13, 2016).

Key parameters:

Parameter Value Bandwidth 180 kHz (single LTE resource block) Frequency Licensed LTE bands (in-band, guard-band, or standalone) Data rate 26 kbps UL, 127 kbps DL (multi-tone) Latency 1.6–10 s (longer than LTE) Battery life ~10 years (with PSM/eDRX) Range ~10–15 km (with repetitions, +20 dB over LTE)

Key features:

  • Coverage extension: up to 20 dB (100×) over LTE via repetitions — the same message sent 2048 times, combined at the base station. Range up to ~15 km.
  • Power Saving Mode (PSM): the device sleeps for up to 413 days, waking only to send data. This is the key to 10-year battery life.
  • eDRX (extended Discontinuous Reception): periodic listening, up to 2.9 hours between wake-ups.
  • Extended coverage but at the cost of latency — messages take seconds to be delivered.

Advantages over LoRa:

  • Licensed spectrum — no interference, guaranteed QoS.
  • Integrated with cellular — the operator handles the network, no gateway needed.
  • Higher data rate than LoRa (~100 kbps vs. ~5 kbps).
  • Global roaming via the operator's network.

Disadvantages:

  • Needs cellular coverage — rural areas without LTE coverage can't use NB-IoT.
  • Operator-controlled — you pay per device, per month.
  • Higher device cost than LoRa.

docs.title: Worked example 6.5 — IoT battery life for LoRa vs. NB-IoT
docs.text:
Scenario: A soil moisture sensor transmits 20 bytes every 30 minutes.

LoRa (SF12, 250 bps):

  • Transmit time: 20 bytes × 8 bits / 250 bps = 0.64 s per transmission.
  • Transmit current (typical): 40 mA.
  • Per transmission: 0.64 s × 40 mA = 25.6 mA·s = 0.0071 mAh.
  • Per day (48 transmissions): 48 × 0.0071 = 0.341 mAh/day.
  • Sleep current: 1 μA × 24 h = 0.024 mAh/day.
  • Daily total: ~0.365 mAh.
  • Battery (2000 mAh): ~5,480 days = ~15 years (theoretical).

NB-IoT:

  • Transmit time: 20 bytes × 8 bits / 26 kbps = 0.006 s per transmission (but with repetitions for coverage, effectively ~1 s).
  • Transmit current: 200 mA.
  • Per transmission: 1 s × 200 mA = 0.056 mAh.
  • Per day: 48 × 0.056 = 2.7 mAh/day.
  • Sleep (PSM): 5 μA × 24 h = 0.12 mAh/day.
  • Daily total: ~2.8 mAh/day.
  • Battery (5000 mAh, typical for NB-IoT devices): ~1,800 days = ~5 years (theoretical).

Realistic: LoRa ~7–10 years, NB-IoT ~3–5 years — battery life is limited by sleep current and self-discharge, not by transmissions.

The takeaway: LoRa is more power-efficient for very low-rate, sparse data. NB-IoT is worth the higher power for higher data rate and licensed spectrum.

docs.title: 6.7.1 5G's three use cases
docs.text:
The ITU defined IMT-2020 (5G) around three broad use cases:

1. eMBB — enhanced Mobile Broadband.

  • Peak rate: 20 Gbps.
  • User-experienced rate: 100 Mbps–1 Gbps.
  • Use: 4K/8K video, AR/VR, cloud gaming.
  • Characteristics: high throughput, moderate latency (~4 ms).

2. URLLC — Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication.

  • Latency: 1 ms (air interface).
  • Reliability: 99.999% (five nines).
  • Use: industrial automation, remote surgery, autonomous driving, smart grid.
  • Characteristics: latency-critical, high reliability, moderate data rate.

3. mMTC — massive Machine-Type Communication.

  • Density: 1 million devices per km².
  • Battery: 10+ years.
  • Use: IoT sensors, smart city, agriculture, asset tracking.
  • Characteristics: high density, low data rate, low power.

The 5G triangle: the three use cases pull in different directions. eMBB wants high rate; URLLC wants low latency; mMTC wants high density and low power. 5G NR is designed to serve all three, often on the same network via network slicing.

docs.title: 6.7.2 5G NR — the new radio
docs.text:
5G NR (New Radio) is the 3GPP air interface introduced in Release 15 (2018). It's a new PHY, not an evolution of LTE.

Key PHY parameters:

Aspect LTE 5G NR Frequency < 6 GHz < 6 GHz (FR1) + mmWave 24–52 GHz (FR2) Subcarrier spacing 15 kHz fixed 15, 30, 60, 120, 240 kHz (scalable) Channel bandwidth up to 20 MHz up to 100 MHz (FR1), 400 MHz (FR2) MIMO up to 8×8 up to 64×64 (FR1), 256 antennas (FR2 massive MIMO) Modulation up to 256-QAM up to 1024-QAM Latency (user plane) ~10 ms ~1 ms Peak DL 3 Gbps (LTE-A Pro) 20 Gbps Spectral efficiency ~6 bps/Hz (LTE-A) ~30 bps/Hz (5G)

Scalable numerology — the key 5G innovation. Unlike LTE's fixed 15 kHz subcarrier spacing, 5G uses different subcarrier spacings for different scenarios:

  • 15 kHz — for wide-area coverage (like LTE).
  • 30 kHz — for urban (typical 5G).
  • 60 kHz — for low-latency (URLLC).
  • 120/240 kHz — for mmWave (high throughput).

Short subcarriers → longer symbols → higher throughput. Longer subcarriers → shorter symbols → lower latency. Numerologies are chosen per application.

Massive MIMO. 5G deploys 64–256 antenna elements at the base station:

  • Beamforming gain: ~18 dB (64 elements) to 24 dB (256 elements).
  • Multi-user MIMO: up to 16 UEs simultaneously.
  • 3D beamforming: both horizontal and vertical steering.

mmWave. FR2 (24–52 GHz) provides 400 MHz channels — 8× wider than sub-6 GHz. This is what enables 20 Gbps peak rate. But mmWave has:

  • High path loss (Chapter 1 worked example 1.1: ~30 dB more than 2 GHz).
  • Blockage (rain, hands, walls).
  • Short range (100–300 m per cell).
  • Requires dense small-cell deployment.

docs.title: 6.7.3 5G Core (5GC) — service-based architecture
docs.text:
The 5G core network is a fundamental redesign from LTE's EPC. Instead of network elements connected by point-to-point interfaces, 5GC uses network functions (NFs) connected by service-based interfaces (SBI) — essentially a microservices architecture.

Key NFs:

Function Role AMF (Access & Mobility) Registration, mobility, connection management (control plane) SMF (Session Management) PDU session setup, IP address, QoS (control plane) UPF (User Plane Function) Packet routing, QoS enforcement, anchor point AUSF (Authentication) 5G authentication UDM (Unified Data Mgmt) Subscriber data, authentication vectors (like HSS) PCF (Policy Control) QoS policy, charging rules NSSF (Network Slicing Selection) Selects the right network slice NRF (NF Repository) Service discovery (NFs find each other) NEF (Network Exposure) APIs for third parties to use 5G capabilities AF (Application Function) Application server (owns the QoS request)

Service-based interface (SBI):

  • All NFs communicate via HTTP/2 + JSON on the SBI.
  • Any NF can expose services that others consume.
  • NRF provides service discovery (like DNS for NFs).

The advantage: flexible, cloud-native — 5GC can run on containers in a data center, orchestrated by Kubernetes, updated without touching the radio.

docs.title: 6.7.4 Network slicing
docs.text:
Network slicing is 5G's flagship feature — the ability to create virtual, isolated networks on the same physical infrastructure, each with its own resources, QoS, and topology.

Each slice has:

  • Its own QoS and KPIs (latency, throughput, reliability).
  • Its own network functions (or shared, isolated by slice).
  • Its own resource allocation (spectrum, compute, backhaul).
  • Its own management and orchestration.

Example slices:

  • eMBB slice — high throughput, moderate latency, for consumer broadband.
  • URLLC slice — 1 ms latency, 99.999% reliability, for industrial control.
  • mMTC slice — massive device count, low power, for IoT sensors.
  • V2X slice — vehicle-to-everything, low latency, high reliability.

The NSSF (Network Slice Selection Function) selects the right slice for each UE based on subscription, requested service, and network policy.

Why slicing matters: before 5G, an operator had one network serving all traffic. An industrial customer wanting guaranteed 1 ms latency competed with consumers streaming video. Slicing lets the operator sell dedicated capacity to an enterprise with strict QoS, without degrading the consumer network — a new business model.

docs.title: 6.7.5 Edge computing and 5G
docs.text:
Edge computing — moving compute resources close to the user, at cell towers or local data centers, instead of centralized cloud.

Why 5G needs it:

  • URLLC latency: 1 ms air-interface latency is useless if the application server is 1,000 km away (adds 20–40 ms round-trip). Multi-access edge computing (MEC) puts the server at the base station or local edge.

Use cases:

  • AR/VR — sub-20 ms end-to-end, must be local.
  • Industrial automation — real-time control loops, local.
  • Autonomous vehicles — safety-critical, local.
  • Cloud gaming — low-latency, local rendering.

5G + MEC = network + compute at the edge = platform for real-time applications.

docs.title: 6.7.6 IoT connectivity in 5G
docs.text:
mMTC in 5G is delivered by three paths:

  1. NB-IoT and LTE-M — the same LPWAN standards, integrated into the 5G core (they become 5G-connected devices via dual-mode radios).
  2. 5G NR RedCap (Reduced Capability) — a lighter 5G NR variant for IoT devices that need more than NB-IoT but not full 5G (wearables, cameras, sensors with moderate data rate).
  3. 5G NR for IoT — for the rare IoT use case that needs URLLC or eMBB.

Network slicing lets operators create a dedicated mMTC slice with massive device density and low power, without impacting eMBB users.

The 5G IoT ecosystem combines:

  • Massive MIMO + beamforming for wide coverage.
  • mmWave small cells for dense IoT deployment.
  • Edge computing for real-time processing.
  • NB-IoT / LTE-M / RedCap for device-side connectivity.
  • Network slicing for isolation and QoS.

docs.title: Worked example 6.6 — network slicing for smart factory
docs.text:
Scenario: A smart factory needs:

  • 500 industrial sensors sending 100 bytes every 1 s. mMTC slice.
  • 20 AGVs (automated guided vehicles) with 1 ms latency control loops. URLLC slice.
  • 10 HD cameras streaming 4K video for quality inspection. eMBB slice.
  • AR glasses for technicians, remote expert assistance. eMBB + URLLC mix.

Without network slicing: one shared network. Under congestion, AGV control latency spikes → safety risk.

With slicing:

  • mMTC slice: 500 sensors × 100 bytes/s = 50 kbps. Trivial. Reserve 1 MHz.
  • URLLC slice: 20 AGVs × 100 kbps with 1 ms latency. Reserve dedicated RBs + UPF at factory edge. 5 MHz.
  • eMBB slice: 10 cameras × 20 Mbps = 200 Mbps. 20 MHz + MU-MIMO.
  • AR/VR slice: mix of eMBB + URLLC. 10 MHz.

Total: 36 MHz reserved, each slice isolated. AGV control latency guaranteed < 1 ms even during video peak traffic. Business model: factory pays for QoS guaranteed slices.

docs.title: 6.8 Choosing the right connectivity
docs.text:
For any given IoT application, choosing between WPAN / WLAN / LPWAN / cellular depends on four variables:

Parameter WPAN WLAN LPWAN Cellular Range 10–100 m 30–100 m 2–15 km 1–30 km Data rate 0.1–3 Mbps 100 Mbps–30 Gbps 0.1–127 kbps 100 Mbps–20 Gbps Power Very low High Very low High (except NB-IoT) Cost Low Moderate Low High (spectrum)

Decision flowchart:

Start
  │
  ├─ Data rate > 1 Mbps?
  │   ├─ Yes → Local → WiFi
  │   │         → Mobile → 4G/5G
  │   └─ No → continue
  │
  ├─ Range > 100 m?
  │   ├─ Yes → Licensed spectrum?
  │   │         ├─ Yes → NB-IoT / LTE-M
  │   │         └─ No  → LoRa / Sigfox
  │   └─ No → continue
  │
  ├─ Battery-powered & low duty cycle?
  │   ├─ Yes → BLE / ZigBee / LoRa
  │   └─ No  → WiFi / Bluetooth Classic
  │
  └─ Latency-critical?
      ├─ Yes → Cellular (4G/5G)
      └─ No  → LPWAN

docs.title: Worked example 6.7 — choosing connectivity
docs.text:
Application: An agricultural sensor measuring soil moisture, sending 50 bytes every hour, powered by a small solar panel with battery backup.

Requirements: - Data rate: 50 bytes/hour = 0.11 bps. Very low. - Range: field is 1 km wide; nearest road/power 5 km. Long range. - Power: solar/battery — should last years. Very low power. - Cost: many devices (100 sensors), so low per-device cost.

Options:

Option Fit WiFi ❌ Range too short (100 m) Bluetooth ❌ Range too short (100 m) ZigBee ❌ Range too short (100 m), no backhaul LoRa ✅ Range 10+ km, low power, low cost NB-IoT ✅ Range 10 km (if coverage), low power, needs cellular subscription Sigfox ✅ Range 30+ km, ultra-low power, ultra-low data rate

Best fit: LoRaWAN — deploy a private LoRaWAN gateway at the farmhouse (powered by solar), sensors use LoRa. No monthly cellular fees, cm-level position (optional), 5+ year battery life on AA cells. If cellular coverage is available and reliable, NB-IoT also works but with monthly subscription cost.

Why not 5G mMTC? Overkill — the data rate, latency, and density are far below what 5G offers; the cost is 10× higher.

docs.title: 6.9 Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. NGN = packet-based, all-IP, multi-service network. It evolved from voice-over-IP convergence (2000s) to fixed-mobile convergence (2010s) to IoT convergence (2020s).
  2. Bluetooth Classic — for continuous data (audio, files). Piconet topology, frequency hopping, 2–3 Mbps. BLE — for bursty sensor data; 40 channels, 3 ms connection, < 1 μA sleep, up to 400 m range (BT 5.0).
  3. ZigBee (IEEE 802.15.4) — mesh network for sensor networks. 250 kbps, AODV routing, 65,000+ nodes, < 1 μA sleep. Dominant in home and industrial automation.
  4. WiFi (802.11) — the local wireless standard. WiFi 6 (802.11ax) brings OFDMA and MU-MIMO uplink for high-density environments. WiFi 7 (802.11be) adds 320 MHz channels, 4096-QAM, and Multi-Link Operation. The 6 GHz band provides clean spectrum for WiFi 6E/7.
  5. UWB — impulse radio using very short pulses (sub-ns) across > 500 MHz bandwidth. Enables ~10 cm precision positioning, used in AirTags, car keys, warehouse tracking.
  6. LPWAN — low-power wide-area networks for IoT. LoRa (unlicensed, chirp spread spectrum, 2–15 km), NB-IoT (licensed, cellular, 10 km, 10-year battery), Sigfox (ultra-low rate, very long range).
  7. 5G NR — new PHY with scalable numerology (15–240 kHz), massive MIMO (64–256 antennas), mmWave bands, 1 ms latency, 20 Gbps peak. FR1 (Sub-6) and FR2 (mmWave) serve different scenarios.
  8. 5G Core (5GC) — service-based architecture with microservices (AMF, SMF, UPF, etc.) communicating via HTTP/2. Cloud-native, orchestrated by Kubernetes.
  9. Network slicing — virtual isolated networks on one physical infrastructure, each with its own QoS and topology. Enables URLLC/eMBB/mMTC coexistence and new business models.
  10. Edge computing (MEC) — brings compute close to the user, essential for URLLC. 5G + MEC is the platform for real-time applications.
  11. IoT connectivity — WPAN (BLE, ZigBee) for local, WLAN (WiFi) for local high-rate, LPWAN (LoRa, NB-IoT) for wide-area low-power, cellular (4G/5G) for high-rate with QoS. Choose based on range, rate, power, and cost.

docs.title: A. Multiple choice
docs.text:
1. Bluetooth Classic operates in which band? (a) 900 MHz (b) 2.4 GHz ISM (c) 5 GHz (d) 60 GHz

  2. The typical range of BLE (Class 2) is: (a) 1 m (b) 10 m (c) 100 m (d) 1 km

  3. ZigBee is based on which IEEE standard? (a) 802.11 (b) 802.15.1 (c) 802.15.4 (d) 802.16

  4. ZigBee's data rate is: (a) 10 kbps (b) 250 kbps (c) 1 Mbps (d) 54 Mbps

  5. WiFi 6 (802.11ax) introduced: (a) OFDM (b) MIMO (c) OFDMA (d) mmWave

  6. WiFi 6E operates in which new band? (a) 2.4 GHz (b) 5 GHz (c) 6 GHz (d) 60 GHz

  7. UWB's main advantage over other technologies is: (a) High data rate (b) Long range (c) Precision positioning (d) Low cost

  8. LoRa uses which modulation technique? (a) OFDM (b) QPSK (c) Chirp Spread Spectrum (d) 8-PSK

  9. NB-IoT's key feature for long battery life is: (a) High data rate (b) PSM (c) MIMO (d) OFDMA

  10. 5G's three use cases are: (a) eMBB, URLLC, mMTC (b) LTE, WiFi, Bluetooth (c) AM, FM, PM (d) FDMA, TDMA, CDMA

  11. 5G NR's scalable numerology allows: (a) Multiple bands (b) Different subcarrier spacings (c) Multiple MIMO orders (d) Coexistence with LTE

  12. Network slicing enables: (a) Higher peak rate (b) Virtual isolated networks with distinct QoS (c) Lower latency (d) Higher density

docs.title: B. Fill in the blank
docs.text:
1. Bluetooth Classic's topology is a ____, with 1 master and up to 7 slaves.
  2. BLE has ____ channels of 2 MHz each.
  3. ZigBee's routing protocol is ____.
  4. WiFi 6 (802.11ax) uses ____ for multi-user scheduling.
  5. WiFi 6E operates in the ____ GHz band.
  6. UWB's pulse bandwidth must exceed ____ MHz (FCC definition).
  7. LoRa's ____ parameter controls the range/data-rate trade-off.
  8. NB-IoT provides up to ____ dB coverage extension via repetitions.
  9. 5G's ____ (three letters) is the ultra-low-latency use case.
  10. 5G Core (5GC) uses ____ (three letters) for service discovery.

docs.title: C. Define / explain
docs.text:
1. What is an NGN? Describe its evolution through the three stages (all-IP, FMC, IoT).
  2. Describe Bluetooth Classic vs. BLE. When would you use each?
  3. Explain ZigBee's mesh topology and AODV routing. Why is mesh important for sensor networks?
  4. Compare WiFi 5, WiFi 6, and WiFi 7. What are the main improvements?
  5. Explain UWB's operating principle. Why does wide bandwidth give high precision?
  6. Describe the three LPWAN technologies (LoRa, NB-IoT, Sigfox). When would you choose each?
  7. Explain LoRa's spreading factor trade-off. Why does higher SF give longer range but lower data rate?
  8. Describe the three 5G use cases (eMBB, URLLC, mMTC). Give one application for each.
  9. Explain 5G NR's scalable numerology. Why is it different from LTE's fixed 15 kHz?
  10. What is network slicing? How does it enable new business models?
  11. How does edge computing (MEC) complement 5G? Which use cases need it most?
  12. A smart city has 100,000 sensors deployed over 50 km². Choose the connectivity strategy — WPAN, WLAN, LPWAN, or cellular — and justify.

docs.title: 6.11 Answer key
docs.text:
A. Multiple choice
  1. (b) — 2.4 GHz ISM.
  2. (c) — ~10 m (Class 2), up to 100 m in Class 1, up to 400 m in BT 5.0.
  3. (c) — 802.15.4.
  4. (b) — 250 kbps.
  5. (c) — OFDMA.
  6. (c) — 6 GHz.
  7. (c) — precision positioning.
  8. (c) — Chirp Spread Spectrum.
  9. (b) — PSM (Power Saving Mode).
  10. (a) — eMBB, URLLC, mMTC.
  11. (b) — different subcarrier spacings.
  12. (b) — virtual isolated networks with distinct QoS.
B. Fill in the blank
  1. piconet.
  2. 40.
  3. AODV (Ad hoc On-demand Distance Vector).
  4. OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access).
  5. 6 (5.925–7.125).
  6. 500.
  7. spreading factor (SF7–SF12).
  8. 20.
  9. URLLC.
  10. NRF.
C. Define / explain — model answers
  1. NGN: a packet-based, all-IP network providing telecommunication services (voice, data, video) with QoS, decoupled from the underlying transport. Three stages: (i) all-IP convergence (2000s) — replacing PSTN with VoIP, circuit-switched cores with IP; (ii) fixed-mobile convergence (2010s) — unify fixed and mobile under one core, VoWiFi, LTE-WiFi; (iii) IoT convergence (2020s) — LPWAN, 5G mMTC, edge computing, network slicing.
  2. Bluetooth Classic: continuous data, piconet topology, 2–3 Mbps, higher power. BLE: bursty sensor data, 40 channels of 2 MHz, 3 ms connection, < 1 μA sleep, up to 400 m. Use: Classic for headphones, audio streaming, file transfer; BLE for wearables, fitness trackers, battery-powered sensors.
  3. ZigBee mesh: any router can forward traffic for any other. AODV: on-demand routing — source broadcasts Route Request (RREQ), destination replies with Route Reply (RREP), routers cache routes for future use. Why mesh: extends range beyond individual node range (multi-hop), improves reliability (redundant paths), and handles node failures gracefully. For sensor networks that can't afford fiber backhaul to every node, mesh is essential.
  4. WiFi 5 (802.11ac): 5 GHz, 80/160 MHz, MU-MIMO DL, 256-QAM. WiFi 6 (802.11ax): adds OFDMA, MU-MIMO UL, 1024-QAM, TWT (Target Wake Time for IoT power), 4× longer OFDM symbol. Better at high density. WiFi 7 (802.11be): 320 MHz channels, 4096-QAM, Multi-Link Operation (MLO — simultaneous transmission on 2.4, 5, 6 GHz), 16×16 MIMO.
  5. UWB: transmits very short pulses (sub-ns) which inherently span > 500 MHz bandwidth. High precision: Fourier transform — pulse of duration τ has bandwidth ≈ 1/τ. Wide bandwidth gives fine time resolution (τ ~ ns), and time of flight directly gives distance: d = c·t/2. So cm-precision ranging is possible, unlike narrowband RSSI (which has ~1 m precision).
  6. LoRa: unlicensed ISM, Chirp Spread Spectrum, 2–15 km, 0.3–37.5 kbps, private or national network. Best for enterprise IoT, agriculture, building automation, remote sensing. NB-IoT: licensed LTE, 180 kHz bandwidth, 1–10 km, ~100 kbps, uses PSM for 10-year battery. Best for operator-managed IoT (smart meters, tracking). Sigfox: proprietary, ultra-low data rate (100 bps), very long range (up to 50 km), ultra-low power. Best for asset tracking, simple telemetry with very infrequent updates.
  7. LoRa SF trade-off: SF7–SF12 correspond to 2^7 to 2^12 chips per symbol. Higher SF: longer symbol time → more signal energy per bit → better sensitivity (−137 dBm for SF12) → longer range (up to 15 km). But: lower data rate (250 bps for SF12 vs. 5.5 kbps for SF7) → longer transmission time → higher energy per transmission. Trade-off: range vs. data rate vs. battery life.
  8. eMBB: enhanced Mobile Broadband — high rate (100 Mbps–1 Gbps user), for 4K/8K video, AR/VR, cloud gaming. URLLC: Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication — 1 ms latency, 99.999% reliability, for industrial automation, remote surgery, autonomous driving. mMTC: massive Machine-Type Communication — 1M devices/km², low power, for IoT sensors, smart city, agriculture.
  9. 5G scalable numerology: LTE uses fixed 15 kHz subcarrier spacing. 5G NR supports 15, 30, 60, 120, 240 kHz. Why: different scenarios need different trade-offs. Short subcarriers (15 kHz) → long symbol duration → robust for high Doppler / wide-area. Long subcarriers (120/240 kHz) → short symbol duration → low latency (for URLLC) but need higher SNR. Deployments choose numerology per scenario — 15 kHz for macro coverage, 30 kHz for urban 5G, 60/120 kHz for mmWave.
  10. Network slicing: ability to create multiple virtual isolated networks on the same physical infrastructure, each with its own QoS, topology, resources, and management. New business models: operator can sell dedicated URLLC slices to industrial customers with guaranteed latency, eMBB slices to consumers, mMTC slices for IoT — each priced for its SLA. Before slicing, all traffic shared one network; the industrial customer's 1 ms latency was at the mercy of consumers streaming video. Slicing provides QoS isolation as a product.
  11. MEC (Multi-access Edge Computing): compute resources placed at cell towers / local data centers, close to the user. Complements 5G: 5G's 1 ms air-interface latency is useless if the application server is 1000 km away (adds 20+ ms). MEC brings the server to the edge → full end-to-end latency in 5–10 ms. Use cases: AR/VR (sub-20 ms), industrial control loops (1 ms), autonomous vehicles (safety-critical), cloud gaming (low-latency rendering), real-time video analytics.
  12. Smart city, 100,000 sensors over 50 km²: 2,000 devices/km². LoRa or NB-IoT are the only viable options. WiFi covers 100 m per AP, would need 5,000 APs and power for each — infeasible. Cellular works but 100,000 subscriptions are expensive. LoRaWAN: 20 gateways cover 50 km² (2.5 km radius each with SF12), private network, low per-device cost, 10-year battery. NB-IoT: if cellular coverage exists and 5–10 year battery acceptable, operator-managed is simpler. Recommendation: LoRa for maximum flexibility, NB-IoT for integration with city's cellular infrastructure.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Bluetooth: Bluetooth SIG's Core Specification 5.4 — free PDF from bluetooth.com. Also Bluetooth Low Energy: The Developer's Handbook by Robin Heydon (Prentice Hall, 2012).
