docs.text: ## ECEG-6412  ### Chapter 6 — Next Generation Networks (NGN)  MSc in Communication Engineering · Year 1, Semester I  Dr. Tesfamichael Gebregziabher  ---  ## Outline  <div class="fragment">  **Part 1 — What is an NGN?**  - From all-IP convergence to IoT - The connectivity landscape  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 2 — Short-range wireless (WPAN)**  - Bluetooth Classic and BLE - ZigBee mesh for sensors - UWB for precision ranging  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 3 — Local wireless (WLAN)**  - WiFi 4/5/6/7 — the OFDMA evolution - 6 GHz band, security  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 4 — Long-range low-power (LPWAN)**  - LoRa, NB-IoT, Sigfox - Battery life and range  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 5 — 5G and IoT**  - The three use cases - 5G NR PHY, 5G Core, network slicing, MEC  </div>  ---  ## Learning outcomes  <div class="fragment">  **LO1 — Explain what an NGN is**  Packet-based, all-IP, multi-service. Evolution from voice convergence to IoT.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO2 — Compare WPAN technologies**  Bluetooth Classic vs. BLE vs. ZigBee — data rate, power, topology.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO3 — Select WiFi generations**  WiFi 4/5/6/7 — the OFDMA step change, 6 GHz band.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO4 — Explain UWB and LPWAN**  UWB's cm-precision; LoRa vs. NB-IoT vs. Sigfox.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO5 — Describe 5G and IoT convergence**  eMBB, URLLC, mMTC; 5GC; network slicing; MEC.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO6 — Choose the right connectivity**  For any IoT application — by range, rate, power, cost.  </div>  ---  ## §6.1 — What is an NGN?  <div class="fragment">  **NGN (Next Generation Network)** — the ITU-T definition (2004):  *A packet-based network able to provide telecommunication services using multiple broadband, QoS-enabled transport technologies, in which service functions are independent of transport technologies.*  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Key principles:**  - Packet-based (all IP, no circuit switching) - Service / transport separation - QoS-enabled - Any-access (fixed + mobile + wireless) - Multi-service (voice, data, video, IoT)  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The NGN concept broadened over 20 years** — from "voice over IP" to "everything over IP."  </div>  ---  ## The three stages of NGN evolution  <div class="fragment">  **Stage 1 (2000–2010) — All-IP convergence**  - Replace PSTN with VoIP - Replace 2G/3G circuit cores with IP - IMS for voice services  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Stage 2 (2010–2020) — Fixed-mobile convergence (FMC)**  - Unified core for fixed and mobile (EPC) - VoWiFi, LTE-WiFi aggregation - 5G NSA/SA  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Stage 3 (2020s) — IoT convergence**  - Billions of devices - LPWAN + WiFi + 5G + edge computing - Network slicing, MEC, ML for network management  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Each stage adds a new connectivity class** — NGN is about making them all work together.  </div>  ---  ## The connectivity landscape  | Category | Range | Standard | Peak rate | Power | |---|---|---|:---:|:---:| | **WPAN** | 10–100 m | Bluetooth, ZigBee, UWB | 0.1–1 Gbps | Very low | | **WLAN** | 30–100 m | WiFi 4/5/6/7 | 100 Mbps–30 Gbps | High | | **WMAN** | 1–50 km | WiMAX, 5G FWA | 70 Mbps–1 Gbps | High | | **WWAN** | 1–30 km | 4G LTE, 5G NR | 100 Mbps–20 Gbps | High | | **LPWAN** | 2–15 km | LoRa, NB-IoT, Sigfox | 0.1–127 kbps | Extremely low | | **Satellite** | global | GEO, LEO | 1–200 Mbps | — |  <div class="fragment">  **Each row is a different trade-off** between range, rate, and power. **No single technology wins everywhere.**  </div>  ---  ## §6.2 — Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR)  <div class="fragment">  **Bluetooth Classic** — designed as a **cable replacement** for audio, peripherals, files.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Key parameters:**  | Parameter | Value | |---|---| | Frequency | **2.4 GHz ISM** | | Channel spacing | 1 MHz, **79 channels** | | Modulation | GFSK (BR), π/4-DQPSK, 8-DPSK (EDR) | | Data rate | 1–3 Mbps | | Range | Class 1: 100 m, Class 2: 10 m | | Topology | **Piconet** (1 master + 7 slaves) |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The piconet:** master controls hopping sequence, slot timing, and access. Up to **7 active slaves**, more can be **parked**.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Frequency hopping: 1600 hops/s.** Resist interference from WiFi, ZigBee, microwaves — a narrowband interferer affects only 1/79 of slots.  </div>  ---  ## BLE — the IoT version  <div class="fragment">  **BLE (Bluetooth Smart)** — introduced in Bluetooth 4.0 (2010), fundamentally different radio optimized for IoT.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  | Aspect | Bluetooth Classic | BLE | |---|---|---| | Target use | Continuous data | Bursty sensor data | | Channels | 79 × 1 MHz | **40 × 2 MHz** | | Connection setup | ~seconds | **~3 ms** | | Peak TX current | 30–40 mA | **~10 mA** | | Standby | 100 μA–1 mA | **< 1 μA** | | Data rate | 1–3 Mbps | 1–2 Mbps (BT 5.0) | | Range | 10–100 m | 10–400 m (BT 5.0) |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **BLE advertising:** peripherals broadcast advertisement packets; centrals scan or connect. **Advertising interval** from 20 ms to 10.24 s.  Lower interval = less power but higher latency.  </div>  ---  ## BLE battery life  <div class="fragment">  **Scenario:** Temperature sensor sends 10-byte reading every 10 s. TX 2 ms at 10 mA. Sleep 5 μA.  **Per transmission:** 2 ms × 10 mA = 0.00556 mAh.  **Per interval (10 s):** ~0.00557 mAh.  **Per hour:** 360 × 0.00557 = 2.0 mAh/h.  **Battery (1000 mAh coin cell):** ~500 hours ≈ **21 days**.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Optimization — 30 s interval + 5 mA TX:**  Per hour: 120 × 0.00278 = 0.334 mAh/h → **~3000 hours ≈ 125 days** (~4 months).  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Realistic for IoT:** with event-driven (not periodic) transmission, **1–3 years** on a coin cell.  Longer life requires LPWAN (ZigBee, LoRa, NB-IoT).  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — Bluetooth Classic vs. BLE  <div class="quiz" data-question="ble-choice">   <p class="quiz-question">Which application is best served by <strong>Bluetooth Classic</strong> (not BLE)?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">Wireless headphones streaming audio continuously</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">A temperature sensor sending 10 bytes every minute</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">A fitness tracker syncing step counts to a phone</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">A smart watch heart-rate monitor</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The rule.** Continuous high-rate data (audio, file transfer) → **Classic**. Bursty, power-critical (sensors, wearables) → **BLE**. Classic provides ~2 Mbps continuous; BLE provides connection in 3 ms with < 1 μA standby.  </div>  ---  ## §6.3 — ZigBee — the mesh sensor network  <div class="fragment">  **ZigBee** (IEEE 802.15.4) — low-power, low-data-rate, **mesh-capable** WPAN designed for sensor networks.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Key parameters:**  | Parameter | Value | |---|---| | Frequency | 2.4 GHz (16 channels), 868/915 MHz | | Modulation | OQPSK | | Data rate | **250 kbps** (2.4 GHz) | | Range | 10–100 m per hop | | Topology | **Star, tree, or mesh** | | Network capacity | **65,000+ nodes** | | Sleep current | < 1 μA |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Three device types:** - **Coordinator** — forms the network (exactly one) - **Router** — forwards traffic, participates in mesh - **End Device** — sensor/actuator; sleeps most of the time  </div>  ---  ## ZigBee mesh and AODV routing  <div class="fragment">  **Mesh topology:** any router can forward for any other. Extends range beyond individual node coverage.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **AODV (Ad hoc On-demand Distance Vector):**  **1.** Source broadcasts **Route Request (RREQ)** — "who has the destination?"  **2.** Intermediate routers forward RREQ, adding their address.  **3.** Destination sends **Route Reply (RREP)** tracing the reverse path.  **4.** Routers cache the route for future use.  **5.** **Route Error (RERR)** propagates back if a link breaks; source sends new RREQ.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **On-demand** — no proactive routing table. Saves energy for mostly-idle sensor networks.  </div>  ---  ## ZigBee vs. BLE  | Aspect | ZigBee | BLE | |---|---|---| | Topology | **Mesh** | Star (BLE Mesh is newer) | | Data rate | 250 kbps | 1–2 Mbps | | Range per hop | 10–100 m | 10–100 m | | Network size | 65,000+ | ~10–20 typical | | Sleep current | < 1 μA | < 1 μA | | Latency | 15–30 ms | 3 ms | | **Best for** | **Sensor networks** | **Phone-tethered IoT** |  <div class="fragment">  **Rule of thumb:** ZigBee when many devices need mesh coverage; BLE when the device talks to a phone or the network is small.  </div>  ---  ## §6.4 — WiFi — the local wireless standard  <div class="fragment">  WiFi (IEEE 802.11) dominates local wireless — home, office, public hotspot.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The naming:** IEEE uses 802.11ac; WiFi Alliance introduced **WiFi 4, 5, 6, 7** for consumers.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  | Standard | Year | Brand | Band | Peak | |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:| | 802.11n | 2009 | **WiFi 4** | 2.4/5 | 600 Mbps | | 802.11ac | 2013 | **WiFi 5** | 5 | 6.9 Gbps | | 802.11ax | 2019 | **WiFi 6** | 2.4/5 | 9.6 Gbps | | 802.11be | 2024 | **WiFi 7** | 2.4/5/6 | 46 Gbps |  </div>  ---  ## WiFi 6 — the OFDMA step change  <div class="fragment">  **WiFi 6** (802.11ax) — the biggest change since WiFi 4:  **OFDMA** — the AP allocates **resource units (RUs)** to multiple users simultaneously.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **WiFi 5 vs. WiFi 6:**  - **WiFi 5:** one user per transmission (MU-MIMO limited to 4 DL streams) - **WiFi 6:** ~30 RUs per 80 MHz channel → **30 simultaneous users** per transmission  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why it matters:** WiFi 6's benefit is **capacity in dense environments**, not peak rate per user. A stadium or airport full of people no longer collapses the network.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **WiFi 6 also adds:** MU-MIMO uplink, 1024-QAM, TWT (Target Wake Time for IoT power saving), 4× longer OFDM symbol (fewer guard bands).  </div>  ---  ## WiFi 6E and WiFi 7  <div class="fragment">  **WiFi 6E** — WiFi 6 extended to the **6 GHz band** (5.925–7.125 GHz).  - **59 × 20 MHz channels**, or 14 × 160 MHz. - **No legacy devices** — every WiFi 6E device supports 6 GHz. - Clean spectrum → much better performance in dense environments.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **WiFi 7** (802.11be) — the next leap:  - **320 MHz channels** (in 6 GHz) - **4096-QAM** (12 bits/symbol) - **Multi-Link Operation (MLO)** — simultaneous transmission on 2.4 + 5 + 6 GHz - **16×16 MIMO**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Peak:** ~46 Gbps theoretical.  **Practical:** MLO aggregation across bands reaches ~20 Gbps — enough for 8K VR, heavy AR.  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — WiFi 6's key innovation  <div class="quiz" data-question="wifi6">   <p class="quiz-question">What is WiFi 6's (802.11ax) <strong>key PHY innovation</strong> for dense environments?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Higher-order QAM (1024-QAM)</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">OFDMA — multiple users served simultaneously via resource units</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">New 6 GHz band</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Wider 160 MHz channels</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why.** WiFi 5 and earlier served **one user per transmission** (OFDM, even with MU-MIMO limited to 4 streams). WiFi 6's OFDMA splits a channel into **resource units** — each serving a different user simultaneously. This doesn't increase peak rate per user, but it **multiplies capacity** in crowded scenarios.  </div>  ---  ## §6.5 — UWB — precision positioning  <div class="fragment">  **Ultra-Wideband (UWB)** — transmits **very short pulses** (< 1 ns) across a **wide bandwidth** (> 500 MHz), at very low power.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **FCC definition:** fractional bandwidth > 20% or absolute bandwidth > 500 MHz, at power below −41.3 dBm/MHz.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why wide bandwidth matters:** a pulse of duration $\tau$ has bandwidth $\approx 1/\tau$. A 1 ns pulse = **1 GHz bandwidth**.  Fourier transform gives the physics for free.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Key property — precise ranging:**  $$ \boxed{\;\Delta d \approx \frac{c}{2B}\;} $$  For $B = 1$ GHz: $\Delta d \approx$ **15 cm**.  For $B = 500$ MHz: **30 cm**.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Timing precision** — a 100 ps timing error → 1.5 cm distance error. Modern UWB chips achieve < 100 ps.  </div>  ---  ## UWB applications  <div class="fragment">  **High-precision indoor positioning:**  - **Apple AirTag, Samsung SmartTag+** — cm-level direction and distance, far better than Bluetooth RSSI (~1 m precision). - **Smart home** — precise location of people and objects. - **Warehouse logistics** — track items to cm.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Secure car access:**  - Digital car keys use UWB ranging to verify the key is actually nearby. - **Defeats relay attacks** — Bluetooth RSSI can be fooled by a remote relay; UWB's time-of-flight cannot.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Industrial positioning:**  - Robots, tools, people in factories, mines, warehouses. - 10 cm precision — better than any narrowband system.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Standard:** IEEE 802.15.4z — supports **HRP** (high rate) and **LRP** (low rate) UWB, with **secure ranging** (STS — scrambled timestamp sequence).  </div>  ---  ## §6.6 — LPWAN — long-range, low-power IoT  <div class="fragment">  **The gap:** between WiFi (short-range, high-rate) and cellular (long-range, high-rate, power-hungry) there's an unfilled niche:  **Long-range, very low power, low data rate, battery-powered.**  That's **LPWAN** — Low-Power Wide-Area Network.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Three main technologies:**  | Tech | Frequency | Rate | Range | Battery | |---|---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | **LoRa** | Sub-GHz ISM | 0.3–37.5 kbps | 2–15 km | 10+ yr | | **NB-IoT** | Licensed LTE | 26–127 kbps | 1–10 km | 5–10 yr | | **Sigfox** | Sub-GHz ISM | 100 bps | 3–50 km | 10+ yr |  </div>  ---  ## LoRa — chirp spread spectrum  <div class="fragment">  **LoRa** = Long Range. PHY is proprietary (Semtech); **LoRaWAN** MAC is open.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS)** — each symbol is a **frequency chirp**.  **Spreading factor (SF7–SF12)** controls chirp rate:  - **Higher SF = longer range but lower data rate** - SF12: 250 bps, −137 dBm sensitivity, 15 km - SF7: 5.5 kbps, −123 dBm sensitivity, 2 km  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The trade-off in one table:**  | SF | Data rate | Sensitivity | Range | |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:| | 7 | 5.5 kbps | −123 dBm | 2 km | | 9 | 1.8 kbps | −129 dBm | 6 km | | 11 | 0.5 kbps | −134 dBm | 10 km | | 12 | 0.25 kbps | −137 dBm | 15 km |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LoRaWAN network:** end devices → gateways → network server → application server.  **License-free** — anyone can deploy a private LoRaWAN network.  </div>  ---  ## NB-IoT — cellular for IoT  <div class="fragment">  **NB-IoT** — the 3GPP IoT standard (Release 13, 2016).  **180 kHz bandwidth** (a single LTE resource block) in licensed spectrum.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Key features:**  - **Data rate:** 26 kbps UL, 127 kbps DL - **Coverage extension:** **+20 dB** over LTE via repetitions (range ~10–15 km) - **Power Saving Mode (PSM):** device sleeps up to **413 days** - **eDRX:** extended DRX, up to 2.9 hours between wake-ups - **Battery:** 5–10 years  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Advantages over LoRa:**  - **Licensed spectrum** — no interference, guaranteed QoS - **Operator-managed** — no gateways to deploy - **Higher data rate** (~100 kbps vs. ~5 kbps) - **Global roaming** via operator's network  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Disadvantages:** needs cellular coverage; monthly fee; higher device cost.  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — LoRa vs. NB-IoT  <div class="quiz" data-question="lora-nbiot">   <p class="quiz-question">A municipality wants to deploy <strong>100,000 water meters</strong> in a city with good cellular coverage. Which LPWAN technology is the simpler choice?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">LoRa — needs custom gateways</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">NB-IoT — uses existing cellular infrastructure, licensed spectrum, operator manages it</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Sigfox — very long range</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">WiFi — better in urban areas</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why.** LoRa is more power-efficient and license-free, but requires deploying gateways (capital + maintenance) and running a private network. **NB-IoT** rides on the operator's existing LTE infrastructure — no gateways, no private network operation, licensed spectrum (no interference), and centralized management. For a city-wide meter rollout, this is far simpler.  </div>  ---  ## §6.7 — 5G and IoT — the converged vision  <div class="fragment">  **5G's three use cases (ITU-R IMT-2020):**  **eMBB** — enhanced Mobile Broadband - Peak: 20 Gbps; user rate: 100 Mbps–1 Gbps - 4K/8K video, AR/VR, cloud gaming  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **URLLC** — Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication - Latency: **1 ms**; reliability: **99.999%** - Industrial automation, remote surgery, autonomous driving  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **mMTC** — massive Machine-Type Communication - Density: **1M devices/km²**; battery 10+ years - IoT sensors, smart city, agriculture  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The three pull in different directions.** 5G NR and the 5G Core are designed to **serve all three on the same network** — via network slicing.  </div>  ---  ## 5G NR — the new radio  <div class="fragment">  **5G NR (New Radio)** — new PHY introduced in 3GPP Release 15 (2018).  </div>  <div class="fragment">  | Aspect | LTE | **5G NR** | |---|---|---| | Frequency | < 6 GHz | **< 6 GHz (FR1) + mmWave 24–52 GHz (FR2)** | | Subcarrier spacing | 15 kHz fixed | **15, 30, 60, 120, 240 kHz** (scalable) | | Channel bandwidth | up to 20 MHz | up to **100 MHz (FR1), 400 MHz (FR2)** | | MIMO | up to 8×8 | **up to 256 antennas** (massive MIMO) | | Modulation | up to 256-QAM | up to **1024-QAM** | | Peak DL | 3 Gbps | **20 Gbps** |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Scalable numerology** — the key 5G innovation. Different subcarrier spacings for different scenarios:  - 15 kHz — wide-area coverage - 30 kHz — urban 5G - 60/120 kHz — low-latency, mmWave  </div>  ---  ## Massive MIMO and mmWave  <div class="fragment">  **Massive MIMO:** 64–256 antenna elements at the base station.  - Beamforming gain: **18–24 dB** - Multi-user MIMO: up to 16 UEs simultaneously - **3D beamforming:** both horizontal and vertical steering  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **mmWave (FR2):** 400 MHz channels → 8× wider than Sub-6 → enables 20 Gbps peak.  But mmWave has trade-offs:  - **High path loss** (~30 dB more than 2 GHz at 1 km — Chapter 1) - **Blockage** (rain, hands, walls) - **Short range** (100–300 m) - Requires **dense small cells**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The combined effect:** massive MIMO beamforming (+18 dB) offsets most of mmWave's path loss penalty. Net: mmWave cells are **dense** but **high-capacity** — the right tool for stadiums, airports, dense urban.  </div>  ---  ## 5G Core — service-based architecture  <div class="fragment">  **5G Core (5GC)** — fundamental redesign from LTE's EPC.  **Instead of network elements with point-to-point interfaces**, 5GC uses **Network Functions (NFs)** connected by **Service-Based Interfaces (SBI)** — essentially **microservices**.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Key NFs:**  | Function | Role | |---|---| | **AMF** | Access & Mobility (registration, handover) | | **SMF** | Session Management (PDU sessions) | | **UPF** | User Plane Function (packet forwarding) | | **AUSF** | Authentication | | **UDM** | Subscriber data (like HSS) | | **PCF** | Policy & charging | | **NSSF** | Network Slice Selection | | **NRF** | NF Repository (service discovery) |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Cloud-native:** 5GC runs on **containers** in a data center, orchestrated by **Kubernetes**. Updated without touching the radio.  </div>  ---  ## Network slicing  <div class="fragment">  **Network slicing** — 5G's flagship feature.  **Virtual, isolated networks** on the same physical infrastructure, each with its own QoS, resources, and topology.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Each slice has:**  - Its own **QoS/KPIs** (latency, throughput, reliability) - Its own **network functions** (or shared, isolated by slice) - Its own **resource allocation** (spectrum, compute, backhaul) - Its own **management**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Example slices:**  - **eMBB slice** — high throughput, moderate latency - **URLLC slice** — 1 ms latency, 99.999% reliability - **mMTC slice** — massive device count, low power  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **New business model:** before slicing, all traffic shared one network. An industrial customer wanting 1 ms latency was at the mercy of consumers streaming video. **Slicing lets the operator sell dedicated capacity** — a new product.  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — Network slicing  <div class="quiz" data-question="nss">   <p class="quiz-question">What does <strong>network slicing</strong> allow a 5G operator to do?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Increase peak data rate beyond 20 Gbps</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">Sell dedicated virtual networks with guaranteed QoS (latency, reliability) on shared infrastructure</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Eliminate the need for base stations</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Reuse LTE spectrum for 5G</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why.** Before slicing, all traffic competed on one network. Slicing creates **isolated virtual networks** on shared physical infrastructure — each with its own QoS, resources, and management. The operator can sell a **URLLC slice** to a factory with 1 ms guaranteed latency, while consumers on the eMBB slice stream video. **Two products, one infrastructure.**  </div>  ---  ## Edge computing — 5G's partner  <div class="fragment">  **MEC (Multi-access Edge Computing)** — compute resources at cell towers or local data centers, close to the user.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why 5G needs it:** 5G's 1 ms air-interface latency is **useless** if the application server is 1000 km away (adds 20+ ms network round-trip).  **MEC** puts the server **at the edge** → full end-to-end latency in 5–10 ms.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Use cases:**  - **AR/VR** — sub-20 ms end-to-end - **Industrial control** — 1 ms loops - **Autonomous vehicles** — safety-critical, local - **Cloud gaming** — low-latency rendering  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **5G + MEC = a new platform** — network + compute at the edge, for real-time applications.  </div>  ---  ## §6.8 — Choosing the right connectivity  <div class="fragment">  For any IoT application, four parameters determine the choice:  | Parameter | Options | |---|---| | **Range** | 10 m (WPAN) → 100 m (WLAN) → 15 km (LPWAN) → global (satellite) | | **Data rate** | 0.1 kbps (Sigfox) → 30 Gbps (WiFi 7) | | **Power** | < 1 μA (BLE sleep) → 40 W (macro base station) | | **Cost** | $1 module (BLE) → $100 module (5G mmWave) |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Decision flowchart:**  1. **High data rate (> 1 Mbps)?** → WiFi (local) or 4G/5G (mobile) 2. **Range > 100 m?** → Licensed? NB-IoT : LoRa 3. **Battery-powered & low duty cycle?** → BLE / ZigBee / LoRa 4. **Latency-critical?** → Cellular (4G/5G)  </div>  ---  ## Worked example — agricultural sensors  <div class="fragment">  **Application:** Soil moisture sensor. 50 bytes/hour. Field 1 km wide. Solar/battery powered. 100 devices.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Requirements:**  - Data rate: 50 bytes/hour = **0.11 bps** (very low) - Range: **1+ km** - Power: **solar/battery — years** - Cost: **many devices — must be cheap**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Options:**  - WiFi → ❌ 100 m range - Bluetooth → ❌ 100 m range - ZigBee → ❌ range too short, needs backhaul - **LoRa** → ✅ 10+ km range, low power, low cost - **NB-IoT** → ✅ 10 km range, low power, needs subscription - Sigfox → ✅ 30+ km, ultra-low rate, ultra-low power  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Best fit:** **LoRaWAN** — private gateway at the farmhouse (solar-powered), 100 sensors use LoRa. No subscription fees. 5+ year battery life on AA cells.  **Alternative:** NB-IoT if cellular coverage is reliable and a monthly subscription is acceptable.  </div>  ---  ## Chapter 6 — key takeaways  <div class="fragment">  **1.** **NGN** = packet-based, all-IP, multi-service. Evolved from voice convergence (2000s) to IoT convergence (2020s).  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **2.** **Bluetooth Classic** for continuous data (audio); **BLE** for bursty sensor data. 3 ms connection, < 1 μA sleep.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **3.** **ZigBee** — mesh, AODV routing, 65,000+ nodes. Dominant in home and industrial automation.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **4.** **WiFi 6** brings **OFDMA** — the biggest change since WiFi 4. Improves capacity in dense environments, not peak rate.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **5.** **UWB** — impulse radio, ~10 cm positioning. Used in AirTags, car keys, warehouse tracking.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **6.** **LPWAN** — LoRa (unlicensed), NB-IoT (licensed), Sigfox (ultra-low-rate). IoT connectivity for years of battery life.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **7.** **5G NR** — scalable numerology, massive MIMO, mmWave. Three use cases: eMBB, URLLC, mMTC.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **8.** **5G Core + network slicing + MEC** — cloud-native, service-based, sells dedicated QoS — the platform for enterprise IoT.  </div>  ---  ## Next — Chapter 7  **Machine Learning for Communications**  <div class="fragment">  - The ETI (Emerging Technology Initiative) mission - ML for the PHY: channel estimation, decoding, autoencoders - ML for the MAC: scheduling, spectrum access, beam management - Federated learning across devices - AI-native 6G vision  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The emerging frontier — how ML is reshaping every layer of the network.**  </div>  ---  <aside class="notes">   <div style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.6;">  **Speaker notes for the whole lecture:**  - Slides 4–7 (NGN definition, three stages, landscape): ~6 min. Emphasize the **broadening scope** — NGN went from "voice over IP" to "everything over IP." - Slides 8–14 (Bluetooth Classic, BLE, battery life): ~8 min. The Classic vs. BLE distinction is critical — audio needs Classic, sensors need BLE. - Slides 15–17 (ZigBee): ~5 min. Mesh + AODV routing is the key concept. Emphasize **on-demand** routing for power saving. - Slides 18–22 (WiFi): ~6 min. **WiFi 6's OFDMA** is the biggest change. Don't dwell on peak rate (9.6 Gbps sounds impressive but the real benefit is capacity). - Slides 23–25 (UWB): ~3 min. Emphasize the **physics** — wide bandwidth → fine time resolution → cm precision. - Slides 26–29 (LPWAN): ~6 min. LoRa vs. NB-IoT vs. Sigfox — the trade-off table is the essential content. - Slides 30–36 (5G/IoT): ~10 min. The three use cases (eMBB, URLLC, mMTC) and **network slicing** are the key concepts. **MEC** completes the story — 5G latency without edge compute is useless. - Slides 37–39 (choosing connectivity): practical. Use the worked example to show students how to reason about the choice.  **The exam will test: BLE vs. Classic, ZigBee mesh vs. BLE star, WiFi 6 OFDMA, LPWAN comparison, 5G three use cases, network slicing.**    </div> </aside>

docs.text: ## ECEG-6412  ### Chapter 7 — Machine Learning for Communications  MSc in Communication Engineering · Year 1, Semester I  Dr. Tesfamichael Gebregziabher  ---  ## Outline  <div class="fragment">  **Part 1 — Why ML for communications**  - The ETI mission - Where classical methods hit limits  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 2 — ML fundamentals**  - Supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement - The data problem  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 3 — ML for the PHY**  - Channel estimation, decoding, autoencoders - Channel modeling with generative AI  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 4 — ML for the MAC**  - Scheduling, dynamic spectrum, beam management  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 5 — Federated learning and practical challenges**  - Privacy-preserving ML - What's deployed, what's not, what's next  </div>  ---  ## Learning outcomes  <div class="fragment">  **LO1 — State the ETI mission**  Foster ML for the PHY and MAC layers — across wireless, optical, satellite, molecular.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO2 — Match ML paradigms to problems**  Supervised (estimation, decoding), unsupervised (sensing), reinforcement (scheduling).  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO3 — Evaluate ML for the PHY**  Where does it beat classical methods? When does it not?  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO4 — Evaluate ML for the MAC**  RL for scheduling, ML for spectrum, beam prediction.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO5 — Explain federated learning**  Privacy-preserving training without centralizing raw data.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO6 — Identify practical challenges**  Data scarcity, generalization, latency, interpretability, standardization.  </div>  ---  ## §7.1 — Why ML for communications?  <div class="fragment">  The **IEEE ComSoc Emerging Technology Initiative (ETI)** on **Machine Learning for Communications** was launched in 2019.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Mission:** foster research and innovation on ML for the **PHY** and **MAC** layers — across wireless, optical, satellite, and molecular communication systems.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The premise:** classical communication theory has reached practical limits in some areas, and ML can solve problems that are:  - **Too complex** for closed-form optimization - **Too data-dependent** for analytic models - **Too slow** for traditional algorithms under real-time constraints  </div>  ---  ## The classical foundation  <div class="fragment">  Classical communication systems are designed from **mathematical models** — each block has a **provably optimal** solution:  | Component | Classical solution | |---|---| | Channel estimation | MMSE (with known covariance) | | Equalization | Viterbi, MMSE | | Detection (MIMO) | ML, sphere decoding | | Channel coding | LDPC, turbo, polar — near-Shannon | | Scheduling | Proportional fair | | Estimation | Kalman filter |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why replace them with neural networks?**  </div>  ---  ## Where ML shines — three properties  <div class="fragment">  **1. Non-linear function approximation.**  Neural networks approximate any continuous function to arbitrary accuracy (universal approximation theorem).  Many communication problems (channel estimation, precoding, detection) are **non-linear** and lack closed-form optima — ML learns the mapping from data.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **2. End-to-end optimization.**  Traditional systems are **independent blocks** (estimate → equalize → demodulate → decode). Each block optimizes its own metric.  ML lets you **jointly optimize the whole chain** for the end-to-end objective.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **3. Data-driven modeling.**  When the environment is too complex for analytic modeling — mmWave channels, molecular propagation, non-linear hardware — ML learns from measurements.  </div>  ---  ## Where ML doesn't shine  <div class="fragment">  **ML is not a replacement for classical methods** — it's an additional tool.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **ML loses to classical methods when:**  - The classical solution is **optimal** (matched filter, LDPC decoder) - Data is **scarce** (new bands, new standards) - **Interpretability and certification** are required (safety-critical — automotive, medical, aviation) - **Generalization matters** (model trained on one channel may fail on another) - Real-time latency is critical (URLLC at 1 ms)  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The best systems combine ML and classical DSP** — ML for the complex, environment-specific parts; classical for the parts with optimal solutions.  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — When does ML NOT beat classical?  <div class="quiz" data-question="ml-limits">   <p class="quiz-question">For which of these is the <strong>classical method already optimal</strong> (ML offers little benefit)?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Channel estimation with unknown statistics</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">MIMO detection in massive MIMO</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">Matched filter for a known signal in AWGN</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Channel modeling with site-specific geometry</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why.** The matched filter is **provably optimal** for maximizing SNR at a specific time — a Cauchy–Schwarz inequality that no learned filter can beat. ML's advantages appear where the optimum is unknown (unknown statistics, non-linear channels, high-complexity problems), not where classical theory already gives the best answer.  </div>  ---  ## §7.2 — ML fundamentals  <div class="fragment">  **Three paradigms:**  | Paradigm | Data | Communications use | |---|---|---| | **Supervised** | (input, label) pairs | Channel estimation, decoding, modulation classification | | **Unsupervised** | input only | Spectrum sensing, anomaly detection | | **Reinforcement** | reward signal | Scheduling, spectrum access, beam management |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Supervised learning:** learn $f_\theta$ from training set $\{(x_i, y_i)\}$.  $$ \boxed{\;\theta^* = \arg\min_\theta \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal L(f_\theta(x_i), y_i)\;} $$  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Reinforcement learning:** learn policy $\pi(a \mid s)$ from reward signal.  $$ \boxed{\;\pi^* = \arg\max_\pi \mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t r_t\right]\;} $$  No labels — just reward.  </div>  ---  ## Deep learning for signals  <div class="fragment">  **CNN (Convolutional Neural Network)** — the dominant architecture for PHY:  - 1-D CNN over signal (time or frequency as "image") - Convolutional layers learn local patterns - Pooling reduces dimensionality - Fully connected layers for classification/regression  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **RNN / LSTM** — for sequential data (channel estimation over time, scheduling).  **Transformers** — attention-based; increasingly used for channel estimation, decoding, end-to-end.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Autoencoders** — for unsupervised and self-supervised tasks, and for **end-to-end learning of communication systems** (see §7.3.3).  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Unfolded networks** — iterative algorithms unrolled into a fixed-depth NN with trainable parameters (deep unfolding).  </div>  ---  ## The data problem  <div class="fragment">  Unlike vision and NLP, communications has a **data problem**:  **Where does training data come from?**  | Source | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---| | **Simulation** (3GPP TR 38.901, Sionna) | Unlimited, controllable | Model-reality gap | | **Measurement** | Realistic | Expensive, limited, site-specific | | **Synthetic augmentation** | Cheap | Doesn't cover all real cases | | **Field data** | Truly representative | Privacy, collection cost |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The model-reality gap:** an ML model trained on 3GPP TR 38.901 synthetic channels may fail on real measured channels.  **This is the fundamental data challenge of communications ML** — much harder than in vision or NLP.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Solutions:** transfer learning, domain adaptation, online learning.  </div>  ---  ## §7.3 — ML for the PHY — channel estimation  <div class="fragment">  **The classical problem:** estimate channel $h$ from received pilots $y_p = h\, x_p + n$.  **Classical methods:** - LS — no statistics, noisy at low SNR - MMSE — optimal, needs covariance - Compressed sensing — exploits sparsity  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **ML approach:** a CNN maps received pilots + context → channel estimate.  **Why might ML help?**  - Channel has structure (sparsity, correlation) - MMSE needs the **covariance** — which must be estimated, and is wrong in new environments - ML **learns** the structure from data, generalizes  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Critical insight:** when the ML model is trained on the **same** channel it's evaluated on, it nearly matches MMSE — **without needing the covariance**.  When trained on a **different** channel (mismatch), it degrades.  </div>  ---  ## Channel estimation — the trade-off  <div class="fragment">  **Typical results (EPA channel, 10 dB SNR):**  | Method | NMSE (dB) | |---|:---:| | LS | −8 | | MMSE (known covariance) | **−14** | | ML (matched training) | **−13** | | ML (mismatched training) | −10 |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The model-reality gap is real.**  When the ML model's implicit channel statistics match the deployment, it wins. When they don't, it loses.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Where ML wins in practice:** when covariance is **hard to estimate** (short windows, non-stationary channels, massive MIMO with many antennas).  **Where classical wins:** when statistics are known and stable.  </div>  ---  ## ML for channel decoding  <div class="fragment">  **The classical problem:** recover information bits from a received noisy codeword.  **Classical decoders:** Viterbi, BCJR, belief propagation (LDPC), SCL (polar) — **near-optimal**.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **ML approach:** learn a decoder that maps noisy codewords → bits.  **Architecture:** RNN or transformer that iterates over the codeword.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Where ML helps:** - **Latency** — a single feed-forward pass may be faster than iterative decoding - **Finite-length performance** — ML can exploit short-code structure - **Joint decoding** across multi-user / multi-antenna  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Where classical wins:** LDPC/turbo/polar are already **within 0.5 dB of Shannon**. At practical block lengths, ML decoders don't reliably beat them.  The main opportunity is **latency**, not raw BER.  </div>  ---  ## Decoding — latency vs. accuracy  <div class="fragment">  **Example:** 5G NR LDPC decoder at rate 3/4, block 8448 bits, target 1 Gbps.  | Decoder | Latency | Energy (pJ/bit) | BER at 2 dB | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | Classical BP (15 iter) | 4.2 μs | 120 | 1.2e-6 | | Neural LDPC (5 iter) | **1.1 μs** | 200 | 1.5e-6 | | Neural LDPC (20 iter) | 4.3 μs | 800 | 1.1e-6 |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The trade-off:** - Neural LDPC **4× lower latency** at similar BER - But higher energy, and depends on fixed code structure - ML decoders are deployed for **latency-critical** applications, not general decoding  </div>  ---  ## §7.3.3 — The autoencoder — the radical idea  <div class="fragment">  **Replace the entire PHY (TX + channel + RX) with an autoencoder** trained end-to-end.  **O'Shea–Hoydis formulation (2017):**  $$ \text{bits} \to \text{Encoder}_\theta \to \text{Channel} \to \text{Decoder}_\phi \to \text{bits} $$  Train encoder + decoder **jointly** to minimize bit-error loss.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why it's interesting:**  - **Joint optimization** — no separate design of TX and RX - **Adapts to any (differentiable) channel** - **Discovers new modulation schemes** — may not match BPSK/QPSK/QAM  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The critical requirement:** the channel must be **differentiable** for backpropagation.  Works when channel is additive Gaussian or a known differentiable function. Fails when channel has hard decisions or unmodeled distributions.  </div>  ---  ## What the autoencoder discovers  <div class="fragment">  **AWGN channel (2 bits/symbol):**  The learned constellation has 4 points, roughly in a **square** — **it learns QPSK**.  BER matches theory within 0.1 dB. **The network discovers the classical optimal.**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Non-linear channel (PA saturation, 4 bits/symbol):**  The learned constellation is **not 16-QAM**. It's stretched and offset to compensate for the distortion.  BER improves **~5 dB** over classical 16-QAM — because the classical constellation was optimized for AWGN, not for the non-linear PA.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **This is where ML genuinely beats classical.**  For the AWGN channel, classical is optimal — ML just recovers it. For non-linear or unmodeled channels, ML learns a better solution.  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — Autoencoder on AWGN  <div class="quiz" data-question="autoencoder">   <p class="quiz-question">When trained on the <strong>AWGN channel</strong> at 2 bits/symbol, what does the autoencoder typically learn?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">A new constellation unlike any classical scheme</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">A QPSK-like constellation — the classical optimal</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">16-QAM</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">It fails to converge</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why.** For the AWGN channel, QPSK is the **optimal 2-bit/symbol modulation** — the constellation that minimizes BER for a given $E_b/N_0$. Gradient descent finds it naturally. **The autoencoder's value appears on non-linear channels** where classical optimal is unknown — there it learns constellations that beat classical QAM.  </div>  ---  ## ML for channel modeling — generative AI  <div class="fragment">  **The classical problem:** 3GPP TR 38.901 is geometric, site-specific, slow to simulate, hard to extend.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **ML approach:** learn a **generative model** of the channel — sample realistic realizations from the same distribution as real channels.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Techniques:**  - **VAE (Variational Autoencoder)** — learns latent representation, samples from it - **GAN (Generative Adversarial Network)** — generator vs. discriminator - **Diffusion models** — similar to DALL-E / Stable Diffusion — sample by progressively denoising  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Use:** - Generate training data for receiver ML models - Generate channels for coverage planning - Augment measured data for rare scenarios  **3GPP Release 18** includes generative-AI channel models for specific scenarios (high-speed train, industrial).  </div>  ---  ## §7.4 — ML for the MAC — scheduling  <div class="fragment">  **The classical problem:** given UEs with channel $h_i(t)$ and queue $q_i(t)$, decide which UE to serve each TTI to maximize utility.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Classical algorithms:**  - **Round-robin** — fair, ignores channel - **Max-throughput** — best channel, unfair - **Proportional fair** — max $h_i(t)/\bar h_i$ — throughput + fairness  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **ML approach:** **reinforcement learning** to learn a scheduling policy.  - **State:** channel qualities, queue lengths, delays - **Action:** which UE to serve - **Reward:** throughput (+ fairness bonus) - **Algorithm:** DQN, PPO, actor-critic  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Advantage over classical:** handles **multiple objectives** (throughput + fairness + latency + energy) that classical heuristics struggle to balance.  </div>  ---  ## RL scheduling — worked example  <div class="fragment">  **Setup:** 10 UEs, Rayleigh fading, full-buffer traffic. Reward = sum throughput, $\gamma = 0.9$.  **Training:** 1 million TTI × 10 UEs.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Results:**  | Scheduler | Cell throughput | Jain's fairness | |---|:---:|:---:| | Round-robin | 22 Mbps | **0.98** | | Proportional fair | 26 Mbps | 0.85 | | **RL (learned)** | **27 Mbps** | 0.82 |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Interpretation.** RL achieves slightly higher throughput (+4%) than PF at slightly lower fairness. **Not a dramatic win** — PF is already near-optimal for this simple scenario.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **RL wins more** with multiple objectives (throughput + delay), non-standard channel models, or bursty traffic. For simple scenarios, PF remains the default.  </div>  ---  ## Dynamic spectrum access  <div class="fragment">  **The problem:** licensed spectrum is often underutilized (15–85% idle). **Cognitive radio** lets unlicensed users access it when the primary user is absent.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Classical approach:** energy detection — measure energy in the band, threshold at occupancy. **Fails** under noise uncertainty, low SNR.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **ML approach:** supervised classification of spectrum occupancy from IQ samples.  **Input:** $N$ IQ samples. **Output:** primary user present/absent, modulation type.  **Network:** 1-D CNN over IQ.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why ML wins:** robust to noise uncertainty, detects weak primary users, generalizes across modulation types.  **Deployment:** CBRS (US) uses a centralized SAS database for primary detection — ML is a candidate for **incumbent detection** in future systems.  </div>  ---  ## Beam management in mmWave  <div class="fragment">  **The problem:** mmWave needs beam alignment. Exhaustive search over an $N \times N$ codebook is $O(N^2)$ — **slow**.  For 64 beams: 64 measurements × 1 ms = 64 ms to align.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **ML approach:** **beam prediction** — predict the best beam from **fewer measurements** or from **context** (position, history, previous beams).  **Input:** a few "probe" beams + GPS + previous beams. **Output:** predicted best beam, or predicted CQI for all beams.  **Network:** CNN or LSTM.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Result:**  | Method | Measurements | Best-beam accuracy | Latency | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | Exhaustive search | 64 | 100% | 64 ms | | Classical hierarchical | 20 | 85% | 20 ms | | **ML (CNN)** | **8** | **92%** | **8 ms** |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **8× measurement reduction**, 8× faster alignment. Enables **high-mobility beam tracking** that classical search cannot support.  **5G-Advanced Release 18** standardizes AI/ML for beam management.  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — Beam management  <div class="quiz" data-question="beam-ml">   <p class="quiz-question">What is the primary benefit of <strong>ML-based beam management</strong> in mmWave?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Higher peak data rate per UE</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">Reduced measurement overhead — faster beam alignment for high-mobility UEs</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Better spectral efficiency per beam</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Eliminates the need for beamforming</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why.** Beam management's bottleneck is **measurement time** — exhaustive search over $N^2$ pairs is too slow for moving UEs. ML predicts the best beam from **fewer probes** + context, reducing measurement from 64 to 8 in the example. That 8× speedup makes beam tracking viable at highway speeds.  </div>  ---  ## §7.5 — Federated learning  <div class="fragment">  **The privacy problem:**  Classical ML trains on **centralized data** — but channel data, location, and usage data are **sensitive**.  Regulations (GDPR, CCPA) restrict moving personal data.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Federated learning (FL):** train a model **without centralizing data.**  **The FedAvg algorithm:**  1. Initialize a global model at the server 2. Broadcast to $N$ participating devices 3. Each device trains **locally** on its data 4. Send model **updates** (weights, not data) to the server 5. Server **aggregates** (weighted average):  $$ w_{t+1} = \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{n_k}{n}\, w_{t+1}^{(k)} $$  6. Repeat  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Privacy:** only model updates leave the device, not raw data. **Differential privacy** can be added for formal guarantees.  </div>  ---  ## FL — trade-offs and applications  <div class="fragment">  **FL applications in communications:**  - **Beam prediction** at mobile devices — learned locally, aggregated - **Channel estimation** — models trained at UEs, aggregated at gNB - **Anomaly detection** — distributed detection of rogue devices - **Spectrum sensing** — collaborative sensing without IQ sharing  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Challenges:**  - **Communication cost** — model updates are large; compression needed - **Non-IID data** — different UEs see different channels; local models diverge - **Stragglers** — slow/offline devices - **Security** — malicious devices can poison the model  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Example:** 100 UEs, channel data 10 GB centralized vs. **50 MB** of model updates — **200× less bandwidth**.  At 0.5 dB accuracy loss. **Privacy is the win** — many applications accept the loss.  </div>  ---  ## §7.6 — Practical challenges  <div class="fragment">  **Data:** - Scarcity — real measurements are expensive - Quality — labels require reference signals - **Distribution shift** — training ≠ deployment  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Generalization:** - ML trained on one channel/band may **fail** on another - Fundamentally different from vision/NLP (data distribution is site-specific and non-stationary) - Solutions: domain adaptation, meta-learning, online learning  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Latency and complexity:** - Inference must fit the TTI (1 ms in LTE, 0.5 ms in 5G, 0.125 ms in URLLC) - Model size must fit in the device - Energy — inference costs power  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Interpretability and safety:** - Black-box models hard to certify - Safety-critical applications need formal verification - Hybrid models, physics-informed NNs, deep unfolding address this  </div>  ---  ## Standardization — what's actually deployed  <div class="fragment">  **3GPP Release 18 (5G-Advanced, 2024):**  - **AI/ML for NR air interface** as a study item - **Beam management** standardized - **CSI feedback** under study - **Positioning** using ML - **Network energy saving** deployed - **Load balancing** deployed  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **O-RAN Alliance** — deployment platform:  - **RIC** (RAN Intelligent Controller) - **xApps** — near-real-time apps - **rApps** — non-real-time apps - First production deployment of third-party ML in RAN  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **ITU-R IMT-2030 (6G)** — **AI-native air interface** as a major theme.  AI is a first-class component of the network — from PHY to network management.  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — Federated learning  <div class="quiz" data-question="fl-privacy">   <p class="quiz-question">Why is <strong>federated learning</strong> considered privacy-preserving?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">It encrypts the raw data during transmission</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">Raw data never leaves the device — only model updates are sent</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">It uses blockchain to verify training</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">It obfuscates the model structure</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why.** Classical ML sends raw data to a server for training. Federated learning keeps **raw data on the device** and sends only **model updates** (gradients or weights). Model updates contain far less information about individual samples — and differential privacy can formalize the guarantee. This is a fundamental architectural advantage for regulated or privacy-sensitive data.  </div>  ---  ## §7.7 — Where ML is deployed today  <div class="fragment">  **Standardized and deployed:**  | Application | Standard | Status | |---|---|---| | Beam management (5G NR) | 3GPP Release 18 | Deployed in 5G-Advanced | | Network energy saving | 3GPP Release 18 | Deployed | | Load balancing | 3GPP Release 18 | Deployed | | Anomaly detection | O-RAN | Deployed in cloud RAN | | Traffic prediction | O-RAN | Deployed for capacity planning |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Commercial (proprietary):**  - **Nokia, Ericsson, Huawei, Samsung** — ML-based beam management, channel estimation in 5G gNB products - **Qualcomm** — ML channel estimation in Snapdragon modems (studied, limited) - **NVIDIA Sionna** — GPU-accelerated simulation for ML research  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The gap between research and deployment is real.** Most papers show gains on simulation; most deployments use small, well-understood ML models for specific tasks.  </div>  ---  ## §7.8 — AI-native 6G  <div class="fragment">  **6G (ITU-R IMT-2030)** is described as **AI-native** — AI from the start, not bolted on.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Expected features:**  - **AI-driven PHY** — learned channel estimation, beam prediction, possibly entire learned PHY for some links - **AI-defined RAN** — xApps, rApps, network automation - **AI-orchestrated core** — self-optimizing, self-healing - **AI for network management** — energy, congestion, slicing - **Federated learning** across billions of devices  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Research projects:**  - **Hexa-X** (EU 6G flagship) — AI/ML as one of six pillars - **NGMN 6G** — operator-driven requirements - **ITU-R IMT-2030** — the framework  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The vision is ambitious — the challenge is delivering it with interpretability, safety, and standardization.**  </div>  ---  ## Chapter 7 — key takeaways  <div class="fragment">  **1.** **ML for communications** is driven by the need to solve problems too complex, too data-dependent, or too slow for classical methods. **IEEE ComSoc ETI** coordinates the research.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **2.** Three paradigms: **supervised** (channel estimation, decoding), **unsupervised** (spectrum sensing), **reinforcement** (scheduling, beam management).  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **3.** ML for PHY: - **Channel estimation** — matches MMSE without covariance, but degrades under model mismatch - **Decoding** — offers latency improvements; classical LDPC/turbo remain near-optimal - **Autoencoder** — discovers new constellations for non-linear channels - **Channel modeling** — generative AI produces realistic training data  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **4.** ML for MAC: - **Scheduling** — RL balances multiple objectives; small gain over PF in simple scenarios - **Spectrum sensing** — ML beats energy detection under noise uncertainty - **Beam management** — 8× measurement reduction  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **5.** **Federated learning** — privacy-preserving training without centralizing data. 200× less bandwidth, 0.5 dB accuracy loss.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **6.** **Practical challenges:** data scarcity, generalization, latency, interpretability, standardization.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **7.** **Standardization:** 3GPP Release 18 includes ML for beam management, energy, load balancing. O-RAN RIC provides deployment platform.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **8.** **AI-native 6G** is the vision — ML across all layers.  </div>  ---  ## Course complete  <div class="fragment">  **ECEG-6412 — Recent Trends in Communication Technologies**  You now understand:  - The wireless propagation channel - Modulation, coding, multiple access - GSM, UMTS, 4G/LTE, 5G - The wired infrastructure - Emerging trends: IoT, LPWAN, ML for communications  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The unifying theme:** every generation adds a new PHY technique and a new application class — driven by the same fundamental Shannon trade-off.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The future:** 6G, AI-native networks, THz communication, integrated sensing — the next decade.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Good luck with your final examination.**  </div>  ---  <aside class="notes">   <div style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.6;">  **Speaker notes for the whole lecture:**  - Slides 4–7 (ETI mission, where ML helps): ~6 min. Emphasize the **three properties** — non-linear approximation, end-to-end optimization, data-driven modeling. And the **three limits** — optimal classical solutions, data scarcity, interpretability. - Slides 8–11 (ML fundamentals): ~5 min. Don't spend too long on the general ML basics — students have seen this in other courses. Focus on **why communications data is different** (model-reality gap). - Slides 12–17 (channel estimation + decoding): ~10 min. Emphasize **where ML wins and where it doesn't** — matched-covariance MMSE is already near-optimal; ML's value is when statistics are unknown or channel is non-stationary. - Slides 18–22 (autoencoder + channel modeling): the most conceptually interesting material. **The autoencoder learns QPSK for AWGN** — a beautiful result showing ML recovers classical optimal. **Where it wins is non-linear channels.** - Slides 23–27 (MAC): scheduling (small gains over PF), spectrum sensing, beam management (big gains — 8× reduction). - Slides 28–30 (federated learning): the privacy story. **200× less bandwidth** at 0.5 dB loss is a real-world trade-off. - Slides 31–34 (challenges + deployment): **the gap between research and deployment** is important. Most papers show simulation gains; most production deployments are small, focused ML models. - Slides 35–37 (AI-native 6G): the future. Keep it brief — it's aspirational.  **The final exam may test: three ML paradigms, when ML beats classical, autoencoder on AWGN, federated learning privacy, three 5G use cases (recap from Ch 6), and the ETI mission.**  **Course complete.** With this deck, ECEG-6412 has:  - 8 content chapters (Ch 1–7 + wired-trends) - 7 slide decks (Ch 1–7) - Exam bank (100 marks) - Solutions for all 8 chapters - Full syllabus, schedule, assessment, resources, feedback  The course site is ready to deploy.    </div> </aside>

docs.title: Wired Technology Trends
docs.text: ## ECEG-6412  ### Part II — Wired Technology Trends  MSc in Communication Engineering · Year 1, Semester I  Dr. Tesfamichael Gebregziabher  ---  ## Outline  <div class="fragment">  **Part 1 — Why wired still matters**  - Every wireless call is mostly wired - Three tiers of wired infrastructure  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 2 — Access loop**  - xDSL vs. DOCSIS vs. PON - FTTH, FTTC, FWA economics  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 3 — Core network**  - DWDM, OTN, IP/MPLS - SDN/NFV, submarine cables  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 4 — Distribution & backhaul**  - Carrier Ethernet - Mobile backhaul, CPRI fronthaul, timing  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Part 5 — Economics**  - Cost per bit: 100–1000× difference - Fiber vs. FWA deployment  </div>  ---  ## Learning outcomes  <div class="fragment">  **LO1 — Explain why wireless depends on wired**  The radio is the last 100 m–1 km; everything else is fiber.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO2 — Compare access-loop technologies**  xDSL, DOCSIS, PON — capacity, distance, cost.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO3 — Analyse core-network capacity**  DWDM wavelength stacking; submarine cables carry 99% of international traffic.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO4 — Design mobile backhaul**  Fiber vs. microwave vs. satellite; CPRI bandwidth; timing requirements.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **LO5 — Evaluate wired vs. wireless economics**  Cost per bit; deployment trade-offs at different densities.  </div>  ---  ## §1 — Every wireless call is mostly wired  <div class="fragment">  ``` UE ──[radio]── gNB ──[fiber]── aggregation ──[fiber]── core ──[fiber]── internet      100 m       10 km          100 km           1000+ km ```  </div>  <div class="fragment">  The **radio link is the last 100 m–1 km.**  Everything else — **fiber** — carries the vast majority of the **distance, capacity, and cost**.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **True of:**  - 4G/5G mobile — fiber backhaul from gNB - WiFi — Ethernet/fiber uplink from AP - Fixed broadband — FTTH, xDSL, DOCSIS all terminate in fiber  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Understanding wireless networks without wired infrastructure** is like understanding city traffic by looking only at parking lots.  </div>  ---  ## Three tiers of wired infrastructure  <div class="fragment">  | Tier | Function | Technology | Distance | |---|---|---|---| | **Access loop** | Connects individual subscribers | PON, xDSL, DOCSIS | 100 m – 20 km | | **Distribution / metro** | Aggregates access traffic | Carrier Ethernet, IP/MPLS, DWDM | 5 – 100 km | | **Core** | Between cities / continents | DWDM, IP/MPLS, OTN | 100 – 10,000+ km |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Each tier** has its own economics and technology — and each has evolved dramatically in 20 years.  </div>  ---  ## Why wired matters in a wireless course  <div class="fragment">  **1. Mobile backhaul is the bottleneck.**  5G sites produce **10–20 Gbps peak traffic**. Backhaul often lags radio capacity by 3–5 years.  **Radio transmits more than the network can deliver.**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **2. Fixed-mobile convergence.**  5G, WiFi, and fiber share a common core. VoWiFi uses the same IMS as VoLTE. Convergence is *wired*.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **3. The economics of data.**  Wired cost per bit: **~$0.001/GB**. Wireless: **~$1–10/GB**.  **1000× difference** — drives WiFi offload, FMC, and fiber deployment strategy.  </div>  ---  ## §2 — Access loop — the last mile  <div class="fragment">  Connects each subscriber to the operator's first aggregation point.  **Historically:** copper twisted pair (phone) → coax (TV) → fiber.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Design constraints:**  - **Dedicated wire** per subscriber (or shared point-to-multipoint) - **Distance-limited** by attenuation - **Cost per subscriber dominated by trenching** — $500–$2,000 per home  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The access loop is the most expensive part of the network** — 40–60% of total capex.  </div>  ---  ## xDSL vs. DOCSIS vs. PON  <div class="fragment">  | Technology | Peak rate | Distance | Sharing | Best for | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:|---| | **xDSL** (VDSL2/G.fast) | 100 Mbps–1 Gbps | 100 m–1.5 km | Dedicated | Reusing copper | | **DOCSIS** (3.1) | 10 Gbps DL | 500 m–2 km | 500–2000 homes/node | Cable operators | | **PON** (GPON / XGS) | 2.5–10 Gbps | 20 km | 32–128 subscribers | New builds, dense urban |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **xDSL** trades distance for rate — the further from the cabinet, the slower.  **DOCSIS** is a shared medium — congestion at peak.  **PON** is passive — no field electronics, lowest maintenance cost.  </div>  ---  ## PON — the fiber access architecture  <div class="fragment">  ``` OLT ──[fiber]── splitter 1:32 ──[fiber]── ONU (home) ```  - **OLT** — Optical Line Terminal at the exchange - **Splitter** — passive optical device (no power, no maintenance) - **ONU / ONT** — Optical Network Unit at the subscriber  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Downstream 1490 nm, upstream 1310 nm, video overlay 1550 nm** (WDM).  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The passive splitter is why PON is cheap.**  No active electronics in the field. No batteries, no cooling, no cabinet. Only the OLT (at the exchange) and the ONU (at the home) need power.  </div>  ---  ## PON generations and split ratios  <div class="fragment">  | Standard | Year | Downstream | Upstream | Split | |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:| | **GPON** | 2003 | 2.5 Gbps | 1.25 Gbps | 1:128 | | **XG-PON** | 2010 | 10 Gbps | 2.5 Gbps | 1:128 | | **XGS-PON** | 2016 | 10 Gbps | 10 Gbps | 1:128 | | **NG-PON2** | 2015 | 40 Gbps | 40 Gbps | 1:64 | | **50G PON** | 2021+ | 50 Gbps | 25–50 Gbps | 1:32 |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Worked example — GPON with 1:32 split:**  Worst case (all 32 active): $2.5 / 32 =$ **78 Mbps** per user.  Realistic (60% active): $2.5 / 19 =$ **131 Mbps** per user.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **XGS-PON with 1:32 split:**  Worst case: $10 / 32 =$ **312 Mbps** per user.  **Ample headroom** for 4K video (~25 Mbps) + multiple HD streams + web.  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — Which access technology for rural?  <div class="quiz" data-question="rural-access">   <p class="quiz-question">A rural area has 500 homes over 30 km². Fiber trenching costs $50,000/km; a 5G FWA base station covers the area at $200,000. Which is likely cheaper per home?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Fiber — always cheaper in the long term</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">PON — passive splitters are free</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">5G FWA — the low home density doesn't amortize trenching costs</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">xDSL — reuses existing copper</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why.** At ~17 homes/km², fiber trenching costs dominate: ~20 km trench × $50K = $1M, plus ONTs → ~$2,200/home. 5G FWA: ~$200K base station + $150K backhaul + $300/CPE × 500 → ~$1,000/home. **FWA wins below the ~70–80 homes/km² crossover.** Above it, fiber is cheaper and higher-capacity.  </div>  ---  ## FTTH vs. FTTC vs. FWA  <div class="fragment">  **Three deployment models:**  - **FTTH** — fiber to the home. 1–10 Gbps per home. - **FTTC** — fiber to the cabinet, copper (VDSL2, G.fast) for last 100–500 m. - **FWA** — 5G wireless to the home. 100 Mbps–1 Gbps per home.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  | Architecture | Capex / home | Peak rate | Deploy time | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | FTTC | $200–500 | 100 Mbps | Weeks | | FTTB | $500–1000 | 500 Mbps | Months | | FTTH | $1000–2500 | 1–10 Gbps | Months | | 5G FWA | $500–1500 | 100 Mbps–1 Gbps | Weeks |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Operators deploy a mix** — FTTH in new builds and dense urban, FTTC in older areas, FWA in rural where trenching is prohibitive.  </div>  ---  ## §3 — Core network — the optical backbone  <div class="fragment">  **The problem:** transport **terabits per second** over **thousands of km**, with **sub-10-ms latency** and **99.999% reliability**.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Two technologies dominate:**  - **DWDM** — dense wavelength division multiplexing (optical transport) - **IP/MPLS** — packet routing  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Layered stack:**  | Layer | Technology | Function | |---|---|---| | L0 | Fiber | Physical medium | | L1 | DWDM | 80+ wavelengths, 100–400 Gbps each | | L2 | OTN | Framing, FEC, monitoring | | L3 | IP/MPLS | Routing, traffic engineering |  </div>  ---  ## DWDM — the capacity multiplier  <div class="fragment">  **DWDM** transmits multiple wavelengths on one fiber — each carries an independent signal.  - **Spacing:** 50 or 100 GHz (ITU-T grid) - **Band:** C-band (1530–1565 nm, ~35 nm → ~80 channels at 50 GHz) - **Per-wavelength:** 100–400 Gbps (coherent detection) - **Per fiber:** **8–32 Tbps**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Worked example — 100 GHz C-band:**  Channels: 4.4 THz / 100 GHz ≈ **44 channels**.  At 200 Gbps each: 44 × 200 = **8.8 Tbps** per fiber.  At 400 Gbps (coherent 64-QAM): **17.6 Tbps** per fiber.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Perspective:** one modern fiber pair carries the **entire traffic of a mid-sized country**.  </div>  ---  ## OTN, IP/MPLS, and SDN/NFV  <div class="fragment">  **OTN** — Optical Transport Network (ITU-T G.709):  - Framing, forward error correction, monitoring - Common rates: OTU4 (111.8 Gbps), OTUCn (n×100 Gbps)  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **IP/MPLS** — carries the actual packets:  - Label switching (fast forwarding) - Traffic engineering (explicit routes) - VPNs, fast reroute (< 50 ms protection)  **Modern evolution:** **Segment Routing** (SR-MPLS, SRv6) — labels encode paths, no per-flow state.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **SDN** — control plane separate from data plane. Centralized controller, programmable network.  **NFV** — network functions virtualized onto commodity servers (containers).  **Together:** the network becomes a **software platform** — new services in minutes.  </div>  ---  ## Submarine cables — connecting continents  <div class="fragment">  **99% of international data travels through submarine cables** — not satellites.  **~450 cables globally**, ~1.4 million km total length.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Modern cables:**  - **8–24 fiber pairs** per cable - **100–250 Tbps** per cable (newer ones) - **Repeaters** every 40–80 km (optical amplifiers) - **Latency:** ~5 μs per km of fiber (speed of light in glass)  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Economics:**  - Capex $100M–500M per cable - **Cost per bit < $0.0001/GB** — the cheapest transport in the network - Lifespan: 25 years (capacity upgrades every 5 years as coherent optics improve)  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The "latency race":** a shorter transatlantic cable saves milliseconds off London–New York round-trip — worth billions to financial trading.  </div>  ---  ## §4 — Mobile backhaul — the critical link  <div class="fragment">  **Mobile backhaul** connects cell sites to the core network.  Often **the bottleneck** — radio capacity grows faster than backhaul.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The capacity gap:**  | Generation | Backhaul requirement / site | |---|---| | 2G | 2–10 Mbps | | 3G | 50–100 Mbps | | 4G | **500 Mbps–2 Gbps** | | 4G (LTE-A, 3-sector, CA) | **2–6 Gbps** | | 5G (sub-6, mid-band) | **5–10 Gbps** | | 5G (mmWave, dense) | **10–25 Gbps** |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Each generation asks for 5–10× more backhaul** — often ahead of what operators can deploy.  </div>  ---  ## Backhaul technologies  <div class="fragment">  | Technology | Capacity | Distance | Latency | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | **Fiber** | 1–100+ Gbps | 40–80 km | ~5 μs/km | | **Microwave** (6–42 GHz) | 100 Mbps–3 Gbps | 1–30 km (LOS) | ~3 μs/km | | **E-band** (70/80 GHz) | 1–10 Gbps | 1–3 km (LOS) | low | | **Satellite** (LEO) | 50–200 Mbps | global | 30–60 ms | | **DSL** | 5–100 Mbps | 1–5 km | low |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Only ~20–30% of cell sites worldwide have fiber.**  The rest use **microwave** or other wireless backhaul.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Fiber preferred** — highest capacity, lowest latency, lowest cost per bit.  **Microwave** dominates rural — deployed in 30–60 days vs. months for fiber.  </div>  ---  ## Backhaul sizing — worked example  <div class="fragment">  **Setup:** 5G gNB, 3 sectors × 100 MHz (Sub-6), 64T64R massive MIMO, peak **10 Gbps per sector**.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Peak per site:** 3 × 10 = **30 Gbps**.  **Busy-hour average:** 40% of peak = **12 Gbps**.  **With 2× headroom for growth:** **~24 Gbps** target backhaul.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Fiber options:**  - 40G (4×10G) — marginal - **100G — comfortable, future-proof**  **Microwave alternative:** 4× E-band (10 Gbps each) = 40 Gbps — viable but weather-sensitive.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Rule:** provision **1.5–2× busy-hour average** to allow for burst and growth.  </div>  ---  ## CPRI fronthaul — the fronthaul tax  <div class="fragment">  **C-RAN** (Chapter 5) splits the base station into RRH (at tower) + BBU (centralized).  The **fronthaul** carries **digitized I/Q samples** — not user data.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **CPRI bandwidth** (per antenna stream):  $$ R_{\text{CPRI}} = f_s \cdot N_{\text{bits}} \cdot 2 $$  For LTE 20 MHz: $30.72 \text{ Msps} \times 15 \text{ bits} \times 2 = \mathbf{921.6\ Mbps}$.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Worked example — 3-sector, 4×4 MIMO LTE:**  Per sector: 4 antennas × 921.6 Mbps = 3.69 Gbps.  **3 sectors:** **~11 Gbps CPRI.**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **User peak per sector: 150 Mbps.**  **CPRI is 24× the user data.** This is the "**fronthaul tax**".  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **eCPRI** reduces this by splitting the PHY between RRH and BBU — different split options give 4×–20× reduction. Essential for 5G massive MIMO.  </div>  ---  ## Checkpoint — Why CPRI is so large  <div class="quiz" data-question="cpri-tax">   <p class="quiz-question">Why is <strong>CPRI fronthaul</strong> bandwidth ~24× larger than the user data it carries?</p>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Because CPRI includes encryption overhead</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="correct">It carries raw digitized I/Q samples — not compressed user data</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Because the fiber is shared among many users</button>   <button class="quiz-option" data-answer="wrong">Because CPRI carries control signalling</button>   <p class="quiz-feedback"></p> </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Why.** CPRI carries the **raw digitized I/Q samples** — 15 bits per I and 15 per Q at 30.72 Msps per antenna — before any demodulation, equalization, or decoding. The user data (150 Mbps) is what's left *after* all PHY processing. **The fronthaul transport carries the signal, not the information.**  </div>  ---  ## Timing — critical for TDD  <div class="fragment">  **TDD** uses the same frequency for uplink and downlink. Cells must align their UL/DL switches precisely.  **Requirement:** **±1.5 μs absolute time** for 5G NR TDD.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Where timing comes from:**  | Source | Accuracy | Notes | |---|:---:|---| | **GNSS** (GPS) | < 100 ns | Primary; vulnerable to jamming | | **IEEE 1588 PTP** | < 1 μs (over fiber) | Backup; hardware timestamping needed | | **SyncE** | < 10 ppb frequency | Frequency only |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The trend:** with 5G's tighter requirements and GNSS vulnerability, operators use **PTP + SyncE as primary**, GNSS as backup.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Without precise timing, a TDD network cannot function** — uplink bursts interfere with downlink in adjacent cells.  </div>  ---  ## §5 — Economics — the 1000× gap  <div class="fragment">  **Cost per bit** across access technologies:  | Technology | Cost per GB | |---|:---:| | **Fiber (FTTH)** | $0.001–0.01 | | **Cable (DOCSIS 3.1)** | $0.01–0.05 | | **xDSL (VDSL2)** | $0.02–0.10 | | **Fixed wireless (5G FWA)** | $0.10–0.50 | | **Mobile 4G/5G** | **$1–10** |  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The economic implication:**  - Operators push traffic to **WiFi offload** (60–80% of smartphone data in urban areas) - **Fixed-mobile convergence** — single core for both - **Femtocells and small cells** — cellular at home, cheaper than macro  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **This is why mobile data is priced to discourage heavy use** — the radio spectrum is the most expensive transport.  </div>  ---  ## Fiber vs. FWA — worked example  <div class="fragment">  **Setup:** 200 homes in 20 km². Compare fiber vs. 5G FWA deployment cost.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Fiber:**  - Trench: ~15 km × $50,000/km = $750,000 - ONT: $200 × 200 = $40,000 - **Total: $790,000 → $3,950/home**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **5G FWA:**  - 2 base stations: $80,000 × 2 = $160,000 - CPE per home: $300 × 200 = $60,000 - Backhaul: $100,000 - **Total: $320,000 → $1,600/home**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **FWA wins at low density** (10 homes/km²).  **Fiber wins above ~70–80 homes/km²** — trenching is amortized.  **Below ~10 homes/km²** — both uneconomical; government subsidy or satellite needed.  </div>  ---  ## The three lessons  <div class="fragment">  **1. Wireless is the tip of the iceberg.**  Every call, every video, every sensor reading — travels mostly on **fiber**.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **2. Backhaul is the bottleneck.**  Radio capacity grows faster than operators can deploy fiber. **Microwave + E-band** fill the gap; 5G will need more fiber everywhere.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **3. Economics dictates architecture.**  Cost per bit (100–1000× gap) drives **WiFi offload**, **FMC**, **small cells**, and **fiber vs. FWA** choices. Every wireless design is really a wired-economics decision.  </div>  ---  ## Chapter summary  <div class="fragment">  **Access loop:** xDSL (copper), DOCSIS (coax), PON (fiber). **PON dominates new builds.**  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Core:** DWDM carries 8–32 Tbps per fiber; submarine cables carry 99% of international traffic.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Backhaul:** fiber preferred, but only 20–30% of cell sites have it. 5G sites need 5–25 Gbps.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Fronthaul:** CPRI carries raw I/Q — 24× user data. eCPRI reduces it for 5G.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Timing:** PTP + SyncE, backed by GNSS, for TDD synchronization.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Economics:** 100–1000× cost-per-bit difference between wired and wireless. **Density determines which wins.**  </div>  ---  ## Course complete  <div class="fragment">  **ECEG-6412 — Recent Trends in Communication Technologies**  **Part I — Wireless basics:** Ch 1, Ch 2  **Part II — Wired trends:** this chapter  **Part III — Cellular:** Ch 3 (GSM), Ch 4 (UMTS)  **Part IV — Emerging:** Ch 5 (4G/LTE), Ch 6 (NGN/IoT), Ch 7 (ML)  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **The full picture:** wireless is the last hop of a mostly-wired network, and every generation pushes deeper into the wired infrastructure's capacity limits.  </div>  <div class="fragment">  **Good luck with your final examination.**  </div>  ---  <aside class="notes">   <div style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.6;">  **Speaker notes for the whole lecture:**  - **This is a survey chapter** — 22 slides for ~90 minutes of content. Pace yourself: 3–4 minutes per slide, don't rush. - Slides 4–6 (the premise, three tiers): **the motivating frame**. Spend 5 min. Emphasize that "wireless is the tip of the iceberg" — students remember this. - Slides 7–12 (access loop): ~15 min. The **PON passive splitter** is the killer insight — no power, no maintenance in the field. The split-ratio worked example shows the trade-off. - Slide 13 (**Checkpoint 1 — rural access**): engages students. Emphasize the **crossover density** (70–80 homes/km²) — this is the "textbook" answer. - Slides 14–18 (core + submarine): ~15 min. **DWDM worked example** — one fiber carries a country's traffic. Submarine cables: 99% of international data is a striking fact. - Slides 19–22 (backhaul): **the core technical content**. Walk through the **backhaul sizing** and **CPRI bandwidth** examples carefully — these are the numbers the exam will test. - Slide 23 (**Checkpoint 2 — CPRI**): test the "raw I/Q vs. user data" insight. - Slides 24–25 (timing): brief — just emphasize **±1.5 μs requirement** and **PTP backup**. - Slides 26–29 (economics): ~10 min. The **cost-per-bit bar chart** is the slide to remember. The fiber-vs-FWA worked example shows the density crossover. - Slides 30–32 (three lessons): the closing summary — connect to the whole course.  **The exam likely tests:** PON split ratio calculation, DWDM capacity, backhaul sizing, CPRI bandwidth, and the cost-per-bit comparison. The **fiber vs. FWA economics** problem is a good exam question.    </div> </aside>
