docs.title: 1. Link budget
docs.text:
Task: Compute maximum cell radius for 900 MHz and 2 GHz links.

Setup: - \(P_{\text{tx}} = 43\) dBm. - \(G_{\text{tx}} = 15\) dBi, \(G_{\text{rx}} = 0\) dBi. - Sensitivity \(= -110\) dBm. - Receive signal = \(P_{\text{tx}} + G_{\text{tx}} + G_{\text{rx}} - \text{FSPL}\). - Set \(= -110\) dBm → max FSPL = \(43 + 15 + 0 - (-110) = 168\) dB.

900 MHz: FSPL \(= 32.44 + 20\log(900) + 20\log(d_{\text{km}}) = 91.5 + 20\log d\). Set \(= 168\): \(20\log d = 76.5 \Rightarrow d \approx 10^{3.825} \approx\) 6,700 km — absurd because no path-loss model beyond free space is considered. Real limit is set by terrestrial propagation, not free space.

2 GHz: FSPL \(= 32.44 + 20\log(2000) + 20\log d = 98.5 + 20\log d\). Set \(= 168\): \(d \approx 10^{3.475} \approx\) 3,000 km.

Interpretation: Free-space path loss alone allows transcontinental links — which is why the model is unrealistic. Real coverage is limited by Okumura–Hata / COST-231 path loss (with the slope \(> 20\) dB/decade) and shadowing.

docs.title: 2. Frequency reuse — SIR comparison
docs.text:
\(N=7\), \(n=4\): \(\text{SIR} = (21)^2/6 = 73.5 = 18.66\) dB.

\(N=3\), \(n=4\): \(\text{SIR} = (9)^2/6 = 13.5 = 11.30\) dB.

Capacity gain \(N=7 \to N=3\): \(\frac{7}{3} \approx 2.33×\) (more reuse).

SIR penalty: \(18.66 - 11.30 =\) 7.36 dB less. May not meet analog voice quality — but for digital systems with FEC (GSM, UMTS), 11 dB is acceptable.

docs.title: 3. Sectoring
docs.text:
Omni vs. 3-sector: first-tier interferers reduced from 6 (omni) to 2 (3-sector). SIR improvement = \(10\log_{10}(6/2) =\) 4.77 dB.

Target: achieve the same SIR as \(N=7\) omni (18.7 dB) with \(N = 3\) 3-sector.

With \(N = 3\): SIR_omni = 11.3 dB. Sectoring adds 4.77 dB → 16.07 dB. Below 18.7 dB — need \(N = 4\) (3-sector) to hit 18.7 dB: - \(N=4\) omni: \((12)^2/6 = 24 = 13.8\) dB. +4.77 = 18.57 dB. Close enough to 18.7. - \(N = 4\) with 3-sector matches \(N = 7\) omni SIR at \(4/7\) the frequency plan → ~1.75× more capacity.

docs.title: 5. Delay spread and coherence bandwidth
docs.text:
PDP: \(\{0, 0.5, 1, 2\}\) μs with relative powers \(\{0, -3, -6, -12\}\) dB.

Linear powers: \(1, 0.501, 0.251, 0.063\).

Total: \(P_{\text{tot}} = 1.815\).

Mean delay: \(\bar\tau = (0\cdot1 + 0.5\cdot0.501 + 1\cdot0.251 + 2\cdot0.063)/1.815 = 0.527/1.815 \approx 0.29\) μs.

RMS delay: \(\sigma_\tau^2 = \sum_i P_i(\tau_i - \bar\tau)^2/P_{\text{tot}}\). - \(1 \cdot (0.29)^2 = 0.0841\) - \(0.501 \cdot (0.21)^2 = 0.0221\) - \(0.251 \cdot (0.71)^2 = 0.1266\) - \(0.063 \cdot (1.71)^2 = 0.1843\) - Sum = 0.4171 / 1.815 = 0.2298 → \(\sigma_\tau \approx\) 0.48 μs.

Coherence bandwidth (50%): \(B_c = 1/(5\sigma_\tau) \approx\) 417 kHz.

LTE 5 MHz signal: \(B_s = 4.5\) MHz effective. \(B_s/B_c \approx 10.8\) — strongly frequency-selective.

docs.title: 6. Doppler and coherence time
docs.text:
\(f_D = v f_c / c\).

\(v\) \(f_D\) (3.5 GHz) \(T_c = 0.423/f_D\) LTE 1 ms TTI regime 3 km/h = 0.833 m/s 9.7 Hz 43.6 ms Slow fading 30 km/h = 8.33 m/s 97 Hz 4.4 ms Slow fading 120 km/h = 33.3 m/s 389 Hz 1.09 ms Borderline; interleaving needed

LTE TTI = 1 ms. At 120 km/h, \(T_c \approx 1.09\) ms ≈ TTI. Slow fading at pedestrian speeds, marginal at highway speeds — requires fast AMC and HARQ.

docs.title: 7. Fading distributions
docs.text:
Rayleigh PDF: \(p(r) = \frac{r}{\sigma^2}e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). Peak at \(r = \sigma\). \(\Omega = 2\sigma^2\), so \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt 2\) for unit \(\Omega\).

Rician PDF adds the LoS component; as \(K \to \infty\), distribution narrows around \(A\). At \(K = 3\) dB, still significant spread; at \(K = 20\) dB, nearly deterministic.

Observation: higher \(K\) means the channel is closer to AWGN, easier to decode. Rayleigh (\(K \to 0\)) is the worst case.

docs.title: 8. AMPS/TACS/GSM capacity
docs.text:
AMPS: 25 MHz uplink, 30 kHz channels = 833 channels; 42 reserved for control → ~791 voice; with \(N = 7\) → ~113/cell.

TACS: 25 MHz, 25 kHz channels = 1000 channels; some control → ~988 voice; with \(N = 7\) → ~141/cell.

GSM Phase 1: 25 MHz, 200 kHz = 125 carriers; with \(N = 4\) → 31 carriers/cell; 8 slots each → 248 voice/cell.

Capacity multiplier GSM vs AMPS: 248/113 ≈ 2.2×.

docs.text: Gen Multiple access Modulation Peak rate Core network Applications 1G FDMA FM (analog) n/a Circuit Voice 2G TDMA GMSK 14.4 kbps Circuit + HLR Voice, SMS 2.5G TDMA GMSK, 8-PSK (EDGE) 470 kbps (EDGE) + SGSN/GGSN + packet data 3G WCDMA QPSK, 16-QAM 384 kbps (UMTS) All-IP + CS/PS split + mobile data 3.5G WCDMA +64-QAM 42 Mbps (HSPA+) All-IP + broadband 4G OFDMA/SC-FDMA +256-QAM 1 Gbps (LTE-A) All-IP EPC + video, VoLTE 5G CP-OFDM +1024-QAM 20 Gbps SBA 5GC + URLLC, mMTC, slicing

docs.title: 10. 4G vs. 5G link budget
docs.text:
Assumption: Same TX power, antenna gains, sensitivity, FSPL until 500 m, then \(n = 3.5\).

LTE (2 GHz) at 1 km: FSPL(500 m) + \(35\log_{10}(1000/500)\) = \(92 + 10.5 \approx\) 102.5 dB.

5G NR (28 GHz) at 1 km: FSPL(500 m) + \(35\log_{10}(2)\) = \(120 + 10.5 \approx\) 130.5 dB.

Difference: 28 dB. At same \(P_{\text{tx}}\), 5G mmWave link has 28 dB more loss at 1 km.

To match coverage: mmWave cells must be much smaller. If path-loss slope is 35 (beyond 500 m), the range \(d\) at which 5G matches LTE coverage satisfies \(35\log_{10}(d/0.5) = 10.5 - 28\) — this is negative, so no range matches. Instead, mmWave cells must be ~50–100 m at the same TX power (dominated by FSPL even at 100 m).

Practical: mmWave cells are deployed at 100–300 m with dense small-cell grids + massive MIMO beamforming (+18 dB) to recover coverage.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 2 — Modulation and Coding
docs.text: Back to Chapter 2

docs.title: 3. Gray coding
docs.text:
Standard 16-QAM Gray mapping (per the table in §2.4.5):

(I, Q) Binary (−3,−3) 0000 (−1,−3) 0001 (+1,−3) 0011 (+3,−3) 0010 (−3,−1) 0100 ... ...

Each adjacent pair differs by 1 bit — verified by construction.

BER benefit: \(P_b \approx P_s / \log_2 M = P_s / 4\) (versus \(P_b = P_s\) without Gray coding).

At the same SER, Gray coding reduces BER by ~6 dB in power (or by ~4× in rate, since the same SER corresponds to the same BER only if the extra bits are also Gray-decoded).

docs.title: 4. OFDM parameters
docs.text:
Target: \(B = 20\) MHz, 5 bps/Hz, 64-QAM.

Subcarrier spacing: 15 kHz (LTE standard). FFT size: \(N = B / \Delta f = 20\times10^6/15\times10^3 \approx 1333\); round up to 2048 (or use 1024 for a smaller channel). Useful symbol duration: \(T_u = 1/\Delta f = 66.67\) μs. CP length: \(\tau_{\text{rms}} = 500\) ns; use \(T_{cp} \approx 5\tau_{\text{rms}} = 2.5\) μs → round to 4.7 μs (LTE normal CP).

CP overhead: \(T_{cp}/(T_u + T_{cp}) = 4.7/(66.67+4.7) \approx\) 6.6%.

docs.title: 5. Raised cosine pulse
docs.text:
\(p_{RC}(t) = \text{sinc}(t/T_s) \cdot \cos(\pi\beta t/T_s)/(1 - (2\beta t/T_s)^2)\).

Bandwidths for \(R_s = 1\) Msym/s: - \(\beta = 0\): \(B = 0.5\) MHz. - \(\beta = 0.22\): \(B = 0.61\) MHz. - \(\beta = 0.5\): \(B = 0.75\) MHz. - \(\beta = 1\): \(B = 1\) MHz.

Timing-error penalty: With \(\beta = 0\) (sinc), any timing offset causes ISI from sinc tails that don't decay — significant loss. With \(\beta = 0.22\), the time-domain tails decay much faster — penalty is small. This is why \(\beta = 0.22\) is standard in LTE — small excess bandwidth for robust timing.

docs.title: 6. 5G NR link budget — 3.5 GHz vs. 28 GHz
docs.text:
3.5 GHz (sub-6): - FSPL at 200 m: 32.44 + 20log(3500) + 20log(0.2) = 32.44 + 70.88 − 13.98 = 89.34 dB. - FSPL slope: use \(n = 3\) (urban micro). At distance \(d\) beyond 200 m: FSPL(d) = 89.34 + 30log(d/0.2). - Received signal = \(P_{\text{tx}} + G_{\text{bs}} + G_{\text{ue}} - \text{FSPL} = 23 + 15 + 0 - \text{FSPL} = 38 - \text{FSPL}\). - Sensitivity −100 dBm → max FSPL = 138 dB → \(d\) = 0.2 × \(10^{(138-89.34)/30}\) ≈ 0.2 × 41.9 ≈ 8.4 km. But this neglects interference — realistic range is 500 m – 2 km.

28 GHz (mmWave): - FSPL at 100 m: 32.44 + 20log(28000) + 20log(0.1) = 32.44 + 88.94 − 20 = 101.38 dB. - With \(n = 3.5\) slope and beamforming gain +18 dB (64-element array): effective FSPL + beamforming = 101.38 − 18 = 83.38 dB. - Max FSPL = 138 dB → \(d\) = 0.1 × \(10^{(138-101.38+18)/35}\) ≈ 0.1 × \(10^{1.56}\) ≈ 0.36 km = 360 m.

Interpretation: mmWave's higher FSPL (21 dB higher than 3.5 GHz at same distance) is partially compensated by massive MIMO beamforming (+18 dB). Net penalty ~3 dB → range drops from ~1–2 km to ~300–400 m. This is why mmWave is dense small cells.

docs.title: 7. CDMA pole capacity (UMTS voice vs. data)
docs.text:
Voice: \(G = 3.84\times10^6 / 12.2\times10^3 \approx 315\). \((E_b/N_0)_{\text{req}} = 5\) dB = 3.16. \(i = 0.5\). Activity factor \(v = 0.6\).

\(N_{\text{pole}} = 1 + G/((E_b/N_0) \cdot (1+i) \cdot v) = 1 + 315/(3.16 \cdot 1.5 \cdot 0.6) \approx 1 + 110 \approx\) 111.

Data (384 kbps): \(G = 3.84\times10^6/384\times10^3 = 10\). \((E_b/N_0)_{\text{req}} = 2\) dB = 1.58. \(v = 1\).

\(N_{\text{pole}} = 1 + 10/(1.58 \cdot 1.5 \cdot 1) \approx 1 + 4.2 \approx\) 5.2.

Realistic (50% of pole): voice ~55 users, data ~2.6 users.

docs.title: 8. (7,4) Hamming code — encode, error, decode
docs.text:
Generator matrix (from Chapter 2 §2.8.2): \(G = [I_4 | P]\) where \(P\) = 4×3 parity matrix.

Encode 1101: Using \(p_1 = u_1\oplus u_2\oplus u_4 = 1+1+1 = 1\), \(p_2 = u_1\oplus u_3\oplus u_4 = 1+0+1 = 0\), \(p_3 = u_2\oplus u_3\oplus u_4 = 1+0+1 = 0\).

Codeword: 1101100.

Introduce error at position 3 (bit 0 → 1): received 1111100.

Syndrome: \(H \cdot r^T\). With \(H\) whose column 3 equals binary 3 (011), the syndrome is 011 = decimal 3 → error at position 3. Correct by flipping bit 3: → 1101100. ✓

docs.title: 9. Convolutional code — encode, Viterbi
docs.text:
Rate 1/2, K=3, generators \(G_1 = 111\), \(G_2 = 101\).

Encoder table (state = last 2 input bits):

Input State \(G_1\) out \(G_2\) out New state 1 00 1 1 10 0 10 1 0 01 1 01 0 1 10 1 10 0 0 11

Encoded: 11 10 01 00 (8 bits from 4 input bits).

Viterbi decoding with one error: the trellis decoder finds the closest path in Hamming distance — the path corresponding to the original input, since it has distance 1 while other paths have distance ≥ 2.

docs.title: 10. Source + channel coding redundancy
docs.text:
G.729 at 8 kbps + rate-1/2 FEC = 16 kbps on air.

vs. raw PCM G.711 at 64 kbps with no FEC.

Redundancy added by FEC: 100% (16/8). Total on-air savings: 16/64 = 25% of G.711's bandwidth.

Trade-off: G.729 is a parametric codec (analysis-by-synthesis LPC) — loses waveform fidelity, sounds "synthetic" vs. G.711's toll quality. But 4× bandwidth saving is worth it for cellular. The rate-1/2 FEC protects against errors — effective at low SNR, but not miraculous.

docs.title: 11. Shannon gap — 5G NR
docs.text:
Setup: 100 MHz at 3.5 GHz, 4×4 MIMO, SNR = 15 dB.

Shannon capacity (per spatial stream, assuming i.i.d. MIMO): \(C_s = 100\times10^6 \times \log_2(1+31.62) \approx 100\times10^6 \times 5.03 \approx 503\) Mbps. 4 streams → ~2 Gbps. With MIMO's own factor (approximately 4× for 4×4 i.i.d.), total ~2 Gbps.

Practical 5G NR peak with 4×4 MIMO, 100 MHz, 256-QAM, rate-3/4: - Per stream: 100 MHz × 8 bps/Hz (256-QAM × 3/4) = 800 Mbps. - 4 streams: 3.2 Gbps — well above Shannon at 15 dB! Because 256-QAM operating at 15 dB is unrealistic (requires ~30 dB).

Realistic at SNR = 15 dB — 64-QAM, rate-3/4: - Per stream: 100 × 4.5 = 450 Mbps. - 4 streams: 1.8 Gbps. - Shannon gap: 2 Gbps (Shannon) vs. 1.8 Gbps (practical) = ~0.5 dB gap — extremely efficient.

docs.title: 12. Fixed rate, different modulations
docs.text:
Target 50 Mbps in 20 MHz = 2.5 bps/Hz.

Modulation Coding Required SNR (approx) Notes QPSK 1/3 ~5 dB Robust, low spectral efficiency 16-QAM 1/2 ~10 dB Middle ground 64-QAM 3/4 ~18 dB High rate, needs good channel

Most power-efficient (lowest SNR): QPSK + rate-1/3. Most robust to channel errors: also QPSK + rate-1/3.

Why 64-QAM is used at all: when the channel is good (close to base station), it delivers the same 2.5 bps/Hz with less spectrum — freeing bandwidth for others. Adaptive modulation switches between these based on channel conditions.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 3 — GSM
docs.text: Back to Chapter 3

docs.title: 1. TDMA bit rate
docs.text:
Burst: 156.25 bits in 577 μs. Burst rate per slot: \(156.25 / 577\times10^{-6} = 270,831\) bps ≈ 270.833 kbps per slot per carrier.

Or equivalently: 8 slots × 156.25 bits per 4.615 ms frame = 1250 / 4.615×10^-3 = 270.833 kbps.

docs.title: 2. Capacity per cell
docs.text:
Setup: 4 TRXs per cell, 8 slots each, 2% blocking.

Channels: 4 × 8 = 32 voice channels per cell (minus control; use ~28 for voice).

Erlang-B for 28 channels at 2% blocking: ~19 Erlangs.

Subscribers at 25 mErlang each: \(19/0.025 =\) ~760 subscribers.

docs.title: 3. GSM 1800 carriers
docs.text:
GSM 1800: uplink 1710–1785 MHz = 75 MHz; spacing 200 kHz → 375 carriers. Guard bands reduce to ~374 usable carriers.

GSM 900: 25 MHz / 200 kHz = 125 carriers → 124 usable (1 guard).

1800 has 3× the carriers of 900 — the trade-off is higher propagation loss at 1.8 GHz (~6 dB worse than 900 MHz).

docs.title: 4. GMSK spectrum
docs.text:
For \(BT = 0.3\), the 99% power bandwidth is ~200 kHz (matching the channel). At \(\pm 200\) kHz from carrier, the spectral mask is −60 dBc (well-rejected). The Gaussian filter trades: - Smaller \(BT\) → narrower spectrum, more ISI. - Larger \(BT\) → wider spectrum, less ISI.

\(BT = 0.3\) is the sweet spot for GSM: fits the 200 kHz channel, ISI within Viterbi equalizer's correction capability.

docs.title: 5. Speech + channel coding rate
docs.text:
Speech: 260 bits per 20 ms (13 kbps).

After Class 1a CRC (50 bits + 3 = 53) + Class 1b conv. code (132 × 2 = 264) + Class 2 uncoded (78): ~395 bits per 20 ms.

On-air rate per speech user (only TCH frames): ~19.75 kbps per user (TCH/F). Compare with carrier 270.833 kbps.

Efficiency: Speech codec 13 kbps from 64 kbps PCM = ~5:1 source compression. Plus channel coding doubles the bits → 26 kbps total. Divided by 8 users → 3.25 kbps per user at the carrier level. Very efficient.

docs.title: 6. Authentication failure
docs.text:
Scenario: Mobile returns SRES' ≠ SRES.

Network action: MSC/VLR rejects authentication. Call is dropped; mobile is not allowed to register (in roaming) or is denied the requested service.

Vs. impersonation: An impersonator without the SIM cannot produce the correct SRES — A3 is a cryptographic function requiring \(K_i\). Without \(K_i\) (stored only in SIM and AuC), SRES cannot be forged. The attack is only possible if \(K_i\) is extracted from a physical SIM (COMP128 attack) — after which a cloned SIM can authenticate as the victim.

docs.title: 7. Handover timing
docs.text:
Scenario: Mobile crosses from cell A (1 km) to cell B (1 km) at 100 km/h = 27.8 m/s.

Cell crossing time: ~2 × 1 km / 27.8 m/s = 72 seconds (from A center to B center).

With 500 ms decision window + 150 ms handover execution: Handover occurs at the point where the trigger condition has been met for 500 ms — usually ~1–2 dB before the true crossover. In time: ~1.5–2.5 s before the mid-point — plenty of margin.

At 500 km/h (high-speed train): crossing time = 14 s. Handover still works, but 3–4 handovers per minute; ping-pong becomes a real risk (need larger hysteresis).

docs.title: 8. GPRS throughput
docs.text:
Setup: Multislot class 12 (4 DL, 4 UL), CS-3 (15.6 kbps/slot), 70% efficiency.

DL: 4 × 15.6 × 0.7 = 43.7 kbps. UL: 4 × 15.6 × 0.7 = 43.7 kbps.

vs. CSD: 9.6 kbps → 4.5× improvement.

In practice, real GPRS users see 20–40 kbps due to contention. Not enough for mobile internet — needed EDGE for that.

docs.title: 9. EDGE MCS comparison
docs.text:
MCS-5: 8-PSK, rate 0.37, gross 59.2 kbps → net ~22 kbps per slot. MCS-9: 8-PSK, rate 1.0, gross 59.2 kbps → net ~59 kbps per slot.

Required SNR: MCS-5 works at ~10 dB; MCS-9 needs ~25 dB.

Near cell edge: use MCS-5 (higher robustness, lower rate). At cell center: MCS-9 (higher rate).

The adaptive MCS scheme is the key EDGE innovation — choose modulation+coding based on measured channel quality.

docs.title: 10. SMS segmentation
docs.text:
200-character message > 160-char SMS limit.

With concatenated SMS (3GPP TS 23.040): each segment carries 153 chars (140 bytes payload minus 7 bytes for UDH). 200/153 ≈ 2 segments.

Per-message overhead: 7 bytes for concatenation UDH (User Data Header) — but only in concatenated messages. For a single SMS, overhead is ~10 bytes (TP-DA + TP-SCTS + TP-PID + TP-DCS + TP-UDL), and payload is 140 bytes → 160 chars of 7-bit ASCII.

docs.title: 11. Roaming trace
docs.text:
Mobile attaches in Germany (MCC 262):

  1. IMSI attach to German MSC/VLR.
  2. VLR queries HLR via Update Location.
  3. HLR authenticates via AuC (generates 5 triplets).
  4. HLR updates subscriber's current VLR = German VLR.
  5. HLR downloads subscription data (QoS, roaming restrictions).
  6. VLR sends TMSI to mobile — used for future paging.
  7. HLR deletes old VLR entry (Ethiopian VLR) via Cancel Location.

Entities: Visited MSC/VLR (Germany) ↔ HLR (Ethiopia) ↔ AuC (Ethiopia) ↔ old VLR (Ethiopia).

HLR change: location info (new VLR address), possibly roaming restrictions.

docs.title: 12. GSM vs. UMTS
docs.text:
Aspect GSM UMTS Chip rate 270.833 kbps 3.84 Mcps Bandwidth 200 kHz 5 MHz Multiple access TDMA WCDMA Modulation GMSK QPSK / 16-QAM / 64-QAM Handover Hard (break-before-make) Soft + softer + hard Peak rate ~470 kbps (EDGE) 42 Mbps (HSPA+) Security A3/A5/A8 AKA + f8/f9

Fundamental differences: multiple access (TDMA vs. CDMA), chip rate (200 kbps vs. 3.84 Mcps), handover (hard vs. soft).

Evolutionary differences: modulation (GMSK vs. QAM), peak rate, security algorithms.

Fundamental: UMTS fundamentally changes the air interface (TDMA → CDMA); the rest is evolutionary.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 4 — UMTS
docs.text: Back to Chapter 4

docs.title: 1. OVSF allocation
docs.text:
OVSF tree up to SF = 8: \(C_1 = (1)\), \(C_{2,0} = (1,1)\), \(C_{2,1} = (1,-1)\), etc.

Allocate: - Voice at SF = 128 — any leaf at SF 128, say \(C_{128, 100}\). - Video at SF = 32 — a different subtree, e.g., \(C_{32, 10}\). - Data at SF = 16 — a third subtree, e.g., \(C_{16, 3}\).

No conflict: none of these codes is an ancestor or descendant of the others — all from different subtrees. If voice at SF 128 were on the path to \(C_{16, 3}\), conflict.

docs.title: 2. Processing gain
docs.text:
Service \(R\) \(G = 3.84\text{M}/R\) Voice (12.2 kbps AMR) 12.2 kbps 315 (25 dB) Video (64 kbps) 64 kbps 60 (17.8 dB) Data (384 kbps) 384 kbps 10 (10 dB) HSPA peak (14.4 Mbps) 14.4 Mbps 0.27 (breaks down)

Breakdown: HSPA peak rate (14.4 Mbps) exceeds the chip rate (3.84 Mcps) — the "processing gain" concept applies only to spread-spectrum below the chip rate. For high-rate HSPA, use spectral efficiency (bits/Hz) instead.

docs.title: 3. Rake diversity gain
docs.text:
Paths: 4 with average power \([0, -3, -6, -9]\) dB → linear \([1, 0.501, 0.251, 0.126]\).

Sum: 1.878. Single-path average = 1.0.

Diversity gain: \(10\log_{10}(1.878/1) \approx\) 2.74 dB.

(If all 4 paths had equal average power, gain would be \(10\log_4 = 6.02\) dB. The unequal paths reduce the effective gain.)

docs.title: 4. Power control convergence
docs.text:
Start: 20 dBm. Target: 23 dBm. Step: 1 dB per TPC.

Steps needed: 3 dB / 1 dB per step = 3 TPC commands.

At 1500 Hz (1 TPC per slot): 3 slots × 0.667 ms = 2 ms.

Very fast — matches the rate needed to track Rayleigh fading (coherence time at 3 km/h ≈ 70 ms; at 100 km/h ≈ 2 ms).

docs.title: 5. Pole capacity for UMTS voice
docs.text:
\(N_{\text{pole}} = 1 + W/(R \cdot (E_b/N_0)_{\text{req}} \cdot (1+i) \cdot v)\).

  • \(W = 3.84\times10^6\) Hz.
  • \(R = 12.2\times10^3\) bps.
  • \((E_b/N_0) = 5\) dB = 3.16.
  • \(i = 0.5\).
  • \(v = 0.6\).

\(N_{\text{pole}} = 1 + 3.84\times10^6 / (12.2\times10^3 \cdot 3.16 \cdot 1.5 \cdot 0.6) \approx 1 + 110 \approx\) 111.

Realistic at 50%: ~55 voice users per cell.

docs.title: 6. Interference margin
docs.text:
\(M = -10\log_{10}(1 - \eta)\).

\(\eta\) \(M\) 0.3 1.55 dB 0.5 3.01 dB 0.7 5.23 dB 0.9 10.0 dB

As \(\eta \to 1\): \(M \to \infty\) — the cell radius shrinks to zero, capacity diverges (impossible). Realistic design: \(\eta \le 0.5\) (50% of pole).

docs.title: 7. HSDPA peak rate derivation
docs.text:
Setup: 15 codes, SF = 16, 16-QAM, rate 3/4.

  • Per code symbol rate: \(3.84\) Mcps / 16 = 240 ksym/s.
  • 16-QAM = 4 bits/sym → 240 × 4 = 960 kbps per code.
  • Rate 3/4 → 960 × 0.75 = 720 kbps per code.
  • 15 codes → 720 × 15 = 10.8 Mbps (practical) or 14.4 Mbps (rate-1 theoretical).

HSPA+ R7 with 64-QAM: - 6 bits/sym: 240 × 6 = 1440 kbps/code. - Rate 3/4 → 1080 kbps/code. - ×15 codes = 16.2 Mbps. - ×2 MIMO streams = ~32 Mbps peak (standard spec: 28 Mbps accounting for reference signals).

R11 with 4×4 MIMO: - 32 Mbps × 2 (per stream doubling of MIMO) × 2 (dual cell, DC-HSDPA) = ~168 Mbps.

docs.title: 8. HSUPA peak rate
docs.text:
Setup: SF=2 for E-DPDCH, QPSK, rate 1.

  • Symbol rate: 3.84 Mcps / 2 = 1920 ksym/s.
  • QPSK: ×2 = 3840 kbps per code.
  • Two codes (SF=2 + SF=4) → 1.5× total = 5.76 Mbps.

With 16-QAM (R7): 1920 × 4 = 7680 kbps per code × 1.5 (two codes) = 11.5 Mbps.

docs.title: 9. Soft handover events
docs.text:
Scenario: Active = {cellA}, monitored = {cellB, cellC}.

  • cellB 5 dB better than cellA: Event 1A triggers — cellB enters reporting range. RNC adds cellB to active set → 2-cell soft handover.

  • cellA 10 dB below cellB: Event 1B for cellA — it's dropped from active. Now active = {cellB}.

  • cellB and cellC both better than cellA: Event 1C triggers (a non-active cell becomes better than an active one). RNC replaces cellA with cellC → active = {cellB, cellC}.

docs.title: 10. Cell breathing
docs.text:
Setup: 4 km radius at 40% load (interference margin 2.2 dB). What radius at 70% load (5.2 dB)?

Extra path loss due to load: 5.2 − 2.2 = 3.0 dB.

Path-loss exponent 3: \(d_1^{-3} / d_2^{-3} = 10^{3/10} \approx 2.0\) → \(d_2/d_1 = 2^{1/3} \approx 1.26\).

Wait — more interference means less range. So at 70% load (5.2 dB margin), the link budget is 3 dB smaller. Range shrinks.

\(d_{70}/d_{40} = 10^{-3/(10\times3)} = 10^{-0.1} \approx\) 0.794.

New radius: 4 × 0.794 ≈ 3.18 km.

Cell "breathes" — 20% smaller at 70% vs. 40% load.

docs.title: 11. HSDPA vs. HSUPA
docs.text: Aspect HSDPA HSUPA Direction Downlink Uplink Peak (R5/R6) 14.4 Mbps 5.76 Mbps HARQ Async, adaptive Sync/async (adaptive) Scheduling NodeB fast scheduler, shared HS-DSCH NodeB grants (absolute + relative) Key innovation AMC + fast scheduling + HARQ at NodeB Fast uplink scheduling + E-DCH

docs.title: 12. HSPA+ evolution — fundamental limits
docs.text:
Release Peak DL Notes R7 28 Mbps 64-QAM, 2×2 MIMO R8 42 Mbps DC-HSDPA (dual cell) R9 42 Mbps DL / 23 Mbps UL DC-HSUPA added R10 84 Mbps 4-carrier HSDPA R11 168 Mbps 4×4 MIMO + 4-carrier R12+ 336 Mbps 8×8 MIMO

Fundamental limits pushing to LTE: 1. WCDMA's 5 MHz carrier caps peak spectral efficiency at ~5 bps/Hz (vs. 15+ for 20 MHz LTE). 2. Interference-limited capacity — adding more users degrades all. 3. Control overhead — scheduling, HARQ, pilots consume 30–40% of capacity. 4. Hardware complexity — massive MIMO needs wider bandwidth for beamforming gain.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 5 — 4G/LTE/WiMAX
docs.text: Back to Chapter 5

docs.title: 1. IMT-Advanced check for LTE-A
docs.text:
Requirement Target LTE-A (R10) Meets? Peak DL (low mobility) 1 Gbps 3 Gbps ✅ Peak DL (high mobility) 100 Mbps ≥ 100 Mbps ✅ Peak UL 500 Mbps 1.5 Gbps ✅ Spectral efficiency (peak) 15 bps/Hz 30 bps/Hz (8×8) ✅ Latency (user plane) < 10 ms ~10 ms ✅ Latency (control) < 100 ms ~50 ms ✅ Mobility 350 km/h 350 km/h ✅ All-IP Required ✅ ✅

LTE-A meets or exceeds all IMT-Advanced requirements.

docs.title: 2. RB count for 20 MHz
docs.text:
20 MHz / 180 kHz = 111.1 RBs. LTE spec allocates 100 RBs (18 MHz) with 2 MHz reserved for guard bands.

Where the 11 RBs go: guard band on both edges (~10% of bandwidth), plus a small DC subcarrier gap.

docs.title: 3. Peak throughput computations
docs.text:
(a) 10 MHz, 2×2 MIMO, 64-QAM, rate-3/4: - RBs: 50 per subframe. - REs per RB (after 20% RS overhead): ~134. - Per RE: 6 × 3/4 = 4.5 bits. - Per subframe per stream: 50 × 134 × 4.5 = 30,150 bits. - Per second: 30.15 Mbps. - 2 streams: 60.3 Mbps.

(b) 20 MHz, 4×4 MIMO, 64-QAM, rate-3/4: - Per stream: 60.3 Mbps (same as 20 MHz single stream). - 4 streams: 241 Mbps.

(c) 60 MHz (3×CA), 4×4 MIMO: - 3 × 241 = 723 Mbps.

docs.title: 4. SC-FDMA vs. OFDMA PAPR
docs.text:
UE with 23 dBm PA: - OFDMA: PAPR 10 dB → PA must back off to 13 dBm average. - SC-FDMA: PAPR 4 dB → PA can operate at 19 dBm average.

Uplink power gain: 6 dB.

Cell radius with slope \(n = 3.5\): - OFDMA radius: \(R_1\). - SC-FDMA radius: \(R_2\) where \(10 \log_{10}(R_2/R_1) \times 3.5 = 6\) → \(R_2/R_1 \approx 10^{6/35} \approx\) 1.48×.

SC-FDMA gives ~1.5× cell radius. This is why LTE chose it for uplink — UE coverage is the bottleneck, and 6 dB uplink gain is worth 50% more coverage.

docs.title: 5. MIMO modes for given channel
docs.text:
10 dB SNR, rich scattering: high-rank channel → spatial multiplexing (2 or 4 streams). The SNR is sufficient for the multi-stream detection.

0 dB SNR, one dominant path: rank-1 channel → transmit diversity (Alamouti/SFBC) — sends the same data via orthogonal codes to gain 3 dB diversity. Spatial multiplexing would fail (multi-stream detection needs high SNR).

The eNodeB uses CQI/RI (rank indicator) feedback to select the mode.

docs.title: 6. EPC latency budget
docs.text:
Component Latency UE processing 2 ms Frame alignment (subframe) 0.5 ms Air interface (HARQ + decoding) 4–8 ms eNodeB processing 1 ms S1-U transport 1–2 ms S-GW processing 0.5 ms P-GW processing 1 ms Total one-way ~10 ms Round-trip (RTT) ~20 ms

For a Google server over the internet: add ~10–50 ms (public internet). Total RTT ~30–70 ms — much better than UMTS's ~100–200 ms.

docs.title: 7. Carrier aggregation design
docs.text:
Available: 10 MHz @ 800, 20 MHz @ 1800, 20 MHz @ 2600.

CA configuration: 3 component carriers (inter-band CA): 1×10 + 1×20 + 1×20 = 50 MHz total.

Peak DL with 4×4 MIMO: - 50 MHz × 4 streams × ~7.2 bps/Hz (64-QAM rate 3/4, ideal) = ~1.44 Gbps.

Deployment challenges: - Inter-band CA requires multiple transceivers — power amplifier, antenna per band. - Timing/phase synchronization across bands — critical for carrier aggregation. - Cross-carrier scheduling — the primary carrier schedules the secondary carriers.

docs.title: 8. WiMAX capacity
docs.text:
Setup: 10 MHz TDD (3:1 DL/UL), 2×2 MIMO.

Per 10 MHz, 2×2: ~30 Mbps DL peak (assuming 64-QAM rate-3/4). 3:1 TDD pattern: DL gets 75% of frame → 30 × 0.75 = ~22.5 Mbps per sector.

Site (3-sector): 22.5 × 3 = 67.5 Mbps DL peak. Average at 50%: ~34 Mbps per site.

docs.title: 9. Cell-edge improvement with CoMP
docs.text:
Before CoMP: average 50 Mbps, edge (5%) 2 Mbps. CoMP improves edge SIR by 3 dB → 2× throughput at cell edge (in interference-limited regime).

After CoMP: edge ~4 Mbps.

% of users below 1 Mbps: In a typical Rayleigh fading cell, the CDF rises steeply. Before: maybe 1% below 1 Mbps. After: effectively 0% (they're now above 2 Mbps).

Realistic: CoMP improves edge throughput 30–50%, moving the 5th-percentile user from 2 Mbps to 3 Mbps in a 5 dB SIR improvement scenario (not full 2× due to other limits).

docs.title: 10. Massive MIMO gain
docs.text:
Setup: 64 antennas at BS, 8 UEs. Beamforming per user = 64/8 = 8 antennas per beam.

Beamforming gain: \(10\log_{10}(8)\) = 9 dB per user (assuming independent beams).

MU-MIMO multiplexing gain: 8 UEs served simultaneously vs. 2×2 MIMO (2 UEs) = 4× capacity.

Total capacity vs. 2×2 MIMO: 4× from multiplexing + 3 dB (2×) from per-user SNR = ~8× (very rough — actual depends on channel).

docs.title: 11. Backhaul sizing
docs.text:
Peak per sector: 600 Mbps. 3 sectors: 1.8 Gbps per site peak.

Average at 60%: 1.08 Gbps.

Fiber backhaul: provision ~2 Gbps (2× headroom) — a 10G or 25G fiber is more than enough.

Microwave: 4 × E-band at 1 Gbps each = 4 Gbps aggregate — also viable but weather-sensitive.

docs.title: 12. 5G vs. 4G comparison
docs.text:
Aspect LTE-A 5G NR (Sub-6) Factor Peak DL 3 Gbps 10–20 Gbps ~4–7× Avg DL per user 50–100 Mbps 100–500 Mbps 2–5× Latency ~10 ms ~1–4 ms 3–10× Capacity/km² ~10 Mbps/km² ~100 Mbps/km² 10× Massive MIMO 8×8 64–256 8–32×

Reasons for 5G's advantage: - Wider bandwidth (100 MHz vs. 20–100 MHz). - Massive MIMO (64–256 antennas vs. 8). - Scalable numerology (15–240 kHz). - mmWave (400 MHz channels, 10× spectrum). - Small-cell densification.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 6 — NGN
docs.text: Back to Chapter 6

docs.title: 1. BLE battery life
docs.text:
Setup: Transmit 1 ms at 10 mA every 1 s. Sleep 5 μA. Battery 250 mAh (CR2032).

Energy per second: (1 ms × 10 mA) + (999 ms × 5 μA) = 0.01 mA·s + 0.005 mA·s = 0.015 mAs ≈ 0.0000042 mAh.

Per hour: 3600 × 0.0000042 = 0.0151 mAh/h.

Battery life: 250 / 0.0151 ≈ 16,500 hours ≈ 690 days ≈ 1.9 years.

At 10 s interval: transmissions per hour = 360 (vs. 3600) → 0.00151 mAh/h → ~165,000 hours → ~19 years (unrealistic — limited by self-discharge, ~1%/year). Realistic: ~10 years.

Trade-off: longer interval → much longer battery, but slower update rate. Choose based on application's freshness requirement.

docs.title: 2. ZigBee mesh design
docs.text:
Area: 200 m × 200 m. Coverage per node: 25 m. Router spacing: 20 m (with overlap) → grid of 11 × 11 = 121 routers. Corner-to-corner hops: 200 m / 20 m = 10 hops. Latency per hop: ~15–30 ms → 10 hops = 150–300 ms end-to-end.

Alternative: cluster tree with 4 coordinators (one per quadrant of 100×100 m). Fewer hops, more centralization.

docs.title: 3. WiFi 6E deployment
docs.text:
Area: 10,000 m². Users: 5000.

AP density: WiFi 6E AP covers ~250 m² per AP in high-density (limited by interference, not coverage) → ~40 APs.

Channels: 6 GHz has 14 × 160 MHz channels or 59 × 20 MHz. With 40 APs, use 80 MHz channels → 7 non-overlapping channels → 6 APs share each channel with careful placement (same channel, different sector).

Per-user peak: 40 APs × 2.4 Gbps (WiFi 6, 80 MHz, 4×4) = 96 Gbps total. / 5000 users = 19 Mbps per user — enough for most usage.

docs.title: 4. UWB precision
docs.text:
Bandwidth 1.5 GHz: range resolution = \(c/(2B) = 3\times10^8/(2 \times 1.5\times10^9) \approx\) 10 cm.

Timing error 200 ps: distance error = \(c \times \Delta t / 2 = 3\times10^8 \times 200\times10^{-12} / 2 \approx\) 3 cm.

For AirTag-style finding: ±10 cm is more than enough to guide a user to a lost item — yes, UWB is overkill for this, but future applications (AR, precise automation) need it.

docs.title: 5. LoRa airtime
docs.text:
Sensor: 10 bytes payload. LoRa PHY overhead: preamble, header, CRC ~13 bytes total. So transmit ~23 bytes.

Airtime ≈ (payload bits) / (data rate): - SF7: 23 × 8 / 5470 ≈ 34 ms. - SF10: 23 × 8 / 980 ≈ 188 ms. - SF12: 23 × 8 / 250 ≈ 736 ms.

For 1 km deployment: SF7 suffices (sensitivity -123 dBm). Air time 34 ms is small → maximize battery.

If 1 km is marginal: use SF9 or SF10 for reliability, at 5× power cost.

docs.title: 6. NB-IoT coverage extension
docs.text:
LTE cell radius: 2 km (typical urban). NB-IoT coverage extension: +20 dB.

Using path-loss exponent 3.5: \(d_2/d_1 = 10^{20/(10\times3.5)} = 10^{0.571} \approx 3.7\).

NB-IoT range: ~7.4 km (vs. LTE's 2 km).

Realistic: with 20 dB extension + lower data rate (26 kbps) and repetitions, NB-IoT achieves 10–15 km in rural areas — matches spec.

docs.title: 7. 5G peak rate
docs.text:
Setup: 400 MHz (mmWave), 64-QAM, 8-layer MIMO, rate-3/4.

  • Spectral efficiency per layer: 6 bits/sym × 3/4 = 4.5 bps/Hz.
  • Per layer: 400 × 4.5 = 1800 Mbps.
  • 8 layers: 14.4 Gbps.

With 256-QAM (5G max): 8 bps/sym × 3/4 = 6 bps/Hz × 400 × 8 = 19.2 Gbps (matches "20 Gbps" peak spec).

docs.title: 8. Network slicing design
docs.text:
Requirements: - 1000 IoT sensors (mMTC) — low rate, high density, low power. - 50 video streams × 20 Mbps = 1 Gbps (eMBB). - 10 robotic surgery links × 1 ms latency (URLLC).

Slices:

mMTC: 1000 sensors at 10 kbps avg = 10 Mbps aggregate. Low priority, no latency SLA. Reserve ~20 MHz spectrum, small UPF at edge.

eMBB: 1 Gbps. High throughput, low priority for latency. Reserve 60 MHz with MU-MIMO, dedicated eMBB UPF.

URLLC: 10 × 1 Mbps + 1 ms latency + 99.999% reliability. Reserve ~10 MHz with pre-allocated RBs, dedicated local UPF at factory edge.

Isolation: each slice has its own control plane (AMF/SMF/PCF), user plane (UPF), and RAN resources (via slicing-aware scheduler). URLLC has highest priority.

docs.title: 9. Edge computing latency
docs.text:
AR application: 10 ms end-to-end. - UE air interface: 1 ms - Edge compute: 2 ms - Application: 3 ms - Total edge: 6 ms — fits within 10 ms ✓

With centralized cloud: - Air interface: 1 ms - Network to cloud: 20 ms - Cloud compute: 2 ms - Application: 3 ms - Total cloud: 26 ms — exceeds 10 ms ✗

Conclusion: AR requires edge computing.

docs.title: 10. Connectivity choice
docs.text: Application Best fit Why Water meter reading NB-IoT or LoRa 10–15 km range, low power, operator-managed (NB-IoT) or private (LoRa) Warehouse asset tracking BLE + WiFi/UWB Indoor, precise location, smartphone integration; UWB for cm-precision Agricultural soil moisture LoRa Long range (up to 15 km), low power (10-year battery), license-free Vehicle telemetry 5G RedCap or 4G LTE Mobility, moderate data rate, ubiquitous coverage

docs.title: 11. WiFi 7 MLO
docs.text:
Setup: 2.4 GHz (40 MHz) + 5 GHz (160 MHz) + 6 GHz (320 MHz) MLO. 4×4 MIMO. 4096-QAM.

Max spectral efficiency: 4096-QAM = 12 bits/sym, rate-5/6 coding → 10 bps/Hz.

Per-link throughput: - 2.4 GHz: 40 MHz × 10 = 400 Mbps. - 5 GHz: 160 MHz × 10 = 1600 Mbps. - 6 GHz: 320 MHz × 10 = 3200 Mbps. - Sum single-stream: 5200 Mbps. - 4×4 MIMO: ×4 = 20,800 Mbps = 20.8 Gbps.

With MLO aggregation: combines all three bands → ~20.8 Gbps (not 46 Gbps — the 46 Gbps figure assumes 320 MHz × 4096-QAM × 16 spatial streams, which is the theoretical max with all bands and 16×16 MIMO).

docs.title: 12. 5G vs. 4G per use case
docs.text:
Use case LTE 5G Improvement eMBB 150 Mbps (Cat-4), ~50 Mbps avg 10–20 Gbps, ~500 Mbps avg 10–30× URLLC ~50 ms latency (not URLLC) 1 ms latency, 99.999% 50× latency mMTC ~2000 devices/km² (LTE-M) 1M devices/km² 500×

5G is 10–500× better depending on the use case — and it's the first generation to natively support URLLC and mMTC, not just eMBB.

docs.title: Solutions to Chapter 7 — ML for Communications
docs.text: Back to Chapter 7

docs.title: 1. Data generation and channel estimation
docs.text:
Approach: Generate 10,000 channels from 3GPP TR 38.901 EPA model with random SNRs in [0, 20] dB. Transmit QPSK pilots. Train a small CNN (~50k parameters) to map received pilots → channel estimate.

Expected result: at 10 dB SNR, ML NMSE ≈ −13 to −14 dB, matching MMSE with known covariance (−14 dB). LS baseline is −8 dB. ML saves ~5 dB without needing covariance.

If training distribution mismatches: if trained on EPA but evaluated on ETU (different delay profile), NMSE drops to ~−10 dB — the model-reality gap is real.

docs.title: 2. Autoencoder for AWGN and non-linear channel
docs.text:
AWGN: Training 4-layer encoder/decoder over 100k random bits. After 10k epochs, learned constellation has 4 points, roughly QPSK. BER vs. SNR matches QPSK theory within 0.2 dB — the network discovers QPSK.

Non-linear channel: Same setup but with clip at amplitude 1.0. The learned constellation is not QPSK — points are stretched and offset to compensate. BER improves ~5 dB over classical 16-QAM (which was optimized for linear AWGN).

docs.title: 3. RL scheduler
docs.text:
Approach: Implement Q-learning with state = (channel quality vector, queue lengths), action = which UE to serve, reward = throughput with fairness bonus.

Result after 1M TTI: - Cell throughput: RL ~27 Mbps vs. PF ~26 Mbps (+4%) - Jain fairness: RL 0.82 vs. PF 0.85 (slightly less fair) - Convergence time: ~100k TTI to reach stable policy

RL wins slightly over PF in throughput, at the cost of fairness. Not a huge win — PF is already near-optimal for simple scenarios. RL wins more when multiple objectives (delay + throughput) must be balanced.

docs.title: 4. Federated learning
docs.text:
Setup: 10 UEs, each with different channel model (EPA, ETU, EVA, etc.).

Results: - Centralized: -15 dB NMSE (but requires all raw data). - FedAvg: -14.2 dB NMSE (0.8 dB worse, but privacy-preserved). - Local-only per-device: -11 dB NMSE (fails on other channels — no generalization).

FL preserves 95% of centralized accuracy while keeping data on devices. Communication rounds: 50 rounds × 0.5 MB per round per device = 25 MB total — vs. 10 GB raw data.

docs.title: 5. Beam prediction with LSTM
docs.text:
Setup: Mobile trajectory through cell, 32-beam codebook, 3 previous beams + GPS position as input.

Results: - Exhaustive search: 100% accuracy, 32 measurements. - Hierarchical (classical): 92% accuracy, 15 measurements. - LSTM (ML): 94% accuracy, 6 measurements.

Measurement reduction: 5×. Latency: 6 ms (beam alignment time) vs. 32 ms exhaustive — enables high-mobility tracking.

docs.title: 6. GAN for channel modeling
docs.text:
Setup: Train GAN on 3GPP EPA channel realizations. Generate 10,000 new channels.

Comparison: - PDP shape: matches (RMS error ~2 dB across delays). - RMS delay spread distribution: matches well. - Doppler spectrum: matches. - Key test: train a channel estimator on GAN-generated data, test on real channels — accuracy within 0.5 dB of training on real channels directly.

Result: GAN can substitute for expensive channel measurements in training data generation.

docs.title: 7. Deep unfolding for sparse recovery
docs.text:
Setup: ISTA algorithm unrolled into 3-layer network. Train on 5000 channel samples (sparse in delay-Doppler).

Results: - ISTA (plain): NMSE −12 dB at 20 dB SNR. - OMP (classical sparse): NMSE −14 dB. - Unfolded ISTA: NMSE −16 dB.

Unfolded network learns better thresholding/regularization than classical ISTA — 4 dB better than ISTA, 2 dB better than OMP.

docs.title: 8. Modulation classification (RadioML)
docs.text:
Setup: CNN on raw IQ, trained on 100k samples across 10 modulations (BPSK, QPSK, 8-PSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM, GFSK, CPFSK, PAM4, QAM16, QAM64), SNR range −20 to 20 dB.

Results: - High SNR (>10 dB): >95% accuracy. - Medium SNR (0–10 dB): 70–95%. - Low SNR (<0 dB): 30–60% (fails on hard cases).

ML matches expert-designed classifiers at high SNR; at low SNR, deep learning has more headroom (learned features are more robust than hand-crafted statistics).

docs.title: 9. DeepMIMO experiment
docs.text:
Setup: Scenario O1 (outdoor urban), 64-antenna BS, downlink 100 MHz. Train CNN for CSI compression: input = 64×64 channel matrix, output = 32-bit compressed, then reconstruct.

Results: - Compressed sensing (classical): NMSE −15 dB at 1/8 compression ratio. - Autoencoder (ML): NMSE −18 dB at same ratio.

3 dB improvement over classical compressed sensing — the learned codebook captures structure that the sparsity prior misses.

docs.title: 10. Explainability of channel estimation CNN
docs.text:
Visualization: First-layer filters of the trained CNN resemble classical DFT basis functions. Deeper layers show more complex, learned patterns.

SHAP analysis: The network's predictions are most sensitive to pilot symbols near the target (as expected), but also to pilots at other frequencies — reflecting the frequency-domain correlation the network learned.

No "shortcuts" (e.g., memorizing specific noise patterns) — the network has learned a generalizable channel estimator.

docs.title: 11. Federated differential privacy
docs.text:
Setup: Extend FL experiment with Gaussian noise addition (σ controls ε).

Results:

ε Privacy NMSE (dB) Utility loss ∞ (no DP) None −14.2 0 10 Weak −14.1 0.1 dB 1 Moderate −13.8 0.4 dB 0.1 Strong −11.2 3 dB

Trade-off: strong privacy (small ε) requires more noise, degrades accuracy. For most practical applications, ε = 1–10 gives acceptable privacy with minimal accuracy loss.

docs.title: 12. Real SDR
docs.text:
Setup: USRP X310 + GNU Radio + Python ML, urban outdoor.

Collect: 30 min of pilot signals at 3.5 GHz with known transmitted pilots → ~100,000 training samples.

Train: Small CNN (30k parameters), int8-quantized for deployment.

Deploy: ML receiver vs. classical LS + MMSE in real-time.

Results: - LS: NMSE −7 dB. - ML (trained on 3GPP simulation): NMSE −10 dB (fails to close the gap — model-reality). - ML (fine-tuned on 100 real samples): NMSE −13 dB.

Key lesson: the model-reality gap is real, but transfer learning with a small amount of real data closes most of it. Domain adaptation is essential for real deployment.

docs.title: Solutions to Wired Technology Trends
docs.text: Back to Wired Trends

docs.title: 1. PON comparison
docs.text:
Standard Total DL Split 1:32 → per user 20× headroom for 4K (25 Mbps)? GPON 2.5 Gbps 78 Mbps 78/25 = 3.1× ✅ XG-PON 10 Gbps 312 Mbps 12.5× ✅ XGS-PON 10 Gbps (symmetric) 312 Mbps 12.5× ✅ NG-PON2 40 Gbps 1.25 Gbps 50× ✅

All support 4K with 20× headroom for GPON's 78 Mbps case (78/25 ≈ 3.1× — meets 20× only if you consider multi-stream). For strict 20× (500 Mbps), need XG-PON or higher.

docs.title: 2. DWDM capacity growth
docs.text:
Initial: 96 fibers × 64 wavelengths × 200 Gbps = 1.23 Pbps total cable capacity.

Upgrade to 400 Gbps per wavelength: 96 × 64 × 400 = 2.46 Pbps.

One 5G call (100 Mbps) uses \(10^8 / 2.46\times10^{15} \approx 4 \times 10^{-8}\) (0.000004%) of the cable.

docs.title: 3. xDSL reach
docs.text:
Plot data: rate vs. distance is roughly \(R \propto d^{-k}\) with \(k \approx 1.5\).

Rate Distance 100 Mbps 500 m 50 Mbps 1 km 25 Mbps 1.5 km

2 km average loop: max 25 Mbps (VDSL2). Not sufficient for 4K video or heavy data. Need FTTC (fiber to the cabinet, then G.fast over short copper) or FTTH.

docs.title: 4. Fiber vs. FWA economics
docs.text:
Fiber cost: 10 km trench × $60K/km = $600K; 300 ONTs × $200 = \(60K; **\)660K** → $2,200/home.

FWA cost: 1 BS × $100K + 300 CPE × $300 + \(100K backhaul = **\)290K** → $967/home.

FWA wins at 15 km² density (~20 homes/km²).

Fiber becomes cheaper when: $1.1M / N homes < $967 → N > 1,140 homes. At 15 km², that's ~76 homes/km².

Crossover: ~70–80 homes/km² for this cost structure. Above that, fiber; below, FWA.

docs.title: 5. CPRI bandwidth
docs.text:
LTE 20 MHz, 4×4 MIMO, 3 sectors: - Sample rate: 30.72 Msps. - Bits/sample: 15 (I) + 15 (Q) = 30 bits. - Per antenna stream: 30.72 × 30 = 921.6 Mbps. - Per sector: 4 antennas × 921.6 = 3.69 Gbps. - 3 sectors: 11.06 Gbps CPRI.

vs. user peak 150 Mbps per sector: CPRI is 3.69 Gbps per sector = 24.6× the user data.

docs.title: 6. eCPRI reduction
docs.text:
5G NR 100 MHz, 64-antenna massive MIMO: - Sample rate: 122.88 Msps. - Per antenna: 122.88 × 30 = 3.69 Gbps. - 64 antennas: 236 Gbps CPRI. - eCPRI split II-D (10× reduction): ~24 Gbps.

Deployable with 100G Ethernet? Yes — 24 Gbps fits easily in 100G.

With split II (4×): ~59 Gbps → still fits in 100G.

With eCPRI + split options: 25G Ethernet viable for most 5G C-RAN deployments.

docs.title: 7. Backhaul sizing
docs.text:
Peak per site: 30 Gbps. Average at 60%: 18 Gbps. With 2× headroom: 36 Gbps.

Fiber options: - 40G (4×10G) — marginal for peak. - 100G — comfortable. - 4×100G — overkill but future-proof.

Microwave: - 4 × E-band (10 Gbps each) = 40 Gbps — viable but weather-sensitive. - 4 × microwave (2 Gbps each) = 8 Gbps — insufficient.

Fiber is clearly preferred for capacity; microwave as backup or where fiber unavailable.

docs.title: 8. Timing — fiber delay
docs.text:
200 km fiber: delay = 200 × 5 μs = 1 ms one-way.

Round-trip delay (PTP): 2 ms.

Without PTP (only local oscillator at 10 ppm): drift after 1 hour = 10 ppm × 3600 s = 36 ms — way off.

With PTP: < 1 μs — matches TDD requirement of ±1.5 μs.

Conclusion: PTP over fiber (with hardware timestamping at every switch) is essential for TDD synchronization.

docs.title: 9. GNSS loss and PTP backup
docs.text:
Scenario: Site loses GNSS for 2 hours.

With rubidium (10⁻¹¹ stability): drift after 2 hours = 10⁻¹¹ × 7200 s = 72 ns — well within ±1.5 μs TDD requirement. Acceptable.

With quartz (10⁻⁷ stability): drift = 10⁻⁷ × 7200 = 720 μs — way over. Not acceptable for TDD.

Real-world: operators use rubidium at critical sites, quartz at less critical ones, always backed by PTP from a neighbor.

docs.title: 10. Mobile vs. fixed cost
docs.text:
User: 20 GB/month mobile. - Mobile cost: $5/GB × 20 GB = $100/month. - Fiber cost: $0.005/GB × 20 GB = $0.10/month.

Offload savings: if 70% of traffic is offloaded to WiFi, mobile traffic drops from 20 GB to 6 GB — saving $70/month for the operator.

Industry data: 60–80% of smartphone data in urban areas is on WiFi. This saves operators billions per year — and is why WiFi offload is a strategic priority.

docs.title: 11. Carrier Ethernet for bank branches
docs.text:
5 branches, private network: need private point-to-multipoint connectivity with security.

Best fit: E-LAN (multipoint Ethernet) — all 5 branches in one broadcast domain, any-to-any connectivity, MEF-standardized QoS.

Alternatives: - E-Line — need one point-to-point link per pair → 10 links. Overkill. - E-Tree — for broadcast (cable TV); not suitable for banking.

E-LAN with MEF 6.2 EPL gives dedicated bandwidth, QoS, and SLA — matches a bank's reliability requirement.

docs.title: 12. SDN service deployment
docs.text:
Goal: deploy a new VPN service in a day (vs. a month).

Required components: - SDN controller (e.g., Cisco Crosswork, Juniper Paragon) for path computation, service provisioning. - NFV infrastructure (OpenStack/Kubernetes) hosting virtual routers and firewalls. - VNFs (vRouter, vFirewall, vCPE) as cloud-native containers. - MANO (e.g., ONAP, OSM) for orchestration. - OSS/BSS integration for service order and billing.

Workflow: 1. Customer orders VPN via web portal (BSS). 2. OSS translates order → service intent → MANO → SDN controller. 3. SDN controller computes optimal path (Segment Routing), provisions the underlay. 4. NFV orchestrator spins up VNFs (routers, firewalls) at customer sites. 5. Configuration pushed via NETCONF/YANG. 6. Service active in minutes to hours, not a month.

Traditional process: weeks of manual config across multiple network teams, each touching their portion. SDN/NFV collapses this to a single automated workflow.
